en: Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 1:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the quest for long life.
Salutations to the three-eyed Lord, the master of the three worlds, who has assumed a triple form through the differentiation of the three qualities and is the source of the three Vedas. (1)
Salutations to Sarasvatī, by whose grace, through meritorious deeds,
the world is perceived as reflected upon the mirror of the intellect, as if before the eyes of its presiding witness.
[Salutations] to Brahmā, Dakṣa, the twin Aśvins, the Lord of the Gods, Bharadvāja, and Punarvasu.
Homage again and again to Hutāśaveśa, Caraka, and the others.
Homage to the Lord of Serpents, who removes the defects of mind, speech, and body through the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya and the revised works of Caraka.
The *Āyurvedadīpikā*, a commentary following the meaning of the *Caraka* as taught by the preceptor Naradatta, is composed by Cakrapāṇidatta.
O learned assembly, whose ears are overflowing from hearing the nectar of the words of the true guru, I am not able to satisfy you with mere rainwater; even the ocean is never satiated.
If, however, even a single drop of the essence of this commentary is found anywhere at all, let it be placed in the ear for a moment.

For here, in the medical treatises (Āyurvedatantra) composed by Brahmā and others for the purpose of pacifying the diseases that obstruct dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, there is no proper comprehension of the meaning for men of the present day—whose lifespan and intellect are diminished—due to their extreme prolixity; and because of that lack of comprehension...

Thinking that if the purposes ordained therein were not carried out, there would likewise be an affliction of diseases, the most compassionate Honorable Agniveśa began to compose this treatise on Āyurveda, which is primarily concerned with the treatment of the body, neither too concise nor too extensive, for the sake of easy comprehension even by those of limited lifespan and intelligence. (7)

And regarding that which is to be explained— consisting of the sections on verses (*śloka-nidāna*), the celestial palaces (*vimāna*), the body (*śārīra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), therapeutics (*cikitsita*), and the accomplishment of rituals (*kalpa-siddhi*)—

it should be understood as being demonstrated by the statement beginning with "are declared" (*uktāḥ*), which expresses the primary subject matter of the entire treatise. Now, as for what was stated— that the declaration of the purpose is for the sake of engaging with the treatise— that is not tenable, because [the engagement] does not occur through the mere declaration of the purpose alone.

The determination that [the scripture] possesses a purpose is made because we observe a lack of purpose even when a purpose is stated in certain treatises, such as those that teach the liberation from a deceptive saṃsāra. Now, if you think: "This is a statement of the purpose by a trustworthy person (āpta), therefore its truthfulness is established here"—well then, sir, how is this so?

If it is argued that the authoritative person (āpta) is one who states the purpose, because the treatise (śāstra) spoken by him is true to reality—alas, as long as there is no ascertainment of the treatise’s possession of a purpose, there is no engagement with the treatise; as long as there is no engagement with the treatise, there is no ascertainment of the treatise’s truthfulness; and as long as there is no ascertainment of the treatise’s truthfulness, there is no [ascertainment of its] purpose.
The authoritativeness of the speaker is determined; yet, if his authoritativeness is not determined, how can there be a determination that what he has stated possesses a purpose?

Thus, a circular argument results. Now, if you think: "Let there be no determination that it possesses a purpose; rather, it is precisely the doubt regarding its having a purpose in the form of a result that will be the motivator for action," [we reply: even in the case of agriculture and the like, activity arises from doubt regarding the result, for it is not the case that...

For farmers, there exists the certainty of obtaining fruit, even though the occurrence of drought and other such obstacles is possible. Now, one might argue: "Even if the purpose is not explicitly stated, since we observe both purposeful and purposeless treatises, the very nature of being a treatise (*śāstratva*) itself shall serve as an indicator of doubt regarding its possessing a purpose;
therefore, enough with stating the purpose. (11)

It is not so; for a general doubt regarding the purpose does not incite one who desires a specific purpose to act in the same way as a doubt whose object is that specific intended purpose. And a doubt concerning a specific intended object does not arise without the recollection of that specific object. Therefore, for those who have not yet ascertained the authority of Agniveśa, [the following applies]:

The statement of the specific purpose is intended to give rise to a doubt regarding the specific nature [of the work], such as whether or not this treatise is a means for achieving the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātusāmyasādhana).

However, for those who have ascertained the authority of the supreme sage Agniveśa from the very beginning, their engagement occurs simply through the ascertainment that it possesses the purpose stated by him; thus, the statement of the purpose is appropriate. 12.

However, in the case of a statement that expresses a purpose (*prayojana*), when that purpose can be understood with very little effort, engagement [with the statement] is justified by the mere doubt regarding the general nature of the purpose; this is not the case, however, for a treatise (*śāstra*) which can only be understood through the hardship of many years.
Thus, the objection that—even for the engagement with a statement expressing a purpose—one must state a further purpose, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), is thereby refuted.

In the aphorism beginning with "atha" (*atha* etc.), the word *atha* [indicates] the lack of determination regarding lifespan, intelligence, and capacity as found in the systems composed by Brahmā and others.

Thus, although the salutation to the chosen deity and the attainment of the teacher’s permission for the purpose of composing the treatise are employed as immediate antecedents [to the composition], they nonetheless constitute an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) by their very nature at the beginning of the treatise, just as the sight of a water-jar filled with water by those setting out on a journey constitutes an auspicious omen. (15) Since authors and listeners whose obstacles have been dispelled by the practice of auspicious rites at the beginning of a work attain their desired goal without hindrance, the inclusion of an auspicious rite is appropriate. (16)

Regarding the auspiciousness of the word *atha*, there is a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "In ancient times, these two—the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—emerged from the throat of Brahmā after piercing it; therefore, both are auspicious. Furthermore, this word *atha* is observed at the beginning of other treatises as being used for the purpose of auspiciousness.

Just as in examples such as "Now, the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*), "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma" (*athāto dharmaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*), and "Verily" (*vai*), [the following applies]. Furthermore, the salutation to one's chosen deity at the beginning of a work is obtained through the practice of the learned; it has indeed been performed by Agniveśa, the most refined of scholars. Otherwise, by transgressing the conduct of the learned, he would not possess the status of a learned person himself, and there would likewise be the fear of obstacles to the exposition.
Furthermore, even though the salutation is not included within the body of the text, it is not inserted therein because it removes transgression (*pratyavāya*).

Just as this composition of the tantra follows immediately after obtaining the teacher’s permission, so too is it clearly evident in the passage beginning with "Then, [he who is] intent on friendliness, [attains] merit," and so forth.
Moreover, by demonstrating the teacher’s authorization for the composition of the work, the worthiness of the text for adoption is shown.
Furthermore, as for the explanation that the word *atha* has the purpose of indicating immediate succession to the student's question—that does not satisfy me;

for a treatise is not composed by first positioning students before oneself. Rather, the composition of a treatise is appropriate when it is intended to be established in the minds of listeners, and those who ask questions do not necessarily have [the subject matter] already established in their minds. (24)

The word "ataḥ" (hence/therefore) indicates the limit preceding the current section; thus, it should be construed as: "that which we shall teach hereafter is the Dīrghañjīvitīya," or else, in the sense of a reason (*hetu*): "because [this treatise] possesses a connection similar to that stated for the Ayurvedic systems composed by Brahmā and others, for this reason we shall explain the Dīrghañjīvitīya. // 25

Regarding the term *Dīrghajīvitīya*: the suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), according to the rule "the suffix *cha* is used after the names of chapters and sections (*adhyāya-anuvāka*), with elision [of the final vowel]," because the word *dīrghajīvita* occurs in this [chapter].

Alternatively, if the intention is that the work—whether in the form of a chapter or a treatise (*tantra*)—was composed concerning the subject of long life (*dīrghajīvita*), then the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule "after a word formed with the sense of 'concerning' (*adhikṛtya kṛte granthe'), [the suffixes *aṇ*, *cha*, etc., are used]," specifically by the sub-rule beginning with *śiśukrandayamasabha*.
In this manner, other cases of a similar kind should also be understood.

And here, although there are other words [that could have been used], the designation was made by the word *dīrghajīvita* (Long-Life) alone, because the word *dīrghajīvita* itself has been introduced at the beginning of the teaching and because it is particularly praiseworthy. By the etymological derivation—either "the word *dīrghajīvita* exists in this" or "it is composed concerning the word *dīrghajīvita*"—the term *Dīrghajīvitīya* is to be applied to both the treatise (*tantra*) and the chapter (*adhyāya*).

By the phrase "therefore we shall explain the Dīrghañjīvitīya," a promise to explain the *tantra* as a whole is established; furthermore, by repeating the word "Dīrghañjīvitīya" and joining it with the word "chapter" (*adhyāya*), it secures a promise to explain that specific chapter. It is observed that a word may be joined [to multiple terms] through repetition, as for example in the *Apāmārgataṇḍulīya*: "in heaviness of the head, in headache, in catarrh," and so forth, where the word "of the head" (*śirasaḥ*) is joined with "heaviness" (*gaurave*) by way of repetition.

And by this [statement] "in the *śūla*," that which was said—that for one who has not made a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) regarding the treatise (*tantra*), the proposition regarding the chapter (*adhyāya*) would be deficient in its body—is thereby refuted.

Or rather, let there be only the proposition regarding the chapter; by that very [proposition], the proposition regarding the treatise is also obtained by implication, for [the treatise] is not [separate from] the chapter.

Since [the treatise] is not distinct from its constituent parts, by explaining a part, there is indeed an explanation of the whole treatise as well, just as by grasping a finger, Devadatta is also grasped.
However, a promise to explain other constituent parts is not obtained; rather, he will do so for each chapter individually.

Regarding the word *adhyāya*: it is derived from the root *iṅ* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *iṅaśca*. Thus, that which is studied (*adhīyate*) is an *adhyāya*.

Nor does this etymological derivation lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to other instances such as the four sections (*prakaraṇa*), the four books (*sthāna*), and so forth; for this designation "chapter" (*adhyāya*) is both etymologically and conventionally established (*yogarūḍhi*) specifically for a chapter.

The term [“chapter”] applies specifically to a particular collection of sections characterized by titles such as “On Longevity” (*dīrghajīvitīya*) and so forth, like the word *paṅkaja* (“lotus”), and does not apply merely through its etymological derivation (*yoga*). For it will be stated: “This designation of the name ‘chapter’ is established with reference to this [collection]”; the meaning is that the designation of the name is a *yogarūḍha* (etymologically derived and conventional) designation.
Alternatively, it refers to the two meanings of the instrumental and locative cases.
The form *adhyāya* is established by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) according to the sūtra "adhyāyanyāyodyāvasaṃhārāś ca.

(41) It is called an *adhyāya* because a particular meaning is studied (*adhīyate*) therein or by means of it. (42) The prohibition against over-extension (*atiprasakti*) follows the previously stated logic. (43)

"We shall explain" (*vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*): this is derived from the root *khyā-* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, with the suffix *lṛṭ*. (44) For if the root *cakṣiṅ-* were used, since the connection between the agent and the fruit of the action is unavoidable even for one who does not wish to explain, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would result according to the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*. (45) The prefix *vi-* signifies "distinction" (*viśeṣa*); and distinctions include both detailed exposition (*vyāsa*) and concise summary (*samāsa*), etc. (46)

Regarding the prefix *āṅ*, we do not understand the intention of those who believe that its application occurs only in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*), while [others] maintain it applies in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) or an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). For if *āṅ* were used in the sense of a limit or an inclusive limit, it would have to be joined with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in "of the lords of the earth as far as the ocean" (*āsamudrakṣitīśānām*) or "it rained as far as Pāṭaliputra" (*āpāṭalīputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ*); and here too, it would be the same. Furthermore, in the absence of connection with a verbal action, *āṅ* would lack the status of a preverb (*upasarga*), because of the rule that "preverbs [occur] in connection with a verbal action. Consequently, due to the intervention of the non-preverb *āṅ*, the preverb *vi-* could not be employed [in the formation of the word *vyāghra*].
50. An *upasarga* (prefix) is that which occurs either immediately before or separated from a verbal root by another word of the same class (*sajātīya*).

51. If both *vi* and *āṅ* were not considered *upasargas*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a cumbersome complexity (*gaurava*) involving the postulation of numerous nominal bases (*prātipadika*) suitable for connection with them; therefore, it is logical that *āṅ* possesses connection with the action (*kriyāyogitva*) alone. 52. Furthermore, in the statement "Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on Longevity," there is a sequence of eight words.
Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya.
[Āyurvedadīpikā:
Now, one might ask: how will Agniveśa explain Āyurveda, which is to be explained through the knowledge of every single detail of all categories of things?

For, first of all, it is not possible to have direct perceptual knowledge of every specific quality of medicinal substances and the like, because the specific qualities of all things are not within the scope of direct perception; furthermore, the determination of all things through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is indeed difficult,

since even a single substance such as honey may, by its very nature, enliven or kill, and when combined with heat and ghee, may be beneficial or harmful for one of a phlegmatic constitution (*kapha-prakṛti*).

For one of a windy (vāta) constitution, that which is wholesome in a marshy region is unwholesome in a desert; what is to be consumed in the cold season is unfit for the summer; what is beneficial when not increased in quantity becomes harmful when increased; a small dose produces only slight benefit while an excessive dose causes affliction; when it has turned into raw matter (āmata), it causes extreme confusion because it contradicts the therapeutic measures for abdominal disease;
furthermore, its consumption combined with *kākamācī* or with ripe *nikuca* leads to death, or else to the destruction of strength, complexion, vigor, and splendor.

Such things as "it exists" and so forth are each appropriate, and he performs them hundreds of times; therefore, when even the nature of a single substance like honey is difficult to comprehend in this manner, what need is there to mention the knowledge of every particularity of all objects?
And since one who explains while not knowing himself would have speech that is not to be accepted, we shall explain what has been understood from a teacher who is a reliable authority (āpta).
Demonstrating this and wishing to dispel such doubt, he shows that his own work is in the form of a restatement of what was spoken by the Guru, saying:
"Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

Here, the word *iti* refers back to the matter about to be stated; the word *ha* is used for emphasis, as in the phrase, "Indeed (*na ha vai*), for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant," where *na ha* means "not at all" (*na eva*).

Regarding this, it is said: by the use of the word *sma* in the phrase "atra smāha," the suffix *laṭ* (present tense) is applied according to the rule *laṭ sme* (Pāṇini 3.2.117), which prescribes the present tense for the meaning of the past (*liṅ*) when *sma* is used; thus, it does not refer to the immediate past (*anadyatana*) or the remote past (*parokṣa*), because Ātreya’s instruction was not remote from Agniveśa's perspective.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate how the *liṅ* (past tense) occurs merely for the past in general.
"Bhaga" is venerated knowledge; one who possesses that [is called Bhagavān]. As has been stated: [He knows] the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going. (5)

He who knows both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) is to be called "Bhagavān. Alternatively, the word *bhaga* denotes the totality of sovereignty, majesty, and so forth, as it has been said: "Of complete sovereignty, valor, fame, beauty, knowledge, and dispassion—these six are designated by the term *bhaga*. (6–7)
"Atreya is the offspring of Atri; by this, his possession of a pure lineage is demonstrated.
(8) Here, others describe that the Sūtra is fourfold: the Guru-sūtra, the Śiṣya-sūtra, the Pratisaṃskartṛ-sūtra, and the Ekīya-sūtra.
(9) Among these, the Guru-sūtra is, for example, "This should not be viewed by one who possesses intelligence, O Agniveśa," and so forth. The Pratisaṃskartṛ-sūtra...

For example, the *śiṣyasūtra* such as "Thus the Blessed One Ātreya spoke," the *ekīyasūtra* such as "O Blessed One, these five hundred [periods of] corruption are not yet filled," and the *kumāraśiras-sūtra* such as "The head of the youth develops first; thus Bharadvāja was Kumāraśiras. // 10 //
Therefore, the first introductory sūtra concerning the promise of exposition belongs to the teacher alone, because the disciple Agniveśa lacks the authority to provide the exposition.
And the second sūtra belongs to the redactor.

By the word *iti*, which denotes manner, the phrase "we shall explain the Dīrghañjīvitīya" is referred to; thus, the expression "he said" (*āha sma*) refers specifically to the past, non-remote, non-present time of the redactor.
Because the instruction of Ātreya himself is beyond direct perception,

by this same principle, the prescription of the *liṅ* (optative) mood is also justified in such passages as "the Blessed One Ātreya said to him. Furthermore, in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, the commentator has established the justification for the *liṅ* mood on the grounds that the phrase "as the Blessed One Dhanvantari said" is a formula used by the reviser (*pratisaṃskartṛ*).
To this we reply: as for what was said—that because the disciple Agniveśa lacks the authority to provide an exposition, this is the aphorism (sūtra) of the teacher—that is not so;
for teacherhood does not exist by birth alone. For that very same Ātreya is a disciple in relation to his own teacher, yet he is a teacher in relation to Agniveśa and the others.
Likewise, at the time of composing the treatise, Agniveśa too is a teacher with respect to those disciples whom he has established within his own intellect.

There is no fault whatsoever. As for the argument that the rule prescribing the *liṅ* affix for the past non-present non-witnessed (*bhūtānadyatana-parokṣa*) is established by means of a second rule acting as a restorative supplement (*pratisaṃskartṛ-sūtra*), it must be examined whether this second rule has attained syntactic unity with the preceding statement or not; for if it has attained syntactic unity—

In that case, [the phrase] "we shall explain in the Suśruta as Dhanvantari said" must be construed; thus, the word "said" (uvāca), having entered into a single syntactical unit with the action "we shall explain," cannot have a different agent. Furthermore, how could there be an injunction using the optative suffix (liṅ) [if they were separate]? On the other hand, if they do not form a single unit, then there is no semantic coherence, just as in the case of "cow, horse, man, elephant. // 16 //

Furthermore, in the case of Jatūkarṇa and others, there is not even a scent of the word "reviser" (pratisaṃskartṛ). Therefore, how could there be an injunctive optative (liṅvidhi) in such passages as: "Then the disciple Jatūkarṇa, whose throat was filled with various scriptures, approached with palms joined and said..."?
By this same logic, even in the Caraka-saṃhitā, if one adopts the position that Agniveśa was the reviser, there is no injunctive optative; therefore, in the Caraka, [Agniveśa is the author].

In the *Suśruta*, Suśruta himself is the author of the aphorisms (*sūtras*). In some instances, in order to praise or censure a certain point, he presents an ancient account (*purākalpa*) in the form of a narrative; he writes some aphorisms as a restatement of what was said by his teacher, and others as a restatement of the opinion of "some" (*ekīya-mata*). However, this [compiler] completes the work as if he were the original author of that initial text. (18)

The prescription of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) should be described as applicable to the mere past non-recent (*bhūtānadyatana*) time even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), as it is ordained in the Vedic hymns (*chandas*);

otherwise, the word "uvāca" (he said) would not occur in works such as the *Jatūkarṇa*. Likewise, in the *Harivaṃśa*, in the *Dhanyopākhyāna*, the expressions "mām uvāca" (he said to me) and "aham uvāca" (I said) would not exist.
As it is said: "That water-dweller, the tortoise, himself spoke to me like a human. (19)
"What is the wonder in me, O Sage? And how am I blessed, O Lord?"—having been addressed thus by the Self-born One (Svayambhū), I approached the Vedas. And he spoke to those four [Vedas] as follows:
"As for the phrase *yad api* and *iti ha smāha*, here the word *iti* refers back to the preceding sūtra; it does not refer only to the sūtras such as the *Dīrghajīvitīya*."

Alternatively, when it is established that the subject matter [of this work] was taught by the Guru, then by stating the title of the subject matter hereafter, it is demonstrated that the entire treatise is a restatement of what was spoken by the Guru; thus, the means for generating faith in the listener is set forth.
(22) However, it is possible to cultivate [faith] in the manner previously explained; therefore, that alone is logical. (23)

Regarding the phrase "we shall explain for Agniveśa," the use of the plural number is justified because the plural form of the pronoun *asmad* (we) is grammatically correct even when referring to a single person; indeed, speakers correctly say, "We shall do it.

[24] However, in the expression "the venerable Ātreya," the singular number is employed, since the honor due to the teacher Ātreya is already demonstrated by the very title "the venerable one" (*bhagavān*). [25]

Seeking long life, Bharadvāja, having recognized Indra— the lord of the immortals and the refuge of those engaged in fierce austerities— approached him. For Prajāpati [received] the Āyurveda exactly as it was proclaimed by Brahmā.
He first grasped it in its entirety, and then again from the two Aśvins.
The blessed Śakra received it solely from the two Aśvins;
Bharadvāja, who had been proclaimed by the ṛṣis, then approached Śakra.
When diseases arise as obstacles to the penance, fasting, study, celibacy, vows, and lifespan of embodied beings,
then the great sages, placing compassion for all creatures foremost, [acted].
Gathered together on the auspicious slopes of the Himalayas were those of meritorious deeds:
Aṅgiras, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu, Ātreya, Gautama, Sāṃkhya, Pulastya, Nārada, and Asita.
Agastya, Vāmadeva, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āśvalāyana, Pārikṣi, Bhikṣu, Ātreya, Bharadvāja, Kapiñjala,
Viśvāmitra, Āśmarathya, Bhārgava, Cyavana, and Abhijit.
Gārgya, Śāṇḍilya, Kauṇḍinya, Vārkṣi, Devala, and Gālava; Sāṃkṛtya, Baijavāpin, Kuśika, Bādarāyaṇa, Baḍiśa, Śaralomā, and both Kāpya and Kātyāyana.
Kāṅkāyana, Kaikaśeya, Dhaumya, Mārīca, Kāśyapa, Śarkarākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Lokākṣa, Paiṅgi,
Śaunaka, Śākuneya, Maitreya, and Maimatāyani.
The Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and other great sages were there—
repositories of the knowledge of Brahman, of self-restraint, and of discipline,
blazing with the splendor of their asceticism like sacrificial fires.
Seated there in comfort, they engaged in this meritorious discourse.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"Who were those great sages? To which he replied, beginning with "Aṅgiras," etc. 1.

The mention of many sages at the beginning of this work is for the purpose of destroying sins, as well as to demonstrate that Āyurveda is worthy of being practiced because it was followed by such great persons.
Among these, some were Yāyāvaras, some were Śālīnas, and some were not born from a womb; all such types should be understood to be included here.
Furthermore, the word "mendicant" (bhikṣu) is a qualification of Ātreya, for he will later say: "That is not so; [it was] the mendicant Ātreya."

"Vaikhānasas" is a designation applied on account of their specific practice of ritual action (karman). (5) The Vālakhilyas, however, are certain sages of very small stature. (6) They are called "treasures" (nidhi) because they are inexhaustible by virtue of being an imperishable locus. (7)

Self-control is the state of being subdued. [8] "This" refers to that which will be explained further on. [9] Health is the supreme root of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. *Caraka Saṃhitā* 1.1.15.
"Diseases are the destroyers of their well-being and their very lives;
this great obstacle has appeared for humanity.
Having said, "What might be the means for their pacification?", they entered into meditative absorption.
Then, with the eye of meditation, they beheld Śakra as their refuge; he,
the lord of the immortals, will explain the means to tranquility exactly as it is.

Dharma is that which upholds; it is inherent in the self and is to be inferred from the observation of its effects. Artha refers to gold and other such objects that are desired. Kāma is the longing for things such as the embrace of a woman. Mokṣa is liberation from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Ārogya is the absence of disease, which is the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Mūla is the primary cause.

"Supreme" means preeminent; therefore, health is the preeminent [factor] among the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*). It has been stated that for one seized by disease, there is an incapacity for any human goal whatsoever. (4) "Their snatchers away" means the snatchers away of health. And this very thing is the snatching away of health by diseases, namely, the non-attainment of one's purpose;
it is not that a disease which has already arisen subsequently snatches away health, because existence and non-existence consist in their mutual absence. (5)

Regarding the phrase "and of a superior life" (*śreyaso jīvitasya ca*): a "superior life" refers to that which is beneficial and pleasant, as will be explained in the *Daśamahāmūlīya*; the construction here is "those who take away such a life. Since an "inferior life" is not to be adopted because it is unbeneficial and a cause of suffering, its taking away is not mentioned in this context.

In this context, the destruction of a happy life is obtained precisely through the destruction of dharma and so forth; therefore, we see that by the word *śreyas* (the good), which denotes prosperity in a general sense, dharma and the other goals are expressed, while by the word *jīvita* (life), mere life itself is meant, since life is desirable to all living beings in its very essence, regardless of qualifications—as it was said: "And he proclaimed the Brahman."
This is the aspiration for oneself: "May I be long-lived.

(7) However, when one seized by extreme suffering desires to give up life, because that suffering—which is so intensely desired to be abandoned—cannot otherwise be relinquished, one wishes to abandon even dear life; this should be understood as not being an obstacle to the accomplishment of dharma and other goals. (9)
"This" refers to the manifestation of disease.
"Of them" refers to those diseases.
"Refuge" means a protector.
He is called Śakra because he is capable (śakta).

Dhyāna is a specific kind of meditative concentration (samādhi); because it is the means for attaining that [concentration], it is like an eye, and thus it is called the "dhyāna-eye. By means of that, the Lord of the Immortals will declare the method of tranquility exactly as it is; such is the construction of the phrase: "they beheld with the dhyāna-eye."
"Who would go to the abode of the Thousand-Eyed One to inquire after the Lord of Śacī?
"I shall be appointed for this purpose"—this was the first word spoken;
therefore, Bharadvāja was commissioned by the sages.

Having gone to the abode of Śakra, he beheld the slayer of Bala, who was seated in the midst of the hosts of celestial sages and blazing like fire. Approaching him, he greeted the lord of the gods with blessings of victory.
The wise one spoke with humility the excellent words of the sages:
"For diseases have arisen that strike fear into all living beings;
therefore, O Lord of the Immortals, tell me truly the means for their pacification."
Having perceived the vast intelligence of that supreme ṛṣi, the Lord Śatakratu proclaimed the Āyurveda to him in few words. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.1.23)

Now, regarding how Bharadvāja approached Indra among these [sages], he says "Who" (*ka*) and so forth. By the term "Lord of Śacī" (*śacīpati*), Bharadvāja demonstrates: "Even though he is absorbed in the enjoyment of Śacī, I am capable of attending upon him. (1) *Arthe* means "for the sake of a purpose" (*prayojana*). (2–3)
"I shall employ" means "I shall apply myself.
Here, the word *atra* refers specifically to the subject matter at hand; the particle *iti* has the sense of "because," as in:
"He has come because there is plenty of food"—that is, he has come because [it is] abundant.
The term *niyojita* belongs to the *cur-ādi* group and takes the suffix *ṇic*, but not in the sense of "impelling.
By this context, it is shown that there was no impelling of Bharadvāja because he possessed a particular longing for the traditional knowledge of Āyurveda.
The word *provāca* means "he spoke correctly," and the prefix *pra-* does not signify elaboration (*prapañca*), as it has already been stated [elsewhere] that [the teaching was given] "in few words."

He explains why he spoke with few words by saying, "having perceived his vast intelligence" (*matiṃ buddhvā vipulām*). The sense is that because he had gained access to Bharadvāja, who possessed vast intelligence, he spoke with few words. Furthermore, "intelligence" (*mati*) is figuratively called "vast" (*vipula*) due to its wide range of objects.
And this intelligence here consists of a desire to hear, hearing, grasping, retaining, reflecting, discerning, and a firm conviction in the truth.
These [topics] are to be understood as extensive.
Here, Indra, having perceived Bharadvāja’s intention beforehand with his divine vision, taught the Ayurveda;
therefore, Bharadvāja’s questions to Indra and so forth are not shown here, or else they were omitted for fear of excessive length of the text, even though they did actually occur.
This has not been written here.

[11] The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) perceived that which is the knowledge of causes, signs, and medicines—the ultimate refuge for the healthy and the sick, consisting of three threads, eternal, and meritorious. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.1.24)
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, he states [the following] regarding that Āyurveda which was taught in brief terms, beginning with "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth:

1. "Knowledge of cause, symptom, and medicine" (*hetuliṅgauṣadhajñāna*): this means that by means of this, the cause and the other factors are known; the sense is that whatever is expressible by Āyurveda is subsumed within these categories of cause and so forth. 2. [The commentary continues: ...the meaning is that everything denoted by Āyurveda is included within the [categories of] cause and the rest.

By the mention of "cause" (*hetu*), the inclusion of both proximate and remote causes of disease is intended; and by the mention of "sign" (*liṅga*), the entire range of signs of both disease and health is expressed. Therefore, even disease and health are denoted by the word "sign" (*liṅga*), because by means of those two [disease and health] as well, that sign is indeed made known (*liṅgyate*). For it will be said: "Fever alone is the characteristic mark of all those whose origins are based on irregular undertakings. (3)

"Fevers are said to be of one type based on irregular onset, primary causes, and so forth," and so on; furthermore, by the mention of "medicines" (*auṣadha*), all wholesome regimens (*pathya*) are included.
(4) Here, the "body" (*śarīra*) is subsumed under both the cause (*hetu*) and the symptom (*liṅga*).

(5) It is called "the ultimate refuge for the healthy and the afflicted" (*svasthāturaparāyaṇa*) because it is the supreme (*parama-utkṛṣṭa*) goal (*ayana*) or path (*mārga*) for both the healthy and the sick. (6)

Is this Āyurveda—consisting of the knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines—different from the Āyurveda of Brahmā-Buddha, or is it non-different? To this he says: "The Three Sūtras," and so forth.

(7) Even Indra taught that which the Grandfather (Brahmā) had understood as the *trisūtra*. (8) That in which or by which the three [topics], beginning with the cause (*hetu*), are strung together (*sūtryante*) is the *tantra-sūtra*. (9)

In this context, it is called a *sūtra* because it indicates (*sūcana*) and strings together (*sūtraṇa*) a series of meanings. By this, he demonstrates that the tradition is unimpaired, showing that just as Brahmā understood the "three threads" (*trisūtra*), so too did Indra proclaim the knowledge of causes, symptoms, and remedies. The word "understood" (*bubudhe*) means that he did not [merely] create it.
Therefore, it is said that "eternal" (śāśvatam) means "constant" (nityam).
That constancy is to be explained at the end of the Sūtrasthāna.
He, the one of great intelligence, [taught] Ayurveda, which has infinite limits and consists of three divisions.
With his mind fixed on that, the sage soon understood everything exactly as it was.
By means of that, Bharadvāja obtained an immeasurable lifespan filled with happiness;
and he proclaimed this to the sages, leaving nothing unsaid.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
Now, he explains how Bharadvāja acquired the Ayurveda that was thus introduced, beginning with the words "He, who is infinite," and so forth.

He whose ends and limits (*anta-pārau*) do not exist is "infinite and boundless" (*anantapāraḥ*). Here, by the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word *pāra* implies the beginning (*ādi*) as well.

It is said that the word *pāra* (the further shore) applies to both banks of a river by virtue of intention; alternatively, since liberation (*mokṣa*) is infinite, that Āyurveda which has this infinite liberation as its supreme fruit (*phala*) is called *anantapāra*.
For it will be stated later: "But that medical treatment which is final is free from ulterior motive. (Verse 3)

In this context, "naiṣṭhikī" refers to that which is the cause for the means of attaining liberation. (4) That which has three parts consisting of the causes and so forth is "triskandha"; a "skandha" is a gross constituent part or a division. (5) One whose mind is fixed upon the acquisition of Ayurveda in that very [context] is "tanmanāḥ. (6)

He is a *muni* because he possesses the excellence of knowledge resulting from reflection. By this it is meant that, since he is of great intelligence and his mind is fixed upon that [knowledge], he—having taken as his objective support the three aggregates beginning with the cause (*hetu*) within the Ayurveda, which is itself infinite in its limits—has correctly realized it in no long time;
"in no long time" means shortly.

And here, by showing that Bharadvāja understood those three sections (skandhas) in the same manner as Brahmā understood the Three Threads (trisūtra) and as Indra proclaimed the knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines, the uncorrupted tradition of Āyurveda is demonstrated; therefore, there is no redundancy between the *Trisūtra* and the *Triskandha*. 10.
"By him" means by [the sage] who received the *Āyurveda* from Indra.
"Immeasurable" (*amita*) means immeasurable as it were, because of its extreme length.

Furthermore, the word "life" (*āyus*) should be understood here as referring to the knowledge of *rasāyana* (rejuvenation therapy), which is the cause of life, since through the subsequent application of *rasāyana*, [longevity is attained].

It should be understood that this Bharadvāja will attain immeasurable life; it must be realized whether he practiced the elixir (rasāyana) before teaching Āyurveda to the sages, or whether Bharadvāja obtained immeasurable life at that very moment through the power of the merit (dharma) born from studying Āyurveda for the sake of benefiting all living beings. // 13
Regarding the phrase "that [which was] heard": when the reading is *tam*, it refers to that Āyurveda.
(14) "Without leaving anything remaining" means in its entirety.
(15) Having studied the Āyurveda, he gave it to the sages immediately thereafter. (16)

And the sages, desiring long life, received from Bharadvāja that [treatise] for the welfare of living beings, which is the Veda that increases longevity. Those great sages perceived it correctly with the eye of knowledge.
Having understood generality, particularity, qualities, substances, action, and inherence—
as taught in that treatise— and having followed its prescribed method,
they attained supreme bliss and a life that is free from decay.
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

"Desiring long life" refers to [the desire] of living beings and of oneself. (1) "The eye of knowledge" (*jñānacakṣus*) means either for the sake of knowledge or the eye whose nature is knowledge; by that "eye of knowledge. (2)
Having acquired that Ayurveda, what did they perceive? To this he says: "And the universal," and so forth.

(Verse 3) Furthermore, the definition of these six categories (*padārtha*), which possess manifold forms, will occur later; therefore, this must be explained in that very place. (Verse 4) "That" refers to the universal and the rest. (Verse 5)
"The procedure taught in the Tantras" refers to the form consisting of the avoidance of what is unwholesome and the adoption of what is wholesome.
"Bliss" (śarma) means happiness.
"Supreme" (parama) means not assailed by suffering.
"Without haste" means without speed.
Then Punarvasu, devoted to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and out of compassion for all living beings, bestowed the meritorious Āyurveda upon his six disciples. *Caraka Saṃhitā* 1.1.30.
Agniveśa, Bhela, Jatūkarṇa, Parāśara,
Hārīta, and Kṣārapāṇi received those words of the Sage.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.1.31)
With the words beginning with "atha," [the author] shows that Ātreya, the disciple of Bharadvāja who also has the alternative name Punarvasu, was the teacher of Agniveśa and the others.

Here, some consider Bharadvāja and Ātreya to be one and the same; however, that is not so, because Ātreya is never mentioned by the name Bharadvāja in any part of this treatise. Furthermore, in the Hārīta [Saṃhitā], Bharadvāja is mentioned as the teacher of Ātreya and others, [where it says]: "From Śakra, I..."
"Having studied [this] from me," and so forth; furthermore, seven great sages—from Ātreya down to Hārīta—know this three-sūtra treatise with its three purposes. (2–4)

Regarding what was stated by Vāgbhaṭa—"Brahmā, having remembered the Veda of longevity, taught it to Prajāpati; he [taught] the two Aśvins; they [taught] the Thousand-eyed One (Indra); he [taught] the sages such as the sons of Atri"—this fact of Ātreya being a disciple of Indra must be justified by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the passage on the origin of Ayurveda in the *Rasāyana-pāda*, because of the connection with his status as a disciple of Indra that will be mentioned there.
In that regard, it must be stated that Āyurveda was subsequently taught by Indra to the great sages.
[7] He was devoted to friendliness (*maitrī*), with friendliness as his primary quality; and friendliness is the perception of all living beings as being like oneself.
[8] Therein, there was a distinction in the Sage’s own realization, not merely another instruction.

Agniveśa was the first author of a treatise (tantra), from whom [the tradition] originated. Then Bhela and others, being highly intelligent, composed their own respective treatises and recited them to Ātreya and the assembly of sages.
Having heard the sutra that sets forth the meanings [of the teachings] of the seers of meritorious deeds,
they rejoiced and approved it, saying, "It has been correctly set forth.
All of them, who desire the welfare of all beings, then offered praise to those [seers].
"Excellent! Compassion toward all beings! they cried out together in a loud voice.
Standing in the heavens, the celestial rishis along with the gods heard that meritorious sound;
having heard it from the supreme rishis, they rejoiced exceedingly.
"Ah, excellent!"— this cry resounded throughout the three worlds,
uttered by beings out of joy, moist and deep in the sky.
An auspicious wind blew, and all the directions were illuminated with light.
And divine showers of flowers fell, accompanied by water.
Then, the deities of knowledge entered Agniveśa and the others:
Intellect, Accomplishment, Memory, Wisdom, Fortitude, Fame, Forbearance, and so forth.
And those tantras, approved by the supreme seers for the welfare of the multitudes of beings, obtained their foundation on earth. [The topics are:
the beneficial and the harmful, pleasure and pain, and the benefit and harm regarding that lifespan.
That in which these [topics] are taught is called Āyurveda.
The union of the body, the senses, the mind (sattva), and the self (ātman) is life;
it is called "āyus" by its synonyms: that which sustains, that which flows constantly, and that which follows as a continuous bond.
Among all forms of longevity, the Veda is considered the most meritorious by those who know the Vedas;
that which shall be declared here is beneficial for humanity in both worlds. (Carakasamhitā 1.1.43)
Sūtrasthāna, 12:
Now we shall expound the chapter on the determination of the strength of the wind (vātakalākalīya).
Thus said the venerable Ātreya. Caraka Saṃhitā 1.12.1–2.

In the preceding chapter of the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, diseases were described by way of their essential nature, pathways, external causes, and remedies; however, the Vāta and other factors which serve as their causes were not mentioned because they require extensive explanation. Therefore, they are now set forth in a separate section titled "The Exposition on the Qualities of Vāta" (*Vātakalākalīya*).

Even there, because of its predominance, *vāyu* alone is mentioned first. *Kalā* means a quality (*guṇa*), as it is said [in the scriptures] that [the self] consists of sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśakala*). *Akalā* is a defect (*doṣa*) opposed to the qualities; therefore, "pertaining to the *kalā-kalā* of *vāta*" means pertaining to the qualities and defects of *vāta*. Alternatively, *kalā* is a subtle portion; the *kalā* of that is *kalā-kalā*, and the *kalā* of even that...
The meaning is "a subtle portion.
[1] Having sat down together, desiring to know one another's opinions regarding the knowledge of the various parts of Vāta, the great seers asked each other:
"What are the qualities of Vāyu? What is its provocation? What are its pacifiers? And how is it that it remains unaggregated?"

Without reaching a state of instability, they provoke or pacify the factors that cause provocation or pacification; and what are the actions of these [humors], whether provoked or unprovoked, as they move within bodies or outside of bodies, traversing both corporeal and incorporeal realms? // Caraka Saṃhitā 1.12.3 [Āyurvedadīpikā]

Here, the description of the qualities of wind and the other [humors] is presented in the form of the words of many sages for the purpose of demonstrating the consensus of numerous seers and to establish that [the doctrine] is consistent with the principles of the medical system (tantra) and traditional authority (aitihya).
"Non-composite" (*asaṃghāta*) means being devoid of a composite of parts, like bile or phlegm. "Unstable" (*anavasthita*) means having a mobile nature.
"It is to be understood that [the term] *anāsādya* refers to both mobility and the lack of dense articulation.
Regarding this, Kuśa Sāṃkṛtyāyana said: "Rough, light, cold, harsh, dry, and clear—these are the six qualities of Vāta. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.12.4) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

Terms such as *rūkṣa* (dry) and so forth have the abstract state (*bhāva*) as their primary meaning; therefore, they should be understood as qualities (*guṇa*), namely dryness (*rūkṣatva*) and the like.

Harshness (*dāruṇatva*) is mobility (*calatva*); because it is precisely due to mobility that what was described in the *Dīrghajīvitīya* chapter is here called "mobility. Alternatively, harshness causes hardness (*kāṭhinya*) through its drying nature (*śoṣaṇatva*). Having heard these words, Bharadvāja Kumāraśiras said: "It is exactly so, just as the Blessed One has said; these indeed are the qualities of wind (*vāta*)."

However, when actions possessing such qualities, such substances, and such powers are practiced, the *vāyu* becomes provoked; for the practice of things with similar qualities is the cause of the increase of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*).
[Āyurvedadīpikā]

*Kumāraśiras* is a qualification of Bharadvāja, intended to exclude the Bharadvāja who was the teacher of Ātreya. "By those of such power" refers to factors that cause dryness (*raukṣya*) and so forth through their influence, such as running, staying awake, and the like; the mention of "power" is because actions themselves are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*).
"By those being practiced" means by those employed repeatedly. [1]

Having heard those words, Kāṅkāyana, the physician of the Vāhlīkas, said: "It is exactly as the Blessed One has said; these very factors are provokers of vāta, and those contrary to them are the pacifiers of vāta, for the reversal of what provokes the bodily constituents is indeed the cause of their pacification."
Having heard those words, Baḍiśa Dhāmārgava said: "It is exactly as the Blessed One has stated; these indeed are the factors that pacify the provocation of *vāta*.

For we shall now explain how, by failing to reach a state of equilibrium or stability, the factors that provoke or pacify actually cause provocation or pacification. Indeed, the factors that provoke *vāta* are those which produce dryness, lightness, coldness, harshness, roughness, clarity, and porosity."
In such bodies, the wind (vāyu), having entered its seat and becoming nourished, falls into a state of provocation; however, when substances that pacify vāta— namely those that are unctuous,
heavy, hot, smooth, soft, slimy, and dense— are applied, the wind, no longer adhering as it moves through such bodies, attains tranquility.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,
"of bodies" (*śarīrāṇām*) refers to the parts of the body;
"causing cavities" (*śuṣirakarāṇi*) means causing apertures (*randhrakarāṇi*).
"Support" (*āśraya*) refers to a locus of similar qualities. "Being nourished" means being accumulated. "Gentle" is the opposite of harsh; "solid" is the opposite of porous.

"Not adhering" means not remaining stationary; that is to say, its constituent parts are wasting away. By this it is meant that although there is no such connection between the wind and the causes of wind or the pacifiers of wind, nevertheless, through those [substances] connected to the body, a connection with the wind moving within the body is established, and consequently—
"Because of its association with qualities similar to those of wind, its increase is logical; and because of its association with contrary qualities, its decrease is likewise established.

Having heard these truthful words of Baḍiśa, which were approved by the hosts of sages, the royal seer Vidyā, who was learned in the nature of wind, said: "All this is exactly as the Blessed One has stated, without exception.
However, as for the functions of wind—whether agitated or unagitated, moving through bodies or not—as it courses within bodies..."

Or rather, those [qualities] exist outside of bodies; having established their constituent parts through perception, inference, and authoritative instruction, and having paid homage to Vāyu, we shall explain them according to our ability. Vāyu is the sustainer of the body's systems and mechanisms; its essence consists of prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, and apāna;
it is the initiator of all high and low movements, the controller and director of the mind, and the stimulator of all the sense organs.
When not provoked, it carries all the sense organs; it arranges the constituents of the entire body, provides cohesion, and initiates the movement of the body;
it is the source of speech and the basis for touch and sound; it is the origin of joy and enthusiasm; it is the wind of the fire [of digestion];

it dries out the humors (doṣas) and expels external impurities; it breaks through the gross and subtle channels; it fashions the forms of the embryo; and it serves as the supporting condition for the continuity of life.
When indeed provoked within the body, it afflicts the body with various kinds of disorders for the destruction of strength, complexion, happiness, and lifespan;

it agitates the mind, impairs all the sense organs, destroys fetuses, causes deformities, or causes them to be retained for too long; it generates fear, grief, delusion, dejection, and excessive lamentation, and it obstructs the vital breaths.

Indeed, for him who exists as the primordial nature (prakṛti) moving through the world, these activities occur: namely, the supporting of the earth, the kindling of fire, the ordaining of the continuous motion of the sun, moon, constellations, and the hosts of planets,
the creation of clouds, the discharge of waters, the setting in motion of rivers, the production of flowers and fruits, and the sprouting of plants.

The differentiation of the seasons, the division of the elements, the manifestation of the forms of the elements and the mind, the sowing of seeds, the growth of crops, non-moistening and drying, and non-disturbing transformation—
these are the functions of this [wind] as it moves through the worlds when it is provoked. For example, the shattering of mountain peaks.

The churning of mountains, the agitation of the oceans, the overflowing of lakes, the reversing of rivers, the shaking of the earth, the swelling of clouds, and the discharge of frost, thunder, dust, sand, fish, frogs, serpents,
alkaline matter, blood, stones, and thunderbolts; the subversion of the six seasons, the failure of crops, the affliction of living beings, and the bringing about of non-existence for all things.

He is indeed the Lord, the source and the imperishable one; the creator of the existence and non-existence of beings; the ordainer of happiness and misery; Death; Yama; the Restrainer; Prajāpati; Aditi; Viśvakarman; the Universal Form; the All-pervading; the ordainer of all systems; the subtle atom of all states of being; the All-powerful; Viṣṇu. He is the emission of the clouds, the sun, fire, and wind, which bring about the end of the four ages.
"The Blessed One is indeed Vāyu, who has traversed the worlds.
[Commentary on the Āyurvedadīpikā:
By stating "of him who moves within bodies and outside of bodies," the true nature of Vāyu is described; thus, there is no tautology between "moving within bodies" and "or outside of bodies."
By saying "the parts" (*avayavān*) here, he shows that it is impossible to state [the definition] in its entirety because of its great complexity. 2. Having established and explained; 3.

Among the actions of the vital air (*vāta*), speech and so forth are perceptible, the impelling of the mind and so forth are inferable, and the formation of the embryo’s shape and so forth are known through scripture (*āgama*). 4.

The "tantra" is the body, as it has been stated: "when the various mechanical contrivances (*yantra*) have fallen apart, [it is for those] desiring to enter the ultimate darkness. That very thing is the "yantra," or alternatively, the "yantra of the tantra" refers to the joints. (5) [The term] "consisting of breath and so forth" means having the nature of breath and so forth. (6) [The phrase] "specification of activity" means various [activities], both high and low; or else, it means auspicious and inauspicious. (7)

He is the controller (*niyantā*) of the mind as it engages with an undesired object, and the guide (*praṇetā*) of the mind toward a desired goal. (8) He is the inciter (*udyojaka*) or the impeller (*preraka*); alternatively, there is the reading *udyogakāraka*, which has the same meaning.

(9) He is the "bearer" (*abhivoḍhā*), as if carrying [everything] along, by virtue of being the grasper of the objects of all the sense organs; and this is because, through his tactile organ (*sparśanendriya*) composed of air, he pervades all the sense organs, according to the principle established in the preceding chapter.
It should be understood [as follows]:

it is the "arranger" (*vyūhakara*), meaning it is the "constructor" (*saṃghātakara*) and the "organizer" (*racanākara*). Its nature (*prakṛti*) is its causality; moreover, air's status as a cause of sound is eternal because of its constant entry into space (*ākāśa*). For it has been stated, after describing the elements beginning with space: "The first [element] possesses one quality, while there is an increase of qualities in each subsequent one."
Furthermore, it has been stated [in the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*]: "Having mentioned earth and the other elements, [it is said] that the subsequent is pervaded by the preceding.
(13) The ear is the root of air because it functions as the specific structural arrangement of the ear-canal; "root" (*mūla*) here means the primary cause.
(14) Enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is the exertion of the mind toward its tasks. (15)
The *yoni* is the cause of manifestation.
[It is] the dryer of the humors (*doṣa*) and the dryer of the bodily fluids (*kleda*).
It is the divider and the maker at the time of the body's production. 16–18.

The word *bhūta* expresses its own essential nature. // 19 The analysis of the compound is "for the purpose of harming" (*upaghātāya*). // 20 And [the word] "embryos" (*garbhān*) is connected with both "brings about a deformity" (*vikṛtim āpādayati*) and "retains for too long" (*atikālaṃ dhārayati*). // 21
The establishment of the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies by way of a continuous, uninterrupted succession is "the establishment of the movement of the continuum" (saṃtānagatividhāna).
[Verse 22] "Of streams" (srotasām) means of rivers.
[Verse 23] "Distinction" (pravibhāga) is the characteristic of being differentiated. [Verse 24]

"Of the elements" means of earth and the others. "Elements" refers to the causal substances such as stones and so forth. "Measure" means dimension; "configuration" means shape. Their "manifestation" is their appearance; that is to say, it is the cause therein.

The "processing" of the seed—such as rice—is its capacity to produce a sprout. (26) "Non-moistening" is the state of not being moistened prior to the time of cooking. And "drying" occurs through cooking in the case of barley and other grains while they are still moist; non-moistening and drying apply specifically to crops. (27)
By means of non-transformative modification (*avaikārika-vikāra*), it declares that *prakṛti* is the cause throughout the entire world. 28.
A mountain is *śikharin*. 29. A tree is *anokaha*. 30.

*Udvartanam* is turning upward. (31) *Pratisaraṇam* is going against [the current]. (32) *Visarjanam* is emission; and that is connected separately with *nīhāra* and the others: *nīhāra* is a mass of cold [mist]; *nirhrāda* is thundering without clouds; *aśani* is fire that pierces like a thunderbolt. (33)

Having established the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) according to the opinions of the sages, the formal determination of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is set forth for the sake of the student's comprehension.

1. The determination of food by way of taste is the "determination of the taste-food" (*rasāhāra-viniścaya*). Alternatively, this is the "determination of taste" (*rasa-viniścaya*), such as [the section beginning] "Furthermore, beyond this, regarding the post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*)," and so forth, which constitutes the determination of food.

2. Bhadrakāpya declared that there is only one taste. That which the experts describe as one of the five objects of the senses, specifically the quality pertaining to the domain of the tongue—that, moreover, is not different from water.
"There are two tastes," said the brahmin Śākunteya, "namely, those that are excising and those that are pacifying.
"There are three tastes," said Pūrṇākṣa Maudgalya, "namely, the excising, the pacifying, and the common to both.
"There are four tastes," said Hiraṇyākṣa Kauśika, "namely, the pleasant and beneficial, the pleasant and harmful, the unpleasant and beneficial, and the unpleasant and harmful."
"There are five tastes," said Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja: "those of earth, water, fire, wind, and space.

"There are eight tastes," says Baḍiśa—namely, sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent, alkaline, and unmanifest. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.8) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
"Only one," and so forth.
(1) In the phrase "of the sense-faculties and objects," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

(2) "Any one" (*anyatama*) means "one"; for this word *anya* is used in the singular, as in "one went by the south" and "another by the north," meaning "one. Furthermore, the suffix *-tamap* is pleonastic (*svārthika*). (3)
"Relating to the domain of the tongue" means that which is perceivable by the tongue.

for by such statements as "the subtle element of taste" and "the subtle element of smell," they assert that substance is not distinct from its qualities. "To be cut" means that which causes emaciation.

"Alleviating" (*upaśamanīya*) means nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*). "Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means that, due to the commonality of both the fiery (*āgneya*) and the lunar (*saumya*) qualities, it performs both lightening (*laṅghana*) and nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*), or, because of their mutual contradiction, it performs neither. "Palatable" (*svādu*) means desired; "wholesome" (*hita*) means not causing harm in the long term.

That which is resorted to is the substratum (*āśraya*), namely the substance (*dravya*); the qualities (*guṇa*) are those such as unctuousness and heaviness; the action (*karman*) is the increasing or diminishing of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*); and the specific taste (*saṃsvāda*) is the internal differentiation of tastes. This means that there are distinctions among these various particulars.

Among these, due to the distinction of the substance—that is, through the difference in the substratum—there occurs a distinction even in the taste that is supported by it. For the substratum is the cause, and from a difference in the cause, a difference in the effect necessarily follows. (14) Furthermore, the distinctions of qualities such as heaviness and so forth, as well as the distinctions of actions, are produced solely by the tastes. (15)

Therefore, the intention of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is that there must necessarily be a difference in the cause due to the difference in the effect. "Nevertheless, even Sarasvatī herself would not be able to describe its distinctions.

Water is the source of these six tastes. There are two types of action: cutting and pacifying; through their combination, there arises the state of being common to both.

Palatability and non-palatability constitute *bhakti* (devotion/attachment); the beneficial and the harmful are the two powers (*prabhāva*); and the modifications of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) are the substrata (*āśraya*), which are subject to the influence of nature (*prakṛti*), transformation (*vikṛti*), processing (*vicāra*), place (*deśa*), and time (*kāla*).

Within those substrata, known as substances (*dravya*), reside qualities (*guṇa*) such as heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, and dry. Alkali (*kṣāra*) is so called because of its caustic action (*kṣaraṇāt*);

The manifestation of the *karana* (the means) results in the non-manifestation of the tastes (*rasa*) within their primary source (*prakṛti*), whether that source is a secondary taste (*anurasa*) or a substance (*dravya*) endowed with secondary tastes. Nor is it logical for them to be anything other than that [mixture], because they consist predominantly of a confluence of various essences (*rasa*). Furthermore, there is no end to the enumeration of these qualities and primary constituents (*prakṛti*) produced from their manifestation; therefore, the wise do not prescribe the medical action of mixed tastes.
Bearing this very reason in mind, we shall explain the distinct characteristics of the six tastes when they are unmixed with one another.

Therefore, the meaning is that for whomever one has a desire, that [object] is sweet-tasting or otherwise (not sweet-tasting) for him; thus, these two properties depend upon the person and do not constitute distinct effects of the taste itself.

What kind of modifications of the elements—earth and so forth—are these substrates? He says: "dependent on nature, transformation, processing, place, and time. "Investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) means the combination with another substance; thus, lightness depends on such investigation, as in the case of honey and clarified butter when combined, which act as poison.

Likewise, poison combined with an antidote produces an effect distinct from its own natural action. Location is of two kinds: the ground and the patient. Regarding the ground, the *śvetakāpotī* plant growing upon an anthill is a destroyer of poison; similarly, medicinal herbs on the Himalayas possess great efficacy. Regarding the location of the body, for example, the flesh of the shoulder, chest, head, and feet is heavier than the flesh of the thigh, and so forth. [This is determined by] the influence of time.

However, just as it was stated regarding radish— that the young variety removes [specific] defects while the mature variety aggravates the three *doṣas*— so too should one take flowers and fruits according to the season,
and so forth. And here,

those things mentioned in this single section that were not explicitly detailed should be included within the categories of "natural properties" (*svabhāva*) and the rest, by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*).

As it has been said: "In this [treatment], the movement (cara), the bodily constituents (śarīrāvayava), the natural state (svabhāva), the elements (dhātu), the actions (kriyā), the gender (liṅga), the measure (pramāṇa), the refinement (saṃskāra), and the dosage (mātrā) are examined.

Among these, the movement, the bodily constituents, and the elements are grasped by means of location (deśa); the dosage enters into the consideration of the [specific] deliberation; and the remainder [is included] within the natural state (svabhāva).

Likewise, that which will be described in the *Rasavimāna* (The Specific Determination of Tastes) regarding the "bases of specific foods" (*āhāraviśeṣāyatana*) should be included here as appropriate, even though it has not yet entered [into this discussion].

(15) By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "unctuous, dry, etc.," he shows that although sharpness (*tīkṣṇa*), mildness (*mṛdu*), and so forth are not mentioned, they are not tastes (*rasa*), but rather distinct qualities (*guṇa*) of substances (*dravya*).

(16) Because of its trickling (*kṣaraṇa*)—that is, its association with the action of moving downward—an alkaline substance (*kṣāra*) is a substance (*dravya*) and not a taste; for it is impossible for a taste, which is itself devoid of action, to possess an action. This is the meaning. (17)

For worldly people say of alkaline substance mixed with water, "We are draining the alkali" (kṣāraṃ srāvayāmaḥ) because it flows downward; and the scripture also states: "Having repeatedly cut [the vessel], the alkali, by virtue of its flowing nature (kṣaratvāt), causes it to flow down from the receptacle.

He states another reason: "produced by an instrument" (*karaṇābhinirvṛttam*). This means produced or made by an instrument such as a strainer for ashes and so forth; the sense is that flavor (*rasa*) is not produced in this manner.
He refutes the position that flavor is unmanifest (*avyaktarasa*) with the words "the state of being unmanifest" (*avyaktībhāva*), etc. (Verse 25).

By the suffix *cvī* in the sense of "becoming what one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāve*), the meaning is that flavors such as sweet and so forth, which are already manifest, simply become unmanifest in some substratum; there is no such thing as an "unmanifest flavor" distinct from the sweet and others.
"Of the tastes" refers to the six, beginning with sweet.
"In the primary cause," and so forth;

And "unmanifestness" (*avyaktatva*) is the perception of the mere generality of taste (*rasasāmānyamātra*), devoid of specific qualities such as sweet (*madhura*) and so forth; and this occurs in water, since it was stated by Suśruta in the description of the qualities of water that "the manifestation of taste (*vyaktarasa*) is a defect of taste," and here too he will say, "and [water] has unmanifest taste. No taste, such as sweet and so forth, is manifested [as a distinct entity].

(31) Just as when an object whose specific color is not discerned from a distance, there is a cognition of the general property of form, but no cognition of specific qualities such as whiteness.

Likewise, there is the state of being unmanifest within a secondary flavor (*anurasa*). Because it follows the primary flavor (*rasa*) while remaining unmanifest, it is called a secondary flavor (*anurasa*).
For example, in the sweet bamboo seed (*veṇuyava*), astringency is the secondary flavor.
As it has been said: "The sweet [flavor] that is dry and has an astringent secondary flavor destroys phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*). (32–33)

"Endowed with secondary tastes" (*anurasasamanvita*) means being joined with all secondary tastes, as in the statement regarding poison: "it is indeed hot and its taste is indescribable," and so forth. Alternatively, there is the reading *aṇurasasamanvite*; by that, in a sugar-drink containing a single minute amount of *marica* (black pepper), the pungency would be unmanifest.
He refutes the position that [tastes] are innumerable with the words beginning "innumerable" (*apari*), and so on.

Regarding the phrase "of these," it is not logical that the flavors (*rasa*) are innumerable; rather, it is because the entities such as their substrata (*āśraya*) are innumerable—that is, because the distinctions among their substrata, qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and tastes (*saṃsvāda*) are innumerable. Here he states the reason: "For even each one... (verse 38).

Even each individual [flavor] such as sweet (*madhura*) and so forth relies upon the distinctions of these substrata, qualities, actions, and tastes; yet, there is no difference in the dependent flavor, such as the sweet, apart from those distinctions of the substrata and so forth.

He thinks as follows: although the substrata of sweetness—such as rice, mung beans, ghee, milk, and so forth—are diverse, nevertheless, there is only one single taste pervaded by the universal (jāti) of "sweetness" therein, just as there is only one white color in cranes, milk, cotton, and the like. Likewise, even though qualities such as heaviness, sliminess, and unctuousness differ, or actions such as the nourishing of taste and so forth, the production of vitality, and the imparting of color differ; [the universal remains one].

Even though there is a difference [among individual instances], there is no otherness in the sweet taste (*madhurarasatva*), because it is the single sweet taste that becomes endowed with various qualities and performs various functions; what contradiction is there? (41) Likewise, even when there is a distinction between sub-varieties of the sweet, there is no transgression of the universal (*jāti*) of sweetness, just as there is no transgression of blackness despite the distinctions among sub-varieties of the color black. (42)

[Objection: "Let it not be so; although the tastes (*rasa*) are indeed innumerable due to their mutual combination, the specific variation in flavor (*āsvādaviśeṣa*) produced thereby also produces a specific effect. The word *saṃsṛṣṭam* (mixed) is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve ktaḥ*). however, those very qualities and natures of the sweet and others that have been individually specified become mixed together.

Or rather, the phrase "of the qualities and natures" means "of the sixfold nature of the qualities consisting of the sweet and so forth. (45) By the word "prakṛti" (nature), "karma" (action) is expressed; therefore, the meaning is "of the actions of the qualities. (46) It should be understood that even the specific internal tastes of sweet and other flavors are produced by their mutual combination. (47)

Among those, substances that abound in the qualities of heaviness, coarseness, hardness, dullness, stability, clarity, density, and grossness are *pārthiva* (earthly); they produce accumulation, cohesion, weight, and stability. Substances that abound in the qualities of heat, sharpness, subtlety, lightness, dryness, and clarity, as well as form (*rūpa*), are... [fiery].
