Those belonging to wind produce dryness, exhaustion, movement, clarity, and lightness; they abound in the qualities of softness, lightness, subtlety, smoothness, and sound.
Those consisting of space produce softness, porosity, and lightness.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,

it is considered whether the word "bahula" (abundant) is connected with each of the qualities beginning with "heavy" (*guru*), or with "odor" (*gandha*) alone; for it is precisely the earth that is abundant in the quality of odor, and for this very reason, even in the definition of other substances, the specific quality (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) is listed at the very end.
Regarding the phrase "abounding in the quality of taste" and so forth, the word "abounding" (*bahula*) should be applied there as well to taste and the other qualities.

(1) Although all effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) consist of the five elements, they are to be understood as "earthy" (*pārthiva*) and so on based on the predominance of earth and the other elements. (2) "Conglomeration" (*saṃghāta*) is solidity, stability, and being immovable. (3)
Bondage (*bandhana*) is mutual conjunction; exhilaration (*prahlāda*) is the gratification of the body and the senses.
The subtle (*sūkṣma*) follows along the subtle channels (*sūkṣmasrotas*).
Radiance (*prabhā*) is the luminosity that reveals color; as it has been said: "Shadow (*chāyā*) pervades color, while radiance (*prabhā*) is the illuminator of color," and so forth.
Vicāraṇa means *vicāra*, which signifies movement.
(7) *Sauṣirya* is the abundance of cavities.

(8) Here, the predominance of space (*ākāśa*) is to be understood as being due to the scarcity of other elements such as earth and so forth within the substance, and because of the extensive manifestation of space; that which possesses abundant cavities is of the nature of space (*nābhasa*), or rather, it is so by virtue of the predominance of the qualities of space.

[9] By this teaching, no substance whatsoever is found in the world that is not some kind of medicinal herb, depending upon its respective application and intended purpose. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.12 [Āyurvedadīpikā])

"By this" means by the instruction regarding specific substances and qualities; the meaning is that whatever substance, such as an earthy one, possesses certain qualities, that substance becomes a medicine when those qualities are to be produced in the body. Furthermore, he states "that particular method," etc., to show that such a substance—whether earthy or otherwise—is not a medicine in every respect nor for every disease.

"Method" (yukti) means the means; "purpose" (artha) means the objective; "with reference to" (abhipretya) means having taken into account. Thus, by some means and for some purpose, a particular substance becomes a medicine, but not in all cases.

Therefore, the statement that "there is no medicinal substance because antagonistic [substances] are always unwholesome" does not constitute a contradiction; for antagonistic substances depend upon combination, processing, place, time, and so forth, whereas in the absence of such antagonistic combinations and other factors,
even [antagonistic substances] may sometimes be wholesome.

Even those things that are always unwholesome by their very nature, such as poison, mild [poison], and so forth, may in certain cases become wholesome when combined with appropriate means, as in the instruction: "One should administer a drop of poison in the case of abdominal swelling," and so on.

As for the claim that grass, dust, and the like are not called medicines because they are not used [internally], that is incorrect; for even these possess the status of medicine by virtue of being employed as medicinal means, such as in sudation therapy (*sveda*).
Furthermore, substances do not become effective solely through the power of their qualities (*guṇa*); rather, substances act through the power of the substance itself (*dravya-prabhāva*).

Due to the influence of qualities (*guṇa*) and the influence of the qualities of substances (*dravyaguṇa*), having encountered this or that occasion (*adhikaraṇa*) at this or that time, and intending this or that method and this or that purpose, that which they do is action (*karman*); that by which they do it is potency (*vīrya*); where they do it is the occasion (*adhikaraṇa*); when they do it is the time (*kāla*); and how they do it is the manner (*yathā*).
The means (*upāya*) is that which accomplishes the result (*phala*). [Commentary on *Caraka Saṃhitā* 1.26.13]:

Since the status of substances such as those of the earth as being medicinal has been stated due to their association with qualities such as heaviness and roughness, the author says "but not merely" (*na tu kevalam*) and so forth, in order to dispel the doubt that a substance would be medicinal solely through the power of its qualities.
1. By the power of the substance (*dravya-prabhāva*), as for example, the purgative quality of *dantī*, or the power of gems to destroy poison and so forth.
2. By the power of the quality (*guṇa-prabhāva*), as for example, a bitter taste in the case of fever, or fire in the case of cold, and so forth.

3. By the power of both substance and quality (*dravya-guṇa-prabhāva*), as for example, "upon a black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇājina*); here too, both the blackness (the quality) and the antelope skin (the substance) are intended.

Or, just as in the case of gold [purified] by means of circular molds (*maṇḍala*), when milk has been boiled therein, only that gold which possesses the quality of the mold attains the state of being a bow;
thus he says "in each respective [instance]" and so forth to explain how they act.
"Resorting to this or that reasoning" means attaining this or that application.

Regarding the phrase "that which they perform," and so forth, the example is as follows: those substances which perform head-purgation (śirovirecana) constitute the action of head-purgation; the specific cause by which they perform head-purgation, such as heat and so on, is the potency (vīrya). Potency...

That potency belongs either to a substance or a quality; the locus where they perform head-purgation (śirovirecana) is the "head," for the substance intended for head-purgation is not effective in any other locus—this is the meaning. As for the phrase "when" (yadā), it refers to the spring season and so forth, as well as times when the head is afflicted by heaviness and similar conditions. By this, it is implied that head-purgation is not effective during the improper time of cold because of stiffness; rather, it should be administered only at its proper time, just as [in the following example].

In whatever manner—by means of fomentation, pressing, and so forth—they cause [the patient] to lie on his back with limbs extended upon a bed covered with a mattress, with the head slightly hanging down and the eyes covered; by such a procedure they perform that which is the *upāya* (means). That which they accomplish—the cessation of heaviness and pain in the head and so forth—is the *phala* (fruit). The *uddeśya* (intended object) is the action to be performed (*kārya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the intended fruit (*phala*) to be achieved (*sādhya*). Just as *dharma* is the *karma* (action) to be produced by a sacrifice (*yāga*), while heaven (*svarga*) and the like, produced by that sacrifice, are the *uddeśya* fruit; so too it is in the case of emetics and other such treatments.

Their classification, such as by karma, legal jurisdiction (*adhikaraṇa*), and so forth, is to be inferred. Furthermore, their division consists of sixty-three types based on substance, location, time, and potency; we shall explain that. [Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.14] (Āyurvedadīpikā)

Having now described substance (*dravya*), he states the classification of the modified tastes (*rasa*) themselves with the words "And their classification... and so forth. The term *prabhāva* (potency) is to be joined with substance, place, and time individually. Among these, by the potency of substance, for example: "sweet due to the predominance of the properties of the moon," and so forth. By the potency of place, for example: "grapes, pomegranates, and the like become sweet in the Himalayas, whereas elsewhere they are sour," and so forth.

Due to the influence of time (*kāla*), for example, a young mango is astringent, when young it is sour, and when ripe it is sweet; likewise, medicinal herbs are sweet in winter and sour during the rainy season, and so forth.
Other causes of taste, such as contact with fire and the like, should also be subsumed under either time or substance.
Sweetness enters into combination with sourness and the other [tastes], and sourness and the others likewise enter into combination individually with the remaining tastes;
these fifteen substances thus possess two tastes each.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.15)

He states the distinctions with the words "sweet" (*svādu*) and so forth. Therein, from the combination of the sweet with sour and the rest, there are five; by "with the remaining ones," he means with those other than the one already employed as the first. Thus, from the combination of the sour with salty and the rest, there are four; likewise, from the combination of the salty with pungent and the rest, three; from the pungent with bitter and astringent, two; and from the bitter [with astringent], one.
Thus, through the combination with the [other] astringent tastes, there are fifteen single [tastes] that possess two flavors.
For the sweet, sour, salty, and pungent tastes, there would likewise be separate combinations with the remaining [tastes]. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.16)
Twenty substances possessing the three tastes have been stated according to their respective numbers. [The *Āyurvedadīpikā* states regarding the three tastes: "He says 'separately' and so forth. 1.

When the sweet taste is combined individually with each of the other four tastes—sour and so forth—it is joined with the remaining tastes, such as salty and the rest. In that regard, there are four combinations for the sweet taste when joined with sour, due to its further union with the remaining salty and other tastes; likewise, there are three for the sweet taste joined with salty, due to its union with pungent and the others; likewise, two for the pungent joined with bitter and the others; and likewise, one for the bitter joined with astringent.

In this way, there is one [type] for the sweet taste when it is combined with itself; there are ten when it is combined with the others. Likewise, for the sour taste when it is combined with itself, there are three when it is combined with salt and so forth; similarly, for that which is combined with pungent, there are two from combination with the remaining two; likewise, for that which is combined with bitter, there is one from combination with astringent.
Thus, there are six for the sour taste. 3.
By this same logic, there are three varieties for salt (*lavaṇa*) and one for pungent (*kaṭu*); thus, combined, there are twenty triads of tastes (*trirasa*).
Furthermore, fifteen substances will be described by means of fourfold combinations:
sweet (*svādu*) and sour (*amla*) joined together with each of the [other] tastes beginning with salt (*lavaṇa*), occurring separately.
The sweet and salty tastes, when combined with the remaining [four] tastes individually, result in four combinations each;

likewise, the pungent and other tastes, when combined individually with the sweet and salty, result in four combinations each. Similarly, the sweet and bitter tastes, when combined with the remaining [four] tastes individually, also result in four combinations each.
The pungent (kaṭu) and others, when combined with the sour (amla) and salty (lavaṇa) respectively,
and joined individually with the remaining [tastes], as well as the sour and pungent joined with the remaining [tastes],
and the salty and hot (uṣṇa) joined with the astringent (kaṣāya) along with the bitter (tikta), are thus combined.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

Among the four tastes, the sweet (*svādu*) and the sour (*amla*), situated at the beginning, become six through their individual combination with salt (*lavaṇa*) and the others, and through their conjunction with the remaining [tastes] such as pungent (*kaṭu*) and so forth.

The sweet and salt combined, situated at the beginning, are joined with "the pungent and the others"—meaning they are joined separately with pungent (*kaṭu*) and bitter (*tikta*)—and with "the remaining," meaning with astringent (*kaṣāya*) and bitter (*tikta*). Therefore, the plural number used here should be understood as referring to the category (*jāti*).
Thus, there are three [types].
By the phrase "likewise sweet and pungent," one [type] consisting of the forms of sweet, pungent, bitter, and astringent is indicated.
In the passage beginning with "by pungent and so forth" as well, the plural number is used in reference to the genus (*jāti*). 4.
Sour and salty combined with pungent, along with the remaining two, make two; likewise, sour and salty combined with bitter, through combination with the remaining, make one.
(5) By the phrase "sour and pungent likewise," one [type] consisting of sour, pungent, bitter, and astringent is indicated. (6) And by the phrase "they are joined," etc., another one is formed. (7)
Thus, there are fifteen [preparations] with four flavors;
however, by the exclusion of one flavor from each, they say there are six with five flavors.
Furthermore, there would be six with a single flavor, and one with all six flavors.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"By relinquishment" means by abandonment.
And here, the coexistence (*samavāya*) of tastes as qualities within a single substance is expressed by the word "conjunction" (*yoga*).]

Thus, sixty-three substances have been specified according to the enumeration of tastes. However, there would be sixty-three [substances] only if the primary and secondary tastes were not taken into account; for tastes, by means of their degrees of intensity (*taratama*), indeed exceed that number.

[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,] he states that the combinations of tastes (*rasasaṃsarga*) are innumerable by another method, beginning with "there would be sixty-three," etc. 1. The secondary taste (*anurasa*) will be explained further on. 2.

And here, regarding the sixty-three-fold [taste], there is no conceptualization of primary tastes (rasa) and secondary tastes (anurasa) because such a distinction is absent in the case of the purely sweet and so forth; therefore, the conceptualization of primary and secondary tastes should be understood as pertaining to the fifty-seven combinations, as far as they occur. Alternatively, even in a single taste, a secondary taste certainly exists, though it remains unexpressed.
He also states their incalculability by another method, beginning with "the tastes, through the degrees of intensity (*taratama*)," and so forth.
The meaning is that the tastes become incalculable due to the distinctions of sweet, sweeter, sweetest, and so on.

Alternatively, this reason—beginning with "the tastes, through the degrees of intensity," and so forth—applies specifically to that incalculability which exists precisely because of the presence of primary tastes and secondary tastes (*rasānura-sa*).
There are fifty-seven combinations, but the formulations are sixty-three;
these have been devised by experts on tastes according to the suitability of the tastes therein.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.24) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

Thus, even though [the combinations] are innumerable, the teachers have devised exactly sixty-three types of conceptualization for the purpose of medical practice; this is stated in the verse beginning with "The combinations" (saṃyogāḥ).

In that context, "because of suitability" (yogyatvāt) means that within the application of medical treatment for the benefit of both the healthy and the sick, these are beneficial by virtue of being neither too concise nor too prolix.
In some cases, a single taste is to be conceived, and in other cases, tastes combined together.
Having carefully considered the humors, the medicines, and other factors, the physician desiring success— whether wise or otherwise—
formulates substances with two or more tastes, combinations of tastes, or even single tastes, according to the specific disease. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.25–26)
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, he states that very same application of treatment beginning with "in some cases" (*kvacid*);
here, by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of those factors not explicitly mentioned, such as place, time, strength, and so forth.

Demonstrating that this very conceptualization of combined and uncombined tastes arises either from the blending of substances with distinct tastes, or from the administration of a single substance with multiple tastes, or from the administration of a single substance with one taste, he says "substances," and so forth. Substances with two tastes (*dvirasādi*) are those established by nature as having two or three tastes; for example, a *mudga* bean has two tastes—bitter and sweet—and a substance with three tastes, such as the *bhavya* fruit, which is sweet, sour, and bitter, and is constipating, heavy, cold, and pacifies *pitta* and *kapha*. Substances with four tastes are sesame seeds (*tila*), as it is said: "It is unctuous, hot, sweet, and bitter."

According to such statements as "the astringent, the pungent, sesame, the five tastes, the *āmalaka*, and the *harītakī*—these are the five tastes," a substance with manifest six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*) is not mentioned here; however, poison (*viṣa*) is endowed with unmanifest six tastes. In the *Hārīta-saṃhitā*, on the other hand, the meat of the black antelope (*eṇa-māṃsa*) is said to be endowed with manifest six tastes.
Thus, from the combination of substances possessing two tastes and so forth, there arises the consumption of those with two tastes and so forth.
(6) Likewise, regarding the phrase "and combined tastes," they prepare and employ combined tastes individually through the blending of substances each possessing one taste and so forth.

(7) Regarding the phrase "for diseases," although this is stated primarily [in the context of pathology], it should be understood as applying even to the regimen for health (*svasthavṛtta*); or else, the distinction of having two tastes and so forth constitutes a disease.

Thus, when one is in a state of health (*svastha*), there is indeed the application of all tastes (*sarvarasa*), as it has been stated: "That which is balanced in all tastes is praised as wholesome (*sātmya*) for one whose *dhātus* are balanced.

(8) This being the explanation, there is no tautology with the statement beginning "sometimes a single taste" (*kvacideko rasaḥ*). (9) Alternatively, the passage beginning "sometimes a single taste" expresses his own view, while the passage beginning "in this very context, substances consisting of two tastes, etc. expresses the agreement of other teachers (*ācāryāntara*) on this same point.
For this very reason, it was stated that [the authors] "formulate [their views] according to the intention of other teachers," and thus there is no tautology.

One who understands the various classifications of tastes (*rasa*) and is a knower of the various classifications of defects (*doṣa*), will not be deluded regarding the causes, symptoms, and pacification of disorders (*vikāra*). (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.27)
[The author] states the fruit of knowing the tastes in the verse beginning with "yaḥ syāt" and so forth.

Here, by the very knowledge of the various permutations of taste, the entire knowledge of substances that cause disease is encompassed; for, as will be explained, almost all the qualities of substances are [determined] by the knowledge of taste alone.

Furthermore, from the knowledge of the variations of the *doṣas* arises the knowledge of the *liṅgas* (signs/symptoms); for as long as there is a *liṅga*, all of it is connected with the variations of the *doṣas*.

From the knowledge of the variations of taste (*rasa*) and the *doṣas*, however, arises the knowledge of the medicine (*bheṣaja*); because from taste comes the knowledge of the essential nature of the medicinal substance, and from the *doṣas* comes the specialized knowledge regarding the scope of the medicinal application. Alternatively, the knowledge of causes (*hetu*) and so forth should be stated separately from the variations of taste and the variations of the *doṣas*; for by means of the distinctions in taste, its effect—the *liṅga*—is also known, as well as the specialized knowledge of the cause and the medicine.

However, it must be stated that this is known precisely through the discernment of the differences among tastes (*rasa*), because it is the substance itself— possessing those specific tastes— that is the cause of the morbid transformations (*vikāra*) and serves as the medicine (*bheṣaja*).
Thus, having understood the difference among the humors (*doṣa*), one recognizes their common cause and that which is antagonistic to the humors.
"Substance is the medicine.
Thus it has been rightly said: "He would not be deluded regarding the causes, signs, and pacification of disorders.
The manifest taste of a substance is perceived both at the beginning and when it is dry.
By contrast, there is no seventh taste that possesses a secondary taste (anurasa).
[The *Āyurvedadīpikā* states:
"Manifest," etc., he now explains the previously mentioned characteristics of tastes and secondary tastes. 1.26.28.

By the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "of the dry," [the text implies] "and of the moist"; by the word "ca" in the phrase "at the beginning," [it implies] "and at the end. Therefore, whether of the dry or the moist, that which is perceived through its manifestation—by way of such conceptual alternatives as "this is sweet" or "this is sour"—either upon the initial contact with the tongue or at the conclusion of the tasting, is the "manifested" (*vyakta*). But what is that which is not perceived as manifested even during the four aforementioned states?

The meaning of the statement is that, therefore, it is measured either by its indefinability, by mere shadow, or by the observation of its effects; thus, it is called a "subtle flavor" (anurasa). Since the sweet and other [primary flavors] themselves take the form of rasa and anurasa through being manifest or unmanifest, there is no such thing as a seventh rasa called "unmanifest.
Furthermore, although this point was refuted previously, it is refuted again here because of the attainment of supporting and clear reasons.

Others, however, say that by the phrase "and of the dry," it is meant that for whichever substance there is usage both in its dry and its moist states, that which is unmanifest in its dry state is called the *rasa*; whereas that which is manifest in its moist state but does not persist in the dry state is not a *rasa*, but rather a *anurasa* (secondary flavor). 5.

Just as the sweet taste of fresh long pepper (*pippalī*) is manifest, whereas the dried long pepper has a pungent taste, therefore the pungent alone is the primary taste of long pepper, while the sweet is its secondary taste (*anurasa*). However, in the case of grapes and the like, where the taste remains sweet both in the fresh and dried states, there is no disagreement; therefore, in those cases, the sweet alone is the taste for those things that are to be used always fresh.

However, regarding substances such as sour gruel (kāñjika) and buttermilk (takra), that taste which is perceived clearly at first and that which is subsequently perceived is logically the "secondary taste" (anurasa), such as bitterness and so forth. Likewise, in the moist state, that which is the opposite of its dry state—such as the sweetness of long pepper (pippalī)—is called the secondary taste. But we observe that even in its moist state, the long pepper possesses a sweet taste itself; for it will be stated later: "The moist [long pepper] is phlegm-increasing and sweet."
Regarding the statement "long pepper is heavy and unctuous," if it were to possess a sweet secondary taste (*anurasa*), then its heaviness and its capacity to produce phlegm would be untenable;
therefore, it is logical that fresh long pepper possesses a manifest sweet taste, whereas dried long pepper possesses a sweet secondary taste.
Furthermore, priority and posteriority, as well as number and conjunction, are established by logic alone.
Separation, distinctness, as well as dimension,
and also refinement or practice— these qualities beginning with *para* (the highest) should be known;
we shall now describe them by their characteristics as the means for achieving success in medical treatment.
In regard to place, time, age, measure, digestion, potency, taste, and so forth,
the application of reasoning regarding priority and posteriority is what constitutes *yojanā* (synthesis).
*Saṃkhyā* (number) refers to calculation (*gaṇita*), while *yoga* is said to be conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with [another].
The disjunction (*vibhāga*) of substances arises from conjunction (*dvandva*), from all [substances], or from a single action, and it is indeed non-eternal.
Disjunction (*vibhakti*) is separation (*viyoga*), the taking apart portion by portion (*bhāgaśo graha*).
Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*), distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*), and manifoldness (*anekatā*).
Furthermore, *parimāṇa* (measure) is considered to be *māna* (measurement), while *saṃskāra* (refinement) is considered to be *karaṇa* (instrumental action).
*Abhyāsa* (practice) is the repeated cultivation of a state (*bhāva*), which is *śīlana* (habituation) or constant performance.
Thus, all the qualities beginning with *para* have been described according to their own specific characteristics.
"Without which [qualities], medical treatment cannot be properly carried out.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.35) [Commentary from the Āyurvedadīpikā:

Now, he states the ten qualities beginning with "para" (remoteness), which are distinct from the previously mentioned qualities such as heaviness (*guru*), and which are to be taught as properties of taste (*rasa*). He says "para... and so forth. 1.

That "remoteness" (paratva) is primacy, and "nearness" (aparatva) is non-primacy. Its explanation begins with "space, time," and so forth. In that context, a desert is remote space and a marshy land is near; the season of release [autumn] is remote time and the season of gathering [spring] is near; and youth is remote age.

Furthermore, there is another [type of] measure regarding the body, which will be explained as follows: in relation to the body, that which is superior is "para" (the supreme), while that which is other than it is "apara" (the inferior).
Regarding a particular yogin, those qualities such as digestion, potency, and taste that are appropriate for him are "para," whereas those not suited to him are "apara.
By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (etcetera), there is the inclusion of factors such as innate nature and strength.

Alternatively, "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "proximity" (*aparatva*), as taught by the Vaiśeṣikas, are to be understood as follows: with respect to space, *paratva* arises in that which is connected to a distant place relative to that which is connected to a proximate place, while *aparatva* arises in that which is connected to a proximate place.
Likewise, with respect to time, *paratva* occurs in an elder and *aparatva* in a youth.

In the case of age and so forth, priority and posteriority—whether produced by time or space—are mentioned here as being metaphorically applied according to their applicability, because no other quality can exist within a quality such as measurement and the like.

Regarding the phrase "and reasoning" (*yuktiśca*) and so forth: "reasoning" (*yojanā*) refers to the proper formulation of a medicine in consideration of the [patient's] doshas and other factors. For this very reason it is said:

"That formulation which is applied and which is appropriate is called 'reasoning' (*yukti*); however, even if a formulation is present, if it is inappropriate, it is not called 'reasoning,' just as a son who is not virtuous is like one who has no son. (8)
And this *yukti* (reasoning), although included within conjunction (*saṃyoga*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), and refinement (*saṃskāra*), is mentioned separately because of its extreme utility.
[Verse 9] He defines number (*saṃkhyā*) with the words "number," etc.
[Verse 10] Here, "calculation" (*gaṇita*) refers to one, two, three, and so forth. [Verse 11]
He states [the definition of] conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with the words "yoga" and so forth.

(12) The meaning is that *saha* refers to the conjunction—that is, the meeting—of substances that have come together; by using the word *saha*, he here excludes a mutual conjunction that is ineffective for this purpose.
(13) He states its divisions with the words "dvaṃdva" and so forth. (14)

Among these, that produced by the action of two [objects] is, for example, like two rams fighting. That produced by all actions is, for example, like beans being poured into a vessel, where many actions of the beans [occur]. That produced by conjunction (*yogaja*) is, for example, like a tree and a crow [where the conjunction arises from the action of one alone].
By stating "it is non-eternal," he shows that conjunction is non-eternal because it is produced by action.
He states the classification: "But the classification," and so forth. (17) *Vibhakti* means division (*vibhajana*).
(18) He explains *vibhakti* itself as separation: *viyoga* is the dissolution of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). (19)
Is disjunction (*viyoga*) merely the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*)? To this he says: "perception by parts" (*bhāgaśo graha*).

The meaning is that it is because there occurs a perception [of objects] as distinct, that is, as divided (*vibhaktatvena*). Therefore, this cognition termed "division" (*vibhakti*) is not a mere absence of conjunction; rather, its sense is that it is endowed with the positive quality (*guṇa*) of division.
Distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), however, is that substance from which such cognitions as "this object characterized as a cloth is distinct from the jar" arise; that is distinctness.
And the Teacher has described it as being of three kinds, beginning with the words "distinctness," etc.
Among these, that distinctness which exists between two things that are in no way conjoined, such as Mount Meru and the Himalayas, is what is expressed by the term "non-conjunction" (*asaṃyoga*).

Likewise, even for things that are conjoined, there is a distinctness among those of different classes, such as buffaloes, boars, and so forth; this he expresses with the words "distinctness" (*vailakṣaṇya*) and so on. (25) The meaning is that the distinctness of things of different classes is characterized by their possession of specific defining characteristics (*viśiṣṭalakṣaṇa*). (26) Similarly, there is also a distinctness among things of the same class that are indistinguishable from one another, such as beans; this he expresses with the word "multiplicity" (*anekatā*). (27)

The meaning is that when things of the same kind are conjoined, there is neither difference nor non-conjunction; nevertheless, multiplicity exists in the form of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*). Alternatively, for one who maintains that distinctness is a separate quality (*guṇāntara*), he demonstrates—just as in the example provided—that distinctness consists precisely in the form of multiplicity characterized by its difference from non-conjunction, for the sake of worldly convention.
Measurable objects include *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and so forth, as well as weights such as the balance scale.

The construction is: "some [substances] are astringent and hot, and bitter and hot. An illustration of astringent, bitter, and salty [substances], even though they were not explicitly mentioned [in the preceding list], has been provided here on account of the context. 2.
The "great five roots" (*mahat-pañcamūla*) here refers to the *bilva* and other five roots.
This is an example of [substances] that are bitter and astringent yet hot in potency; whereas the meat of aquatic and marshy animals is an example of those that are sweet yet hot in potency.
For some slightly sour substances are constipating (*saṃgrāhin*), while others that are slightly sour are purgative (*bhedana*).
Just as the wood-apple (kapittha) is astringent, so too is the emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) laxative.
Pippalī and ginger (nāgara) are aphrodisiacs, whereas pungent substances are said to be non-aphrodisiac.
A decoction is astringent and cooling; however, in the case of abhayā, it is the opposite.
Therefore, one should not prescribe every substance based solely on its taste;
for it is observed that even among substances of identical taste, there are differences in their specific qualities (guṇa). (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.52)
In connection with the discussion of *vīrya* (potency), he states something else regarding the contradictory qualities of *amlā* and other [substances], beginning with "kiñcit" and so forth.
[Verse 1] Regarding *abhayā*, it is otherwise; that is to say, in *abhayā*, the taste is astringent (*kaṣāya*), it is disintegrating (*bhedana*), and it is hot (*uṣṇa*).
[Verse 2] Due to its dryness (*raukṣya*), the astringent taste is the best among dry substances, while the pungent (*kaṭu*) is middling.
Among hot substances, bitter is the lowest, while salty is the highest due to its heat;
sour is middling, and pungent is the last. Among unctuous substances, sweet is the highest; sour is middling, and salty is said to be the lowest in terms of their unctuousness.

In terms of coldness (*śaitya*), [the tastes] are middling, superior, and inferior [respectively as astringent, sweet, and bitter]; salt is superior to astringent due to its heaviness (*gurutva*), while sour is inferior to it. Bitter is superior to pungent because of its lightness (*laghutva*), and thus it is the very best of all.
Among light substances, they consider salt to be the least [heavy] taste;
however, in terms of both heaviness and lightness, it is the least of both.
"Due to dryness," and so forth.

(1) Among these, the astringent taste is the best because of its dryness, meaning it is the driest; the bitter taste is dry; the pungent taste is middling, being drier than the former; and the same applies elsewhere.
(2) "And the pungent is last" means it is the lowest. (3)

Thus, "salt is the last" means it is the lowest (avara). "Salt is the lowest" means [lowest] in terms of heaviness. Regarding the sequence beginning with "pungent is lighter than sour," pungent is lighter than sour; therefore, bitter is the highest of all because it is lighter than even the highest [of the preceding], namely pungent. Thus, bitter is the most excellent (uttamottama) among those that are already excellent (uttama). 6.
He states the opinion of some with the words "some say," and so forth.
Accepting the opinion of some through a particular turn of phrase, he says "in weightiness," and so forth.

By this, while accepting the inferiority of salt both in weightiness and lightness, [he shows] that by the phrase "inferior in weightiness," [salt is inferior] compared to sour, pungent, and bitter [tastes].
By the statement "it accepts the heaviness of salt and is an obstacle to its lightness," he accepts that salt possesses less lightness than even sour [taste], which is itself light.
Nor should it be argued that earth is the cause in sourness while water is the cause in salt; therefore, [salt] is lighter than earth because it is produced from water.
Lightness is indeed appropriate for salt, since heaviness and lightness cannot be determined by its placement alone;
for instance, that which is sweet due to an excess of water becomes heavier than that which is astringent due to an excess of earth.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the post-digestive effects (vipāka) will now be explained.
The post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) of pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes is generally pungent;
the sour taste is digested as sour, while the sweet and salty tastes are likewise digested as sweet. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.58)
Now, since even the post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) possesses the nature of taste, he states its definition beginning with "param" and so forth.

(1) By the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*), he demonstrates that long pepper (*pippalī*), horse gram (*kulattha*), and others undergo a transformation that is inconsistent with their [original] tastes.

(2) Furthermore, by the term "pungent" (*kaṭuka*) and so forth, the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of those tastes is meant; for it is not the tastes themselves that are transformed, but rather the substance itself. (3)
"Salt is likewise," meaning that salt also generally has a sweet post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
As for the definition of *vipāka*: the quality that arises at the time of the food's final digestion through contact with the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) is *vipāka*. For it is said:
"That other taste which arises from contact with the digestive fire [is the post-digestive transformation]."
That [result] is proclaimed as the transformation at the end of digestion.
The three tastes—sweet, salty, and sour—are considered pleasant during the discharge of wind, urine, and feces, owing to their unctuous nature. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.59)
Furthermore, the three tastes— pungent, bitter, and astringent—
are seen to lead to suffering during liberation [from the body] due to their dry nature, as they cause the discharge of wind, feces, urine, and semen.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.60)

Now, regarding the characteristics of post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) that will be described, he states the reason why sweet and sour tastes do not obstruct wind, urine, and feces during their digestion, whereas pungent taste causes the obstruction of wind, urine, and feces:
"sweet," and so forth.

Here, the meaning of the sentence is that sweet, sour, and salty tastes, even when they have reached the state of final digestion (*niṣṭhāpāka*), facilitate the easy elimination of wind and feces due to their association with the quality of unctuousness (*sneha*).
Therefore, this same characteristic applies to those that undergo sweet and sour post-digestive transformations (pāka).
Likewise, the meaning of the statement regarding pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] is the same, even when there is a reversal [of their properties].
Pungent [taste], when it has undergone transformation, is destructive of semen, causes the retention of feces and urine, and increases vāta.
The sweet [rasa] promotes the excretion of feces and urine; its post-digestive effect (vipāka) increases kapha and semen.
The sour [rasa] produces pitta and promotes the excretion of feces and urine; its post-digestive effect destroys semen.
Among these, the sweet is heavy, while the pungent and the sour are otherwise [light].
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

Now, in order to state the characteristics of post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) as established by its causes, endowed with specific qualities such as the destruction of semen (*śukra-hatva*), etc., he says "śukra-hat" and so forth. 1.
Therefore, otherwise [it is] light. 2.]
One should observe the mild, moderate, or predominant nature of the maturation (vipāka) of substances in each respective case,
based on the specific qualities of those substances.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.63)

Now, he explains how, among the various substances characterized by the aforementioned results of digestion (*vipāka*), there occurs at times a small degree, at times a middling degree, and at times a superior degree: "The result of digestion," and so forth.

(1) The meaning is that one should observe the small, middling, or predominant nature of the characteristic of digestion for each individual substance, due to the specific excellence of their qualities (*guṇavaiśeṣya*).

(2) By this, it is stated that because of the specific excellence of qualities among substances—such as being sweet, sweeter, or sweetest—the distinctions such as the smallness of the results of digestion arise.
On this point, some say that there is a transformation (pāka) for each individual taste, such that the six tastes—sweet and the rest—undergo six transformations, namely sweet and so forth;
others say that the weaker tastes fall under the influence of the stronger tastes, and consequently, the transformation is not fixed.
In this regard, disregarding both these systems for determining transformation, Suśruta accepted two types of transformation: sweet and pungent.
Furthermore, in a substance composed of the five elements, there are two types of digestion: when there is an excess of the heavy elements, earth and water, a sweet digestion occurs;

however, when there is an excess of the remaining light elements, a pungent digestion occurs, as it has been said: "In substances being digested, those in which the qualities of water and earth [predominate]... (Verse 6).
When the qualities of fire,
wind, and space predominate among those being digested,
that digestion is called pungent. Thus it is said.

In the case of both *pratirasa-pāka* (counter-taste digestion) and *anavasthita-pāka* (unstable digestion), the substance remains identical to its taste and qualities even during the state of digestion; therefore, no distinction is perceived there through the action of *vipāka*. Thus, it was rightly done that Suśruta disregarded those two positions. 10.

The rejection of the third [position], namely that there is no sour digestion (*amlapāka*), however, brings about a logical flaw; for it is observed that rice, horse-gram (*kulattha*), and other such grains produce bile (*pitta*) due to their having a sour digestion.

Now, if you think that the production of bile in the case of rice and so forth is due to their hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*), that is not correct; for according to that view, even though sweet rice possesses hot potency while having a sweet post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), the production of bile is not logically tenable on account of both its taste and its post-digestive transformation.
Because a single potency (vīrya) cannot be obstructed.

Furthermore, because rice and other grains have an acidic digestion (amlapāka), they produce bile with an acidic quality; if that [bile] were caused by a hot potency, then the bile would be predominantly pungent in quality. However, it is observed that from eating rice, there is an abundance of acidic qualities, such as acid eructation and so forth.

Furthermore, if it is argued that a sweet post-digestive transformation (pāka) results from the predominance of the qualities of earth and soma, while a pungent one results from the predominance of air, fire, and space, then how can the production of sourness— which consists of both soma and agni— be rejected when there is a predominance of mixed qualities? // 13 //

Alternatively, what need is there for these two authors of the Tantras to concern themselves with this mere contradiction in their words? For, that which Caraka describes as having an acid transformation (*amlapāka*) is reconciled by Suśruta on the grounds that its potency (*vīrya*) is hot; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the qualities of substances. As for the objection raised in the Suśruta to refute the acid transformation—beginning with "bile, when improperly digested, attains acidity" and so forth—that is refuted simply by not accepting [that premise].

Now, one might object: "If salt has a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), its capacity to produce *pitta*, blood disorders, and so forth, is untenable; likewise, if bitter and astringent tastes have a pungent post-digestive effect, their capacity to destroy *pitta* is untenable. This is not so. Even though salt has a sweet post-digestive effect, because it possesses a salty taste and a hot potency (*vīrya*), it produces *pitta*, blood disorders, and the like by means of those two qualities; however, its post-digestive effect therein is characterized by the removal of *pitta* and blood.
Being sublated in its effect, it is indeed characterized by such defining marks as "having emitted feces and urine" and so forth.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "If salt has a sweet post-digestive transformation (vipāka), yet, being sublated by its [original] taste and potency, it does not perform its own function, then what is the point of teaching that [transformation]?"

Since it is indeed observed that salt produces the emission of feces and urine and so forth, its quality of having a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) must be inferred therein. (18) By this same method, the refutation of the prima facie argument regarding bitter and astringent tastes is also established.

(19) Others, however, fearing this objection, explain that even salt is digested as sour (*amla*), because in the phrase "salt is likewise" (*lavaṇas tathā*), the word "likewise" (*tathā*) draws in the distant term "sour" (*amla*). (20)
Therefore, according to the statement of Jatūkarṇa, "the pungent [taste] has a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka), the sour has a sour, and for the remaining two,

it is sweet," one should not ask why there are only three post-digestive effects and not bitter ones as well; for this is simply the nature of the elements (bhūtasvabhāva), by which only these three— sweet and so forth— exist, and the nature of the elements is not subject to questioning.

Now, one might object: let that transformation of taste which is contrary to the original taste—such as the sweet post-digestive effect (pāka) of salt, or the pungent effect of bitter and astringent substances—be described; but what is the purpose of stating that which shares the same qualities, such as the sweet effect of a sweet substance, the sour of a sour, or the pungent of a pungent?
For in those cases, the quality of the post-digestive effect will already be known through the qualities of the taste itself. (23)

It is not so; for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that a dissimilar secondary taste might arise—as in the case of salt and other substances—a corresponding *vipāka* (post-digestive transformation) must indeed be stated even in those cases. Furthermore, the taste born of *vipāka* occurs at the end of the digestion of food, whereas the natural (*prākṛta*) taste is to be understood as contrary to the *vipāka*, except during the period of transformation itself. Therefore, the pungent taste of long pepper (*pippalī*) acts first by clearing the phlegm located in the throat and cleansing the mouth.
The state of having a sweet post-digestive effect (*madhuravipākatva*) is purposeful because it indicates, through its transformation (*pariṇāma*), qualities such as aphrodisiac power (*vṛṣyatva*).

(24) Likewise, it should be understood that where the tastes (*rasa*) of the post-digestive effect are concordant with the primary taste by virtue of possessing similar qualities, the resulting action is powerful; however, in the opposite case, it is weak.

(25) Furthermore, these three types of digestion (*pāka*) are restricted to substances (*dravya*); therefore, they are distinct from the "digestion of the state of food" (*āhārāvasthāpāka*) which will be discussed in the chapter on the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-adhyāya*).

Thus, in that regard, three types of digestion (pāka) must be stated for all tastes without distinction, according to their state, by means of the passage beginning with: "Of food consisting of the six tastes, immediately upon being eaten, through its full digestion...
[26] ...[the qualities are] mild, sharp, heavy, light, unctuous, dry, hot, and cold.
Some maintain that potency (*vīrya*) is of eight kinds, while others hold it to be of two kinds.
Potency is defined as that by which an action is performed—whether cold or hot;
nothing can be accomplished without potency, for every action is produced by potency.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, the definition of *vīrya* according to one school of thought is stated as "soft," etc. (verse 1).
This pair of opinions from one school proceeds by taking the technical designation (*pāribhāṣikī saṃjñā*) of *vīrya* as its basis. (Verse 2)

In medical science (*vaidyaka*), the term *vīrya* (potency) refers to a quality distinct from taste (*rasa*), post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and specific action (*prabhāva*), which performs numerous functions.

Therefore, according to the view that there are eight types of potency, qualities such as sliminess (*picchila*) and clarity (*viśada*) generally do not produce effects contrary to those of taste and the other factors;

consequently, they are understood through the very instruction of taste and so forth. However, qualities such as softness (*mṛdu*) and the like possess the capacity to override taste and the other factors.

Just as in long pepper (*pippalī*), the action of its pungent taste—which is to aggravate *pitta*—is overcome by its soft and cold potency (*vīrya*) residing therein, so that it pacifies *pitta* itself; likewise, in the great five roots (*pañcamūla*), which are astringent with a bitter aftertaste, the action of wind-aggravation is overcome, and by means of their hot potency, an action contrary to that [aggravation]—namely, the pacification of wind—is produced. Similarly, in sweet sugarcane, there is an increase of wind due to its cold potency, and so forth. (3)
As stated in the *Suśruta*: "Indeed, these potencies (vīrya), by the excellence of their own strength and qualities, overcome the taste (rasa) and manifest their own specific actions," and so forth.

The doctrine of those who maintain that there are cold and hot potencies should be understood as arising from the fact that the world is composed of Agni and Soma, and because cold and heat alone are predominant.
And it has been said:
Even though a substance consists of multiple natures, it never transcends the two great powers, Agni and Soma,
just as the world does not transcend the manifest and the unmanifest.

And these two views are indeed accepted by the Teacher as established by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), since later on— in passages such as "where a similarity of taste, potency, and post-digestive effect is observed"— only this technical terminology is employed.
He will explain *vīrya*.
However, by abandoning the conventional designation of *vīrya*, he states the definition of *vīrya* as a synonym for power (*śakti*) in the passage beginning with "But *vīrya*... and so forth.
*Vīrya* means power.

"By which" means that in whatever action—consisting of satiation, exhilaration, pacification, and so forth—is performed by means of taste (*rasa*), post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), potency (*prabhāva*), or qualities such as heaviness and lightness, that taste and so forth constitute the *vīrya* (potency) in that action.
For this very reason it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "That by which they act is *vīrya*."
Right here, he states the reasoning well-known in the world, beginning with "not without vigor" (*nāvīryam*), and so forth.
(12) "Without vigor" (*avīryam*) means "incapable.
(13) "Produced by vigor" (*vīryakṛtā*) means "produced by one possessing vigor," that is, produced by vigor. (14)

The taste of substances is perceived at the moment of ingestion; their transformation (vipāka) results from the completion of the action; and their potency (vīrya) is perceived through both the latent impression (adhīvāsa) and the act of ingestion itself. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.66)

He states the definition of taste (*rasa*) and the other [qualities] which reside in a single substance, distinguishing them by their respective functions, beginning with "taste is [that which occurs] during contact," and so forth.
1. "During contact" (*nipāta*) means during the engagement of the sense of taste (*rasanā*).

2. "By the completion of the action" (*karmaniṣṭhayā*): the completion (*niṣṭhā*) of an action is its accomplishment; "completion of the action" refers to the conclusion of the activity involved in the utilization of the taste.
When present, that specific transformation of the final food which is characterized by the increase of phlegm, semen, and so forth, determines the maturation (*vipāka*).

(3) *Adhīvāsa* means coexistence; "as long as there is *adhīvāsa*" means as long as there is residence in the body. This is to be understood as occurring prior to the maturation (*vipāka*) and subsequent to the falling away [of the body].
(4) "And from the falling away" means from the mere conjunction with the body; thus, some potency (*vīrya*) is perceived from *adhīvāsa*, as in the case of the meat of marshy animals and the like.

Some degree of heat is obtained from the very moment of ingestion, as in the case of *marica* and similar substances; some degree [of heat] is obtained both from ingestion and from subsequent habituation, as in the case of those same substances. By this it is shown that while taste (*rasa*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) is always imperceptible and is inferred from its effects, whereas potency (*vīrya*) is in some cases known through inference.

The meaning of the statement is as follows: just as the coldness inherent in rock salt or the heat inherent in the meat of marshy animals is perceived through direct experience, and just as the heat in mustard seeds is determined by the sense of smell, while qualities such as sliminess, clarity, oiliness, and dryness are ascertained by both sight and touch.
And this vigor should be understood as being both innate and acquired.
(7) And this should be understood as the characteristic of vigor, as it applies to heavy, light, and other such [degrees], according to their occurrence.
(8) "Of substances" means of those substances being employed. (9)
And that characteristic of potency (*vīrya*) pertains exclusively to the technical definition of *vīrya*.

Where the commonality of taste, potency, and post-digestive effect (*rasa-vīrya-vipāka*) is observed, as well as the distinction of actions, that is traditionally known as its power (*prabhāva*). (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.67)
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,] he states the definition of *prabhāva* (specific potency) beginning with "rasavīrya" and so forth. 1.
*Sāmānya* means similarity or equality. 2.
"Specificity of actions" refers to [qualities] such as purgation and so forth, which depend on dental and other [articulatory] places.

By the phrase "the general is characterized," he indicates that whatever effect cannot be determined through its being an effect of taste and so forth is produced by *prabhāva* (potency). For this very reason it is said: "Potency is called inconceivable"; the meaning is that it is inconceivable by way of being an effect of taste, *vīrya* (potency), and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
Citraka is considered pungent in taste, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and hot in potency (vīrya).
Similarly, Dantī causes purgation due to its specific inherent power (prabhāva).
Regarding poison that is said to be an antidote for poison, its specific inherent power is the cause therein.
That which leads upward and in accordance with the natural order,
as well as the various kinds of effects produced by the wearing of gems,
are brought about by their power; indeed, their power is said to be inconceivable.
The correct maturations, the potencies, and the specific actions have also been described:

some [substances] perform their function through taste, others through potency, some substances through post-digestive effect (pāka), and others through specific action (prabhāva). Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.71.
Taste, post-digestive transformation, and potency—potency sets these aside;
this is the inherent strength of taste and the other factors when their strength is equal.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.72) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
Because this very [subject] is difficult to comprehend, he states many examples beginning with "bitter" (kaṭuka) and so forth.

(1) "In that same way" means possessing qualities similar to those of a painter. (2) "It is said to be an antidote to poison" refers to the passage beginning with "therefore, the primary poison is from the fangs. (3)
"Upward and downward-moving" (ūrdhvānulomika) means that which simultaneously eliminates [impurities] from both parts, or else that which moves upward and likewise moves downward.
"Action which is of two kinds" (karma yadvividhātmakam) refers to such things as the removal of poison and the removal of colic.

This is merely an illustration; by this, it should be understood that the entire inconceivable range of effects—such as the taste and other qualities of substances like life-giving or purifying agents—is known as *prabhāva* (specific potency).

In this context, "potency" (*prabhāva*) is intended to mean the power of a substance (*dravya-śakti*). Furthermore, this is the general-specified nature (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) of substances; it is the very individual (*vyakti*) endowed with properties such as being *dantī*. For potency is indeed the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of entities, not some other distinct attribute. This same principle should be stated regarding the "power of qualities" (*guṇa-prabhāva*) and so forth mentioned in other passages, as it has been said: "For substances [produce] the power of qualities through the power of the substance," and so on. (7)
Nor should it be argued: "Since *dantī* itself, by its very nature, causes purgation, why does it not do so when impaired by water and the like?

For it is the power (*prabhāva*) as qualified by the absence of obstructing factors that constitutes the cause; thus, one must follow the reasoning that in the case of *dantī* impaired by water, the impairment by water acts as the obstructor.

The argument stated in the Naiyāyika theory of potency (*śakti*) regarding the counteraction of poison by another poison—characterized as a contradiction between upward and downward movement—occurs precisely because of the internal presence of a specific power (*prabhāva*).
[9] The same should be said even when describing qualities such as being earthy (*pārthivatva*) in relation to the upward or downward movement of substances.
[10] Hereafter, I shall teach the knowledge of the six tastes (*rasa*). (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.73)
Located in the mouth, it is perceived through its qualities of unctuousness, refreshing, exhilarating, and softening; being sweet, it pervades the mouth and seems to coat it.
It is characterized by a tingling sensation in the teeth, salivation from the mouth, perspiration, and a sense of clarity in the face.
One should declare that the salty taste, having tasted it, causes a burning sensation in the throat;
it dissolves quickly, producing moisture, exudation, and softness in the mouth, and is known by its burning of the mouth. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.75–76)
That which causes agitation upon contact, stings as it were, burns the mouth,
nose, and eyes, and flows out [as a discharge] is known as pungent (kaṭu).
That which strikes back against the tongue upon contact and does not taste sweet is also [pungent].

That bitter [taste] produces clarity of the mouth, dryness, and refreshment. That taste which, through clarity, astringency, and numbness, engages the tongue and binds the throat as it were, though it is expanding, is astringent (kaṣāya).
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, "vijñāna" means that by which something is known; the meaning is "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*).
(1) "Pralīyan" means becoming dissolved. (2)
It is called *saṃsrāvī* because it causes [the morbid matter] to flow out (*saṃsrāvayati*).
It is called *vikāsī* because it has the nature of expanding the heart; for it is stated in the Suśruta that "it afflicts the heart.
To the Blessed Ātreya who had spoken thus, Agniveśa said: "Blessed One, this which we have heard is unerring and endowed with the perfection of its meaning."

"O Blessed One, we wish to hear your authoritative discourse on the categories of substances, qualities, and actions as they truly are; however, we also desire that you teach us, without excessive brevity, the characteristics of incompatible dietary combinations."

Now, he says "thus, etc. in order to speak of incompatible food (*viruddhāhāra*). 1. They are called *vairodhika* because they produce a contradiction of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is that by which the incompatible is characterized; thus, the very text that expresses the term *vairodhika* constitutes the definition. 2.
Whatever [food] provokes the humors (*doṣa*), and so forth—this is to be understood as the definition of the incompatible. 3.

The Blessed Ātreya said to him: "Substances that are antagonistic to the bodily constituents (dhātus) enter into opposition with those constituents; some do so because their qualities are mutually contradictory, others through combination (saṃyoga), others through processing (saṃskāra), others through place, time, measure, and so forth, and still others by their very nature."

"Being antagonistic to the bodily constituents (*dehadhātu*)" means having a nature that is opposed to the bodily constituents—such as *rasa* and the rest—as well as to *vāta* and the rest when they abide in their natural state. "They come into conflict" means they act in opposition to the bodily constituents; that is to say, they vitiate them.

When substances, as they truly are, come into conflict with the constituent elements of the body, he says: "Some are mutually contradictory," and so forth. (3) Among these, those whose qualities are mutually contradictory are as stated in the passage beginning, "One should not consume fish with milk, for both of these... and so on. (4) That which is contradictory due to combination is as stated in the passage beginning, "That same *nikuca* fruit when ripe [is forbidden], but not the *māṣa* bean," and so forth; that which is called contradictory merely by being taken together, without mentioning a contradiction in qualities such as processing (*saṃskāra*) and the like, is this [type]. (5)
[This refers to] that which is incompatible with combination.

(5) Although the simultaneous consumption of fish and milk is stated to be incompatible, it is nevertheless described as being due to a contradiction in their qualities (*guṇa*); therefore, this is an illustration specifically of that which possesses a contradiction of qualities.

Furthermore, even when there is a contradiction of qualities, incompatibility occurs only in certain cases due to the specific power (*prabhāva*) of the substances; thus, in the consumption of a diet containing all six tastes, there is no incompatibility between the sweet and the sour [tastes], despite their having contradictory potencies (*vīrya*), such as cold and hot.
Contradiction by way of preparation (*saṃskāra*) is, for example: "not pigeons fried in mustard oil," and so forth.

(7) Place (*deśa*) is twofold: the ground and the body. (8) Among these, contradiction by way of place is, for example, that same [food] covered with ashes or dust; or whatever is produced in an unsuitable environment—that is contradiction by way of place. Contradiction by way of the body is, for example, honey for one afflicted by heat.

9. Contrary to time (*kālaviruddha*): for example, stale *kākamācī* leads to death. 10. Contrary to measure (*mātrāviruddha*): for example, honey and ghee taken in equal proportions leads to death. 11.

"One should not consume fish together with milk; for both of these are sweet and have a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), yet they are highly obstructive to the channels (*mahābhiṣyandi*).

Honey that is warm, or honey given to one afflicted by heat, leads to death.

Honey and ghee taken in equal proportions; the atmosphere (the sky) taken in equal proportions with honey; honey followed by lotus seeds; honey followed by warm water; *bhallātaka* with warm water; *kampillaka* prepared with buttermilk; stale *kākamācī*; and the meat of the *bhāsa* bird roasted on charcoal—these are incompatible combinations (*viruddha*).
Thus, this has been explained according to the questions asked.

(1) That which is brought in is *āhāra* (nutriment), and this includes medicinal substances (*bheṣaja*) as well. (2)
"Having caused the discharge of the *doṣas*" means that after having provoked the *doṣas* into their manifest forms, one does not eliminate them.

By this, he rejects emetic and purgative substances, for those indeed cause the discharge and then eliminate the *doṣas*. Furthermore, [the fault applies] when [the treatment is administered] due to [inappropriate] place, time, digestive fire (*agni*), dose, unwholesome suitability (*asātmya*), wind (*anila*), and so forth.
That which is contrary due to processing, effort, the stages of digestion within the stomach,
avoidance, application, ripening, or combination—
and that which is unsuitable due to the heart, excellence, or ritual procedures— is not beneficial.

First, that which is contradictory by way of place (*deśa*) is as follows: the use of dry, sharp, and similar qualities in a desert (*dhanvana*), or the use of unctuous, cold, and similar medicinal substances in a marshy region (*ānūpa*). Furthermore, that which is contradictory by way of time (*kāla*) is the practice of consuming cold, dry, and similar qualities [during the hot season].

Likewise, the consumption of pungent and excessively hot substances during cold weather, or similarly, food and drink that is incompatible with the digestive fire (*anala*)— whether it be of the four types [of taste, combination, processing, or nature]— is contraindicated. Furthermore, honey and ghee taken in equal proportions are mutually incompatible when consumed in such a measure.

The consumption of sweet and cold substances by one who is habituated to pungent and hot ones is what is called "contrary to habituation" (*sātmyaviruddha*); however, that which is contrary to the bodily humors such as *vāta* is "contrary to the humors" (*anilādibhir viruddha*).
Furthermore, any dietary practice or medicinal treatment that is contrary to the habitual practice of similar qualities is also considered contrary.
That food which, due to its processing (*saṃskāra*), becomes like poison is known as incompatible by processing;
it is just like the meat of a peacock when combined with castor oil and lead.
That which is incompatible by potency (*vīrya*) should be understood as that which is of a cooling nature by virtue of its potency.
That [purgative] is administered together with a substance that possesses a heating potency (uṣṇavīrya) to facilitate its union;
for one with a hard bowel (krūrakoṣṭha), it should be very small in dose and mild in potency, yet non-purging (abhedana).
For one with a soft bowel (mṛdukoṣṭha), it may be heavy, purgative (bhedanīya), and likewise large in dose.
However, that which is incompatible with this [specific] constitution may become incompatible due to one's state [of health].
For one who is addicted to fatigue, sexual intercourse, and physical exercise, food causes the provocation of *vāta*;
for one who is drowsy and lethargic, it causes the provocation of *kapha*. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.26.95–96)
That which one eats without having first voided feces and urine, that which one eats while not hungry,
that which follows the sequence of digestion in reverse, and that which is consumed under the influence of excessive hunger;
furthermore, that which is contrary to avoidance consists of consuming the flesh of pigs and other such forbidden animals.
Having consumed hot ghee and other substances, one then partakes of the cold; likewise,
food that is contrary in its digestion, poorly prepared with inferior wood,
undercooked, overcooked, or burnt.
That which is incompatible due to combination is, for example, sour [substance] with milk.

Food that has lost its flavor, or whose flavor has become spoiled,
should be known as contrary to the rules when it is eaten without being properly concealed;
such food, when consumed, is considered "contrary" (viruddha).

furthermore, it is inferred from the scriptural injunction that the combination [of garlic and other substances] is incompatible only when they are not combined with other substances.

as do emesis, pacification, or the prior adoption of wholesome practices;
this applies especially to those who are habituated to it, those with small dosages, or those who are young and possess a keen digestive fire.
For those who are unctuous, accustomed to exercise, and strong, [the aforementioned] contraries would be ineffective and false.

The determination of the superior, inferior, and middling qualities of tastes based on their heaviness and other attributes; the signs of post-digestive transformation (*pāka*) and potency (*prabhāva*); the ascertainment of the number of potencies (*vīrya*);
and the specific characteristics of the six tastes as they are being experienced—[these are the subjects].

Whatever is antagonistic, from whatever [cause], by whatever [means], and whatever action it performs— the Sage spoke of all that, as well as the remedies for diseases caused by antagonistic factors, in the chapter concerning Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.112–113)

Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 27: [The Rules for Food and Drink] Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for food and drink. Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya.
[Āyurvedadīpikā:

Now follows the section on food and drink (annapānavidhi), intended to describe the specific qualities and actions of individual substances that are useful, which have been mentioned only in general terms according to their qualities and actions, but not described for each individual substance.
2. Here, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha* when it has arisen [after a word ending in *anna*].

3. In this context, because of the commonality of solidity, solid food (*khādya*) is to be understood as being included within "food" (*anna*), and because of the commonality of fluidity, edible liquids (*lehya*) are to be understood as being included within "drink" (*pāna*).

4. The "regimen of food and drink" (*annapānavidhi*) is prescribed; it is explained as that by which food and drink are presented through their association with specific qualities and actions. Indeed, the regimen of food and drink is precisely the description of the qualities and actions of substances (*dravya*), for it is that [which effects such presentation].
Having understood this, food and drink are prescribed.
Experts declare that food and drink—possessing desirable color, fragrance, taste, and texture, and prepared according to rule—are the "life" (*prāṇa*) of living beings, those designated as sentient;
for they see the visible result of this: it is indeed by means of them that the internal fire is maintained, and it is that which invigorates the vital essence (*sattva*).
When that which produces the arrangement of the bodily elements, strength, complexion, and clarity of the senses is consumed as prescribed, it becomes the opposite and leads to harm.
To the question "What does that food and drink do?", he says: "Desirable," and so forth.

It is by that rule [that food and drink act].

Sakoradūṣa śyāmāka is astringent and sweet, light, increases vāta, destroys kapha and pitta, is cold, constipating, and desiccant. Hastiśyāmāka, nīvāra, toyaparṇī, and gavedhukā [are similar].
*Praśāntika*, *ambhas*, *syāmāka*, *lauhitya*, *aṇu*, and *priyaṅgu*;

although barley (*yava*) is heavy, it possesses an abundance of *vāta* due to its dryness; alternatively, since barley is described as light (*laghu*) in the *Suśruta*, it should be understood here also as not heavy (*aguru*). Wheat (*godhūma*) promotes healing, alleviates *vāta*, and is sweet and cold.

Nāndīmukhī and madhūlī are sweet, unctuous, and cooling.

Due to the consumption of wheat (godhūma), which possesses qualities such as being sweet, cold, and unctuous, it indeed acts as a producer of phlegm (śleṣman); for this very reason, it is stated in the Suśruta Saṃhitā that it is "phlegm-producing" (śleṣmakara).
As for the statement that one should eat barley and wheat in the spring when phlegm predominates, that refers to old wheat;

In this very chapter, by means of the text:

Mudga is considered the best of the pulses (sūpya); it is slightly astringent and sweet, dry, cold, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), light, non-slimy (viśada), and it destroys phlegm (śleṣman) and bile (pitta). (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.27.23)
Māṣa is highly aphrodisiac, an excellent alleviator of vāta, unctuous, hot, sweet, and heavy; it is strengthening, produces abundant waste, and quickly bestows virility.
Rājamāṣa is laxative, appetizing, and alleviates kapha, semen-related disorders, and āmlapitta.
They are sweet, increase vāta, are dry, astringent, clear, and heavy.
Kulattha beans are hot, astringent, sour in their post-digestive transformation (pāka), and they destroy kapha, semen, and vāta;
they are constipating and beneficial for cough, hiccups, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids.
Makuṣṭhaka beans are sweet in digestion, constipating, dry, and cold;
they are praised for use in cases of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), fever, and similar conditions.
So too are chickpeas (caṇaka), lentils (masūra), khaṇḍika, and hareṇu.
Light, cold, sweet, slightly astringent, and drying,
they are recommended for use in soups and as external applications for the pacification of pitta and kapha.
Among them, masūra is constipating, while kalāya is excessively provocative of vāta.
Sesame is unctuous, hot, sweet, bitter, and astringent;
it is pungent, beneficial for the skin, hair, and strength; it subdues Vāta while increasing Kapha and Pitta.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.30) It is sweet, cold, heavy, strength-depleting, and drying in nature.

Various types of pulses should be eaten with fats by those who are strong. The pulse (śimbī) is dry and astringent; it aggravates the wind (vāta) in the digestive tract, is neither aphrodisiac nor beneficial for the eyes, and undergoes digestion after causing flatulence.
Āḍhakī destroys kapha and pitta but increases vāta; avalguja, iḍagaja, and niṣpāva alleviate kapha and vāta but increase vāta and pitta.
One should prescribe the fruit of kākāṇḍa, umā, and ātmaguptā as being like that of māṣa.
This second group of pulse-grains (śamīdhānya) has been declared by the Great Sage.

(2) Regarding the qualities of mung beans (*māṣa*) beginning with "aphrodisiac" (*vṛṣya*), since their capacity to remove wind (*vāta*) is already established by their possession of qualities such as being unctuous, hot, and sweet, their explicit mention again is for the purpose of demonstrating that they are specifically effective against wind. Those that dwell on the ground are called *bhūśaya* because they live in burrows; those that frequent marshy lands are *ānūpa* because they take refuge in such places; those born in water are *jalaja* because they reside in water; and those that move in water are *jalecara* because they roam in water.

He states the definition by means of the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the terms *prasaha* and so forth. 1.
*Prasahya* means "by force. 2.

Regarding the phrase *ānūpānūpasaṃśrayāt*, since the rule [of *vṛddhi*] is not established in the preceding case, one should understand the *saṃhitā* in the word *ānūpāḥ* as being established precisely because the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is considered optional. 3.
Regarding "from those that move in water" (*jalecaryāt*), it should be understood that this refers only to water-dwellers such as swans and the like, whose movement is restricted solely to the water.

(4) When "land-born" (*sthalaja*) is mentioned, there might be the implication that elephants and other such land-born creatures are also included; therefore, he says "those that roam the wilderness" (*jāṅgalacāriṇaḥ*).

(5) Regarding the word "scattering" (*vikīrya*), the word "they eat" (*bhakṣayanti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Similarly, regarding "piercing" (*pratudya*), it means having struck [the prey] in many ways. (6)

Goat meat, being neither too cold, heavy, nor unctuous, does not aggravate the *doṣas*.
Due to its similarity with the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), it is non-obstructive and nourishing.
Sheep meat, because it is sweet and cold, is heavy and nourishing.
In the womb, goats and sheep are indeterminate because they share a common habitat;
[as stated in the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"because of the similarity of the bodily constituents," meaning they are identical to human flesh.]
By this it is stated that even though goat meat possesses cold, heavy, and unctuous qualities, it does not produce *kapha* because of its similarity to the constituent elements (*dhātu*) of the body.
(2) Sheep meat should be understood as removing *pitta* due to its sweet and cold nature; for this very reason, it is mentioned among the animals of the autumn regimen as "the ram and the *śarabha*.

(3) However, in the section on the etiology of hemoptysis (*raktapitta*), one should understand that sheep meat causes *raktapitta* only when combined with other substances, as indicated by the passage beginning with "boar, buffalo," and so forth. (4)
"In the womb" (yonau) refers to the eightfold birth resulting from forceful entry [into the womb].

"Because of their mixed range of activity" means that because they sometimes frequent marshy lands, sometimes frequent arid lands, and sometimes frequent both, goats and sheep have an indeterminate origin (*aniścitayonitva*).
Here, "indeterminate" (*aniścita*) is either a qualifier for "womb" (*yoni*), or it means that these two—the goat and the sheep—are themselves indeterminate.
[Objection: If this is so, then the partridge (*tittiri*) should also not be listed among the *viṣkira* birds, since it frequents both arid and marshy lands. [Response:

Since some [animals] move about only in both [land and water], it is not possible to establish a distinction between those two based on their restricted mode of movement.
