It is excellent for sight, hearing, intellect, digestive fire, youth, complexion, voice, and lifespan.
Peacock flesh is most beneficial, strengthening, wind-alleviating, and increases muscle mass and semen.
It is heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet, and it bestows voice, complexion, and strength.
Swans are said to be nourishing, semen-prolific, and destroyers of wind (vāta);
they are unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and clarifiers of the voice.
Peacocks are supremely strengthening, pacifiers of wind, and sudorific.
The partridge (*tittiri*) is hot, sweet, and not excessively dry due to its frequenting of both arid and marshy lands;
it quickly subdues the three *doṣas* when wind (*vāta*) is predominant.
As for the grey partridge (*kapiñjala*), it is beneficial in disorders of bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*) accompanied by blood.
Lavas are recommended during mild winds because of their coolness, sweetness, and lightness;
they are astringent and sweet, light, and increase the digestive fire (*agni*).
They pacify the derangement of the three humors (*saṃnipāta*) and are pungent in their post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
The iguana (godhā) is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), while being astringent and pungent in taste;
it pacifies wind and bile, is nourishing, and increases strength.
The porcupine (śallaka) is known to be sweet and sour in taste, and pungent in its post-digestive effect.

The pigeons that dwell in houses destroy wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as cough and dyspnea; they are astringent, cleansing, cooling, and eradicators of hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta); furthermore, they are sweet in their post-digestive effect (vipāka).
Slightly lighter than those are the forest-dwelling pigeons;
they are cooling, constipating, and produce very little urine.
The flesh of the parrot is astringent and sour, and is dry and cold in its post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
Quail is beneficial for consumption, cough, and wasting; it is astringent, light, and digestive-stimulant.
Quail is sweet and unctuous, increasing strength and semen;
it pacifies the derangement of the three humors (saṃnipāta) and alleviates vāta.

The hare (śaśa) is astringent, clear, dry, cold, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and light. It is sweet, highly recommended for the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (saṃnipāta) and for vāta-predominant disorders.
[The meat of] the rabbit is sweet, sweet in its post-digestive effect, pacifies the three doṣas, and is auspicious.
The meat of the deer is declared to be light, binding for the feces and urine, and cooling;
it is unctuous, nourishing, aphrodisiac, fatiguing, and pacifies Vāta.
The flesh of the boar is strengthening, appetizing, sudorific, and heavy.
Cow’s milk is beneficial in cases of simple wind disorders, chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), and irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
It is also wholesome for dry cough, exhaustion, excessive digestive fire, and wasting of muscle tissue.
Buffalo’s milk is unctuous, hot, sweet, aphrodisiac, heavy, and satiating.
They produce firmness, bulk, enthusiasm, and even sleep;
they are heavy, hot, sweet, strengthening, nourishing, and subdue the wind (vāta).
Fishes are declared to be unctuous, aphrodisiac, and productive of many doṣas.
Because it feeds on moss and young grass, and because its dreams are avoided,
the rohita fish is digestive-stimulant, easily digested, and very strengthening; it improves the complexion,
alleviates wind, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and increases physical strength.
The meat of the tortoise (kūrma) is said to promote intelligence and memory, is wholesome, and cures consumption (śoṣa).
The meat of the rhinoceros (khaḍga) is known to cause secretions (abhiṣyandi), increases strength, and is sweet.
It is emollient, nourishing, improves the complexion, removes fatigue, and subdues Vāta.
The eggs of the peacock,
the partridge, the cock, and the sparrow— which are wholesome—
should be used for those with diminished semen, coughs, heart disease, and chest wounds.
Sweet, non-burning, and providing immediate strength—
no other solid food excels meat for the nourishment of the body.
Thus, this third group of meats has been fully described.
"In some" refers to peacocks and others that will be mentioned later.
"Due to the excellence of qualities" means because they possess distinguished qualities.
The heaviness and unctuousness of the peacock are already established by its inclusion in the *vartakādi* group; that they are stated again is for the sake of specifying particular qualities.
In other cases as well, when a quality already obtained through its mention in a group is stated again, it should be explained in this same manner.
(4) The cock is the "foot-weaponed" (*caraṇāyudha*). (5)

By stating the reason "due to frequenting arid and marshy lands," it should be understood that the partridge (*tittiri*) which frequents such arid and marshy lands is precisely what possesses the aforementioned qualities.

(6) Likewise, other animals such as cows and so forth that frequent arid and marshy lands also possess qualities similar to those of the partridge; however, since the partridge possesses these qualities to a superior degree, the partridge is mentioned explicitly.

(7) Alternatively, it should be understood that while frequenting arid and marshy lands is the cause for the partridge alone having such qualities, this is not the case for others, such as cows, whose habitats are different. (8)
"House-dwelling pigeons" refers to *pārāvata* (doves).

Some read "sweet sparrows" (*caṭakā madhurā*) and so forth; however, for those who do not read this, the aphrodisiac quality (*vṛṣyatva*) obtained through the general qualities of the *pratuda* (pecking) category is acquired solely from aphrodisiac preparations such as: "Having eaten the flesh of sparrows, he who drinks milk afterwards... and so on. However, because the many qualities of peacocks and other such birds exceed those mentioned in the collective list [of meats], they have been listed separately.

(11) Since the nourishing quality of meat is already established by the statement "meat is the foremost among nourishing substances," the subsequent statement beginning with "for the nourishment of the body there is nothing else" should be understood as being introduced by the context and intended to reinforce that very point. One should know that pāṭhā, āśu, śaṭī, śāka, vāstuka, and suniṣaṇṇaka are astringent and destroy the three doṣas; however, vāstuka specifically breaks up constipated stools. Kākamācī pacifies the three doṣas, is aphrodisiac, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).

The *rājakṣavaka* vegetable is neither excessively hot nor cold in potency; it is a laxative that destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). It pacifies the three *doṣas*, is light, is constipating, and is especially recommended for those suffering from disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*) and hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
Black potherb (kālaśāka), however, is pungent, digestive, and overcomes artificial poisons and edema.
The potherb known as kālāya is said to be light, hot, wind-increasing, and dry.
It is digestive, hot in potency, and constipating for kapha and vāta.
The sour *cāṅgerī* is praised; it is beneficial for disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*) and for hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
It is sweet, sweet in its post-digestive transformation (*pāka*), a laxative, and increases phlegm (*śleṣman*). *Upodikā* is aphrodisiac, unctuous, cold, and a destroyer of pride (*mada*).
It is dry, destroys intoxication and poison, and is praised for those suffering from *raktapitta*.
*Taṇḍulīyaka* is sweet and sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and is cooling;
so too are *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, the tips of *vetra*, *kucelā*, and *vanatiktaka*.
Karkoṭaka, avalguja, paṭola, śakulādanī, vṛṣapuṣpa, śārṅgeṣṭā, kembūka,
kaṭhillaka, nāḍī, kalāya, gojihvā, vārtāka, and tilaparṇikā.
Kaulaka, kārkaśa, naimba, and pārpaṭaka vegetables are bitter, cold, and pungent in their post-digestive effect;
they alleviate kapha and pitta.

Regarding *vāstuka* and *ṭaṅkavāstuka*:
"Its potency is neither excessively hot nor cold" means that its heat has not reached a state of intensity, nor does it possess coldness.

As for what was stated in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*, that "the bitter *kākamācī* pacifies wind because of its hot potency," that is according to the view of those who prioritize potency (*vīrya*); for this very reason, even in the *Suśruta*’s section on the qualities of substances, it is stated exactly thus: "it is neither excessively hot nor cold."
It is recited [as follows]: 6. *rājakṣavaka* is *dugdhikā*. 7.

Leafy vegetables (śāka) that are heavy and dry generally digest with flatulence;
they are sweet, cold in potency, and cause the breaking up of the stool.
However, when steamed, their juice squeezed out, and enriched with fats, they are highly recommended.
The flowers of the *śaṇa*, *kovidāra*, *karbudāra*, and *śālmali* are astringent and highly recommended, especially in cases of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders).
Likewise, the tender leaves of the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *padma*, and others are [recommended].
Astringent decoctions that are cooling and stabilizing are beneficial for those suffering from pitta-type diarrhea.
Vatsādanī destroys vāyu, while gaṇḍīra and citraka destroy kapha.
Śreyasī and bilvaparṇī are also beneficial; however, bilva leaves specifically alleviate vāta.

Bhaṇḍī, the leafy vegetable of śatāvarī, balā, and jīvantikā; as well as the vegetables of parvaṇī and parvapuṣpī, are known to alleviate vāta and pitta. The vegetables of lāṅgalakī and uruvūka are light, purgative, and bitter.

The vegetables *tilavetasa* and *pañcāṅgula* increase *vāta*; they are pungent, bitter, and sour, and they promote downward movement [of the humors]. *Kausumbha* is dry, sour, and hot; it destroys *kapha* and increases *pitta*.
Trapusa and ervāruka are sweet, heavy, constipating, and cooling;
they are pleasant to the mouth, dry, and highly diuretic.
Furthermore, when fully ripe, ervāruka relieves burning sensations, thirst, fatigue, and distress.
Alābu gourds break up the stool and are dry, cold, and heavy;
likewise, cirbhaṭa and vāruka are similar, yet they are beneficial for breaking up the stool.
Ripe kūṣmāṇḍa is alkaline, sweet and sour, and light.
Once the urine and feces have been eliminated, it [the regimen] removes all the *doṣas*.

In that regard, although the qualities of alleviating pitta and increasing kapha have been mentioned, they should be understood here as applying to *sannipāta* where pitta is predominant or where kapha is predominant. Kelūṭa, kadamba, nadīmāṣaka, and ainduka are said to be clear (*viśada*), heavy (*guru*), cold (*śīta*), and highly obstructive to the channels (*abhiṣyandi*).
Blue lotuses and astringent decoctions alleviate *rakta-pitta* (hemorrhagic disorders).
Likewise, *tālapralamba* (the hanging fruit of the palmyra palm) removes pain from chest wounds. Dates and the grain of the palmyra palm cure *rakta-pitta* and consumption (*kṣaya*).
Tarūṭa, bisa, śālūka, krauñcādana,
kaśeruka, śṛṅgāṭaka, and aṅkaloḍya are heavy, constipating, and cold.
The stalks of the kumuda and utpala lotuses, along with their flowers and fruits, are likewise considered [to have these same properties].
Cold, sweet, and astringent, they aggravate phlegm and wind;
the astringent variety is known to cause slight constipation and to alleviate hemorrhaging and bile disorders.
The seed of the lotus (*pauṣkara*), however, is sweet in both its taste and its post-digestive effect.

Muñjātaka is mild, cold, heavy, unctuous, satiating, and nourishing; it pacifies vāta and pitta, is sweet, highly aphrodisiac, vitalizing, bulk-promoting, and beneficial for the throat, being especially recommended for rejuvenation (rasāyana). Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.119–120.
The root of vidārī is strengthening, diuretic, sweet, and cooling.
The root of amlikā is considered beneficial for disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids;
it is light, not excessively hot, subdues kapha and vāta, is constipating, and is recommended in cases of alcoholism (madātyaya).
The mustard leaf (*sārṣapa-śāka*) is said to aggravate the three *doṣas* and cause the binding of feces and urine.
Likewise, the red-stalked variety (*rakta-nāla*) is especially dry and sour.
One should know that the elephant-yam (*piṇḍāluka*) is similar, being a tuber and pleasant to the palate.
With the exception of the *sarpacchattra* (snake-umbrella), there are many other varieties of mushrooms;
they are cooling, cause nasal catarrh (*pīnasa*), and are sweet and heavy.
This is the fourth group of vegetables (*śākavarga*), which consists of leaves, tubers, and fruits.

The phrase "based on leaves, stalks, and fruits" indicates that, by way of prominence, the vegetable group should also be understood as being based on flowers and other parts.
[Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.125] It cures thirst, burning sensations, fever, dyspnea, hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta),
chest wounds, consumption, wind-pitta disorders, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), hoarseness of voice, and alcoholism.
The grape (*mṛdvīkā*) quickly removes a bitter taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, and cough;
it is nourishing, aphrodisiac, sweet, unctuous, and cold.
The date palm fruit (*kharjūra*) is sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, heavy, and cold.

It is beneficial in cases of wasting, injury, and burning, as well as for disorders of vāta and pitta. The *tarpaṇa* (satisfying) and *bṛṃhaṇa* (nourishing) fruits—namely *phalgu*, *parūṣaka*, and *madhūka*—are heavy, cause flatulence, and are cold; they are recommended for disorders of vāta and pitta.
The *āmrātaka* fruit is sweet, nourishing, strengthening, satiating, and heavy;
it is unctuous, increases *kapha*, is cold, aphrodisiac, and digests slowly by causing flatulence.
Cooked *tāla* grains and *nārikela* fruits are likewise [sweet and nourishing].
[The fruit] is nourishing, unctuous, cooling, strengthening, and sweet.
The *bhavya* fruit is sweet, sour, and astringent; it causes constipation, is heavy and cooling, increases *pitta* and *kapha*, is astringent, and cleanses the mouth.
Amla, parūṣaka, grapes, jujubes, and āruka fruits,
as well as karkandhu and nikuca, aggravate pitta and śleṣman. When fully ripe, they are not excessively hot, are heavy, predominantly sweet, and pleasant to the mouth.
Āruka is nourishing, digests quickly, and does not excessively increase the *doṣas*.
Pigeon meat (*pārāvata*) is known to be of two kinds—cold and hot—and sweet and sour; it is heavy, suppresses the appetite, and destroys excessive digestive fire.
The fruit of the *kāśmarya* is said to have qualities only slightly inferior to those of the *bhavya*.
Likewise, the sour *tūda* has qualities only slightly inferior to those of the *parūṣaka*.
The *ṭaṅka* is astringent and sweet, increases *vāta*, and is heavy and cold.
Unripe *kapittha* destroys the throat, is anti-toxic, constipating, and increases *vāta*.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.136) Because it is sweet, sour, and astringent, and because of its fragrance, the ripe fruit stimulates the appetite;
it also subdues the *doṣas*, is anti-toxic, constipating, and though heavy, is beneficial. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.137)

The ripe *bilva* fruit is difficult to digest, aggravates the *doṣas*, and produces putrid wind (*pūtimāruta*). It is unctuous, hot, and sharp. When young, it stimulates digestion and overcomes *kapha* and *vāta*. When fully grown, it causes *rakta-pitta* and increases *pitta*.
Ripe mango overcomes wind (vāyu) and bestows flesh, semen, and strength.
The rose-apple (jāmbava) is predominantly astringent and sweet, heavy, constipating, and cold;
it destroys phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta), is absorbent (grāhi), and is an excellent producer of wind.
The jujube fruit (badara) is sweet, unctuous, laxative, and subdues vāta and pitta;
when dried, it destroys kapha and vāta and is not contraindicated in cases of pitta.
The fruit of the simbitikā is astringent-sweet, cooling, and constipating.
Gāṅgerukī, karīra, bimbī, todana,
and dhanvana are sweet, slightly astringent, cooling, and alleviate pitta and kapha.
So too are ripe jackfruit (panasa), plantain (moca), and rājādana fruits.
The fruit of the *lavalī* is sweet, slightly astringent, unctuous, cold, and heavy;
due to its astringent clarity and fragrance, it stimulates the appetite,
is suitable for use as a side dish (*avadāṃśa*), is pleasing to the heart, and increases *vāta*.
Nīpa, śatāhvaka, pīlu, tṛṇaśūnya,
and vikaṅkata destroy the doṣas and remove poison.
Aiṅguda is bitter and sweet, unctuous and hot, and it conquers kapha and vāta.
Tinduka destroys kapha and pitta; it is astringent, sweet, and light.
One should know that in the āmalaka all tastes are present except for salt.
It is dry, sweet, and astringent, and is the best remedy for kapha and pitta.
The vibhītaka fruit destroys the humors (doṣas) arising from the lymph-chyle, blood, flesh, and fat;
it cures hoarseness of voice, excessive secretion of phlegm, and diseases of pitta.
It is sour, astringent, and sweet, subdues vāta, is constipating, and stimulates digestion.
The unctuous and hot pomegranate is pleasing to the heart and antagonistic to *kapha* and *pitta*.
However, that pomegranate which is dry and sour aggravates *pitta* and *vāyu*.
Among these, the first type of pomegranate is the best; it is sweet and subdues *pitta*.
Vṛkṣāmla is astringent, dry, and hot; it is recommended for disorders of vāta and kapha.
The ripe fruit of amlikā is similar in its qualities to that, with only slight differences. Amlavetasa, however, possesses those same qualities but is also laxative.

It is prescribed for all conditions arising from Vāta and Kapha: in cases of colic, anorexia, constipation, weak digestion, intoxication, hiccup, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and diseases of the feces. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.153)
The filaments of the *mātuluṅga* are light; the rest [of the fruit] is otherwise.
Devoid of its bark, *karcūra* is appetizing, digestive, cordial, and fragrant;
it destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, and is beneficial for asthma, hiccup, and hemorrhoids.
The fruit of the *nāgaraṅga* is sweet and slightly sour, pleasant to the heart, and an appetizer; it is heavy to digest, pacifies *vāta*, and is heavy [in its action].
*Vātāma*, *abhiṣuka*, *akṣoṭa*, *mukūlaka*, and *nikocaka* [are also mentioned].
The urumāṇa fruits are heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet;
they bestow strength, subdue vāta, promote corpulence, act as aphrodisiacs, and increase kapha and pitta.
One should know that the priyāla fruit is similar to these in its qualities, except for its heat.
The fruit of the *śleṣmātaka* increases phlegm, is sweet, cold, and heavy.
The fruit of the *aṅkoṭa* increases phlegm, is heavy, causes constipation, and subdues the digestive fire (*agni*).
The fruit of the *śamī* is heavy, hot, sweet, dry, and destroys the hair.
The *kārañja* fruit causes constipation and is not antagonistic to *vāta* and *kapha*.
One should know that *āmrapātaka*, *dantaśaṭha*, sour *karamardaka*,
and *airāvataka* produce *rakta-pitta*.

One should know that the fruit of the *parpaṭakī* is wind-alleviating, digestive, pungent, and bitter; it increases wind and subdues phlegm and bile. The fruit of the *akṣikī* is sour, subdues bile and phlegm, and increases wind.
The fruits of the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and nyagrodha are sweet, sour in their post-digestive transformation (pāka), and they pacify pitta and śleṣman;
they are astringent, sweet, and sour, increase vāta, and are heavy.
The stone of the *bhallātaka* is like fire, while its flesh is sweet and cooling.
This fifth group of fruits has been described as generally useful. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.165) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

It is "equal to fire" because it generates a bursting sensation and other such effects.
Ginger is appetizing, digestive, aphrodisiac, and a universal medicine;
its juice is prescribed for obstructions caused by wind and phlegm. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.166)
The jambīra fruit is brightening, illuminating, sharp, fragrant, and a cleanser of the mouth;
it destroys phlegm and wind, kills worms, and digests food.
The young fruit removes the *doṣas*, while the mature fruit aggravates all three *doṣas* and alleviates wind.
Radish that has been prepared with fats and then dried conquers *kapha* and *vāta*.
It destroys hiccup, cough, poison, dyspnea, and pain in the flanks.
*Surasa* increases *pitta*, destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, and removes foul odors.
Yavānī, arjaka, śigru, śāleya,
and mṛṣṭaka are pleasant to the heart and palatable, yet they aggravate pitta.
Gaṇḍīra, jalapippalī, tumbaru, and śṛṅgaverikā [are likewise].
Sharp, hot, pungent, and dry substances remove phlegm and wind.
Bhūstṛṇa is destructive to virility, pungent, dry, and hot, and it cleanses the mouth.
Kharāhvā destroys phlegm and wind, and it alleviates diseases of the bladder and pain.
Dhānyaka, ajagandhā, and sumukha are brightening (rocanā) agents;
they are fragrant, not excessively pungent, and do not aggravate the bodily humors (doṣas).
Gṛñjanaka is astringent, sharp, and beneficial for wind (vāta), phlegm (śleṣman), and hemorrhoids (arśas).
One should employ it for fomentation and as food for those who do not have pitta.
Onions increase kapha and subdue vāta, but they do not pacify pitta;
they are suitable for dietary use, strengthening, heavy, aphrodisiac, and appetizing.

Garlic destroys worms, skin diseases, and leucoderma; it subdues wind (vāta), destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), is unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, pungent, and heavy. The dried fruits of these [plants] likewise destroy kapha and vāta.
And this sixth section on green vegetables (*harita*) is concluded.
[Commentary from the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

Regarding green vegetables such as ginger (*ārdraka*) and others, because they are consumed before and after meals without undergoing cooking by fire like fruits, they are discussed immediately after the fruits; however, their mention after the fruits is for the sake of [logical] sequence.]
Because green [ginger] does not provide satiety;

(1) the qualification "fresh" (*ārdraka*) is for the purpose of excluding dried ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and the qualities of dried ginger will be discussed in the section on substances associated with food.
(2) *Jambīra* is a variety of *parṇāsa*; the fruit of the *jambīra* is fragrant. (3)
"Raw radish removes the *doṣas*" means that in its young state, when its flavor is unmanifest, it removes the three *doṣas*.

For there is a statement from another treatise: "As long as radishes are newly sprouted and possess unmanifest flavors, they are light, digestive stimulants, and removers of *pitta*, *vāyu*, and *kapha*.
"Aged [radish] aggravates the three *doṣas*" refers to that same radish when fully grown; this is stated with reference to this very stage of the radish.

Regarding the unsuitability of bulbs as food, [the term] "most excellent" refers to their quality as a remover of wind (*māruta*), while "prepared with unctuous substances" applies generally to both the young and the old.

(6) Since it will be stated later in the text that "these dried ones destroy phlegm and wind," and the capacity of the dried variety to counteract phlegm and wind is already established, this repetition is for the purpose of attaining excellence.
(7) "Destroying putrid odor" means it removes the foul smell of the body as well as that of meat used as a condiment. (8)

*Arjaka* is *śvetaparṇāsa*. *Śigru* is *viṭapa-śobhāñjana*. *Śāleya* is the root of *cāṇakya*, well-known in Maru; or rather, it is called *śāleya*, as there is a saying well-known among the *pāṭakas*: "Indeed, they call the root of *cāṇakya* by the name *śāleya* in the context of theft."
*Mṛṣṭaka* is black mustard (*rājikā*).

*Gaṇḍīra* is of two kinds: red and white. Of these, the red one is listed in the group of pungent herbs (*kaṭu*) because of its pungency; however, the white variety that grows in water is listed in the group of leafy vegetables (*śāka*). Thus, there is no single item being listed in two groups.

Jalapippalī is that which has the form of long pepper (pippalī) in water. 12. Śṛṅgaverī is gojihvikā, or it has the appearance of ginger (ārdraka); it is called śṛṅgaverī because its shape is like that of ginger (śṛṅgavera), as it is said:
"They call tumburu those things that have the same appearance as kustumburu. 13–14.
Bhūstṛṇa is gandhatṛṇa;
kharāhvā is black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka);
ajagandhā is wild yavānī.

Sumukha is a variety of *parṇāsa*. (18) This refers to the qualities of coriander (*dhānyaka*) and other such items when fresh; however, for their dried forms, he will describe the qualities later in the section on foodstuffs (*āhārayogigaṇa*) beginning with "black cumin (*kāravī*), caraway (*kuñcikā*)," and so forth. (19) Gṛñjanaka is simply an onion (*palāṇḍu*) characterized by small stalks and leaves. (20)
"These" refers to those mentioned in the section on the green group (haritavarga).

[21] Although by the words "dried" and so forth the qualities of dried ginger and other such items are already stated, they are mentioned again for the purpose of describing their specific additional qualities; since this will occur in the section on combinations of foods (āhārasaṃyogivarga), there is no redundancy. [22]
Carakasaṃhitā,
Sūtrasthāna,
Chapter 28: [On Various Foods and Drinks] (Vividhāśitapītīya)
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on various types of food and drink.
Thus said the venerable Ātreya.

In the preceding chapter, it was stated that "food is the life-force" (*annaṃ prāṇāḥ*). This chapter, titled "The Various Things Eaten and Drunk" (*vividhāśitapītīya*), is taught for the purpose of explaining the manner in which food becomes the cause of the life-force. [1] This title, too, is based on its meaning. [2] The various things eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed, when beneficial to a living being, are [transformed] by the power kindled by the internal fire through their respective heat (*uṣman*).

When properly digested at the appropriate time, it brings about the maturation of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) without causing them to become unstable; it endows the body solely with nourishment, strength, complexion, happiness, and longevity, and invigorates the bodily constituents.
For the constituents, being nourished by their own respective foods, follow their natural state.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*]:
"Vividha" (various), etc.

By the word "vividha," he shows the internal subdivisions of the [categories] beginning with food (*aśita*). Among those beginning with food, whichever is most commonly used has been mentioned first. 2.
The statement "for the benefit of the living being" is made because that which is unwholesome, such as food and so forth, lacks the capacity to produce strength, complexion, and other such qualities.

(3) By the phrase "by one whose strength is kindled by the internal fire," it is meant: by one whose strength is stimulated by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) within. (4) Regarding the expression "by its own heat": the heat belonging to the ingested substances such as earth and so forth—which takes the form of the terrestrial fire and so on—is meant; for it is said: "There are five heats—earthy, watery, fiery, airy, and ethereal. (5)
For indeed, they cook their respective five qualities of food, such as the earth-element and so forth.
(6) "Being properly digested" refers to what has been eaten and so on.

(7) Or rather, "by its own heat" means that the food which has been eaten and so on is being properly digested by whichever heat belongs to blood and the other constituents—that is, by the fire of the constituent (*dhātu-agni*).

When that which has attained the state of *rasa* reaches the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) such as blood, it is then cooked by the very heat of the blood and other constituents; thus being digested, the food and so forth joins, invigorates, and increases the body through accumulation and the like—this is the construction [of the sentence].
To the question "Of what kind of body?", he says: "Like time," and so forth.

Just as time is non-abiding by virtue of its constant movement, so too is that body in which the maturation (*pāka*) of all the *dhātus* is non-abiding and uninterrupted. By this, he demonstrates that it is logical for a body—whose *dhātus* are constantly being depleted by the digestion of its own internal fire (*svāgni*)—to undergo processes such as nourishment through food and drink. For if the body were not subject to depletion through digestion, then growth and other such processes would be established spontaneously.
The sense is: what would eating and so forth accomplish?

Or rather, "like time" is a qualifier for eating and so forth; therefore, the meaning is "eating and so forth performed at the prescribed time," because eating at an improper time does not produce accumulation and other such results. Likewise, "the digestion of all the *dhātus* being unsettled" is also a qualifier for eating and so forth; by this, it means [a state] where [the digestion] is unsettled among all the *dhātus*.

"That whose digestion [has occurred] regarding what was eaten and so forth is thus. By this, he shows that when the essence of what was eaten and so forth has been obstructed in any given element (*dhātu*), there is no further accumulation and so on due to the cessation of its digestion. (12) Furthermore, this explanation is not very elegant; since this meaning is already obtained by the qualification of the body itself through the term "unimpaired" and so forth, the repeated application of a qualification to the body is untenable. (13)

"Unimpaired," and so forth: that [body] in which the heat (*ūṣman*), the winds (*māruta*), and the channels (*srotas*) of all the *dhātus* are unimpaired is described as such. For when even a single digestive fire (*pācakāgni*) among the *dhātus* is impaired, or when the wind (*māruta*)—which nourishes the *dhātus* and carries the nutrient juices (*rasa*) in the form of *vyāna*—is impaired somewhere, or when a channel carrying the nutrient juices that nourish the *dhātus* is impaired, then [the food] eaten and so forth...
The meaning is that because [the food] does not cause the elements (*dhātu*) to increase, it does not perform the function of nourishment and so forth.

(14) "Only" (*kevalam*) means either the entire body, or else "only" means free from demerit (*adharma*); for when the body is joined with demerit, what is eaten and so forth becomes fruitless. (15) Now, one might object: since the elements existing in their natural state undergo nourishment and so forth by themselves, what is accomplished by what is eaten and so forth? To this he says: "For the elements... and so forth. (16)

Those for whom the elements (*dhātu*) are the nourishment are called "element-nourished" (*dhātvāhārāḥ*). The meaning is that the elements—such as the *rasa* and so forth—which are constantly being consumed, maintain their supreme state of health only when they exist as the nourishment of the elements produced by eating and so forth, and not otherwise.
In that process, the *rasa* known as the essence of food (*āhāraprasāda*) and the waste product known as *kiṭṭa* (excrement) are produced.

From the *kiṭṭa*, sweat, feces, wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), and the impurities of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, hair-follicles, and the genitals, as well as the body parts such as the hair of the head, beard, body hair, and nails, are nourished.

From the essence of food (*āhārarasa*), they nourish the plasma, blood, muscle, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and vitality (*ojas*); the substances of the five sense organs known as the pure elements (*dhātuprasāda*); and the bodily parts such as the ligaments, joints, and mucous secretions.

All these constituents—both those called impurities (*mala*) and those called pure elements (*prasāda*)—nourished by the essence and the waste products, maintain their own respective proportions according to the age and body.
Thus, when the essence and the waste products remain within their own measures, they maintain the equilibrium of the constituents (*dhātusāmya*) for one whose body has balanced constituents.

From the perspective of its causal function (*nimitta*), however, rasa produces equilibrium for the sake of health through the increase and decrease of the elements known as *prasāda* (pure essence), which have been diminished or increased by food—the root cause of these fluctuations—and it likewise produces waste (*kiṭṭa*) for the excretions.

In this same way, the excretions (*mala*), when they exceed their own proper measure, are observed to bring about equilibrium among the body's elements when they are expelled and when they are treated with alternating qualities of cold and heat.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.4) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
Regarding that which is the nutriment of the elements, he says "therein," and so forth. 1.
"Therein" refers to the ingested food and the like. 2. The grammatical connection is: "nutriment and waste are produced. 3.
That which is called *āhāraprasāda* (the essence of food) is thus *prasāda*, meaning the essential part.
*Kiṭṭa* is the non-essential portion.

From *kiṭṭa*—that is, from the portion consisting of waste—arise urine and feces; and from the *rasa* being digested, the impurity (*mala*) arises as phlegm (*kapha*), and so forth, as will be explained in the chapter on the *grahaṇī*.
For he will state what must be followed:
"The dregs of food are feces and urine; those of the nutrient essence (rasa) are phlegm; of blood, bile; of flesh, its own excrement; and of fat, sweat. (6)
There may be waste from hair, body hair, and bone; oil from marrow; and excrement and skin from the eyes.
(7) By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the oil of the eyes and so forth are to be understood. (8)
And although wind is indeed perceived even from fasting, it nevertheless certainly arises from the impure portion of food such as dry matter and dregs;

thus, the production of wind from dregs is entirely logical. Nor is there a fixed rule that it arises only from waste products, since wind and other humors are also present due to physical exercise, immersion in water, and so forth.
The male organ is the sign of procreation.
[Regarding] that which is nourished by the nutrient essence (*rasa*), he says "they nourish," and so forth.
The five material substances of the sense organs are earth and the other elements, which are the causes of the sense organs such as the nose and the rest.
"Those called the clarity of the elements" indicates that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are initiated by the extremely pure clarity of the elements (*dhātuprasāda*).

(13) "It binds the body" refers to the bodily bond (*śarīrabandha*), consisting of tendons, veins, and so forth. (14) By the inclusion of "and so forth," the inclusion of menses, breast milk, and other such substances is intended. (15)

Regarding this, some say that from the essence of food (*āhārarasa*), there is the nourishment of blood and the other constituents; namely, that the essence transforms into the form of blood, blood into the form of flesh, and so on, with each subsequent constituent transforming into the form of the next.

(16) Furthermore, regarding this position as well, some say that just as curd is produced entirely from milk, so too the entire essence becomes blood, and likewise blood and the others become the form of flesh and the rest.

Others, however, say that the nourishment of the tissues (*dhātu*) by the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) follows the analogy of water from a field-channel: the nutrient fluid produced there from food, having reached the tissue-fluid (*rasa-dhātu*), increases that tissue-fluid by a certain portion; and another mass of nutrient fluid, having reached that place, becomes like blood because it possesses the smell and color of blood, and thus [increases] the tissue-form by a certain portion equal to blood.

The remaining portion nourishes the blood, and that [blood] in turn passes into the flesh; in this regard, the arrangement is the same as for the blood. This applies likewise to the fat and the other [dhātus].
For this very reason, this text has its primary meaning [in this context], as it says:
"From rasa comes blood, from that comes flesh, from flesh comes fat, and from that, bone."
"From bone comes marrow; from that, semen; and from semen, the embryo is produced from the pure essence.

(19) Thus it is also stated in the *Hārīta*: "The nutrient fluid (*rasa*), circulating within seven days, undergoes a transformation of color according to the sequence of days—resembling white, pigeon-grey, green, yellow, lotus-colored, kiṃśuka-flower colored, and lac-dye colored—and through the influence of the heat of bile (*pitta*), it attains the state of blood (*śoṇita*)."

It occurs thus; likewise it is stated in the *Suśruta* as well: "That aqueous rasa indeed remains for three thousand and fifteen *kalās* in each constituent element (*dhātu*); in this manner, within a month, the rasa becomes semen.

Others, however, say that according to the maxim of the pigeon in the threshing floor, this essence of food (*annarasa*), having entered the respective channels of the constituents, [transforms] the rasa and the others.
It nourishes [the tissue], yet the portion of rasa that nourishes this specific tissue does not even experience a connection with other tissues.

The channels (*srotas*) that nourish rasa and the other elements become progressively narrower and longer; therefore, by virtue of traveling through the path of rasa, the portion of rasa that nourishes rasa nourishes only the rasa. In this way, after the time of nourishing the rasa, the portion of rasa that nourishes blood [nourishes the blood].

Just as [the nutrient essence] nourishes blood, so too, after the period of nourishing the blood, the portion of the essence that nourishes flesh nourishes the flesh because it travels through distant and subtle channels; this should be understood to apply likewise to the nourishment of fat and the other tissues.

Therefore, the meaning of the statement "from essence comes blood, from that flesh," and so forth, is that blood is produced after the period of the nourishment of the essence, and likewise, flesh is produced after the period of the nourishment of the blood.
And so forth.
(22) In this same manner, the statements of Suśruta and Harīta are also to be explained.

(23) Furthermore, regarding what will be stated in the section on *rājayakṣman*—that blood, because its path is obstructed, does not reach the muscles and other tissues—that refers to the blood circulating within the heart (*hṛdayacāri-śoṇita*), and not to the nourishing blood (*poṣaka-śoṇita*).

Furthermore, in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma-pakṣa*), semen is produced only after a very long time through the gradual process of the aphrodisiac substance assuming the form of blood and so forth;

yet substances such as milk are observed to be aphrodisiacs immediately. However, in the "crow-at-the-grain-field" model (*khalekapota-pakṣa*), it is logical that the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) produced by the aphrodisiac, through its specific power (*prabhāva*), becomes connected with the semen very quickly and thereby nourishes it. This same logic applies when there is a corruption of the nutrient fluid (*rasa-duṣṭi*) in the theory of transformation.

There would be a corruption of all the blood and other elements produced from that [corrupted] birth, because they are born from a corrupted cause. However, according to the "crow-on-the-threshing-floor" analogy, only that portion of the nutrient-fluid (*rasa*) which nourishes a particular tissue becomes corrupted; the others do not, because their causes are not corrupted. Likewise, when there is an increase in fat (*medas*), one might expect the bone (*asthi*) also to become abundant due to its being a substantial cause; yet, in reality, we observe an abundance of fat.

"The depletion of other constituents (*dhātu*) and the statement that 'in a person with excess fat (*medasvin*), only the fat increases and not the other constituents'—such [arguments] constitute the refutation of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*).

Furthermore, among these positions, the theory of the transformation of the entire self (*sarvātmapariṇāmavāda*) is indeed contradictory; for if the entire self were to transform, the body would die from becoming sapless after only three or four fasts, whereas [according to the opponent], in the case of a month-long fast, only..."
The body would consist of semen alone. However,

the analogy of the irrigation channel in a field (*kedārīkulyā-nyāya*) possesses equal force to the analogy of the sparrows in the threshing floor (*khalekapota-nyāya*), because regarding the potency of aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya-prabhāva*), it is stated that even according to the irrigation channel analogy, by virtue of its specific potency (*prabhāva*) alone, [the substance] quickly reaches the blood and other tissues and [produces] semen.

It will produce virility even in the case of a "crow-on-the-threshing-floor" [which is a weak seed], because of its power. As for the claim that the vitiation of blood occurs when the *rasa* (nutritive fluid) is vitiated—that is not so; because the portion of *rasa* that nourishes the part of blood which has become a *dhātu* (tissue element) remains unvitiated. This is the same as the previous argument.
For even in this view, not all *rasa* turns into blood in the form of a *dhātu*; rather, only a certain portion becomes similar to blood.
The remaining portion, however, is called blood because it has reached the site of blood and because its color and other qualities are somewhat similar to those of blood.

By this same logic, the increase of bone upon the increase of fat is also refuted; for bone is not nourished by fat, but rather by the nutrient essence (*rasa*) located in the site of fat, which resembles fat. (30)

Thus, since these two positions are equally respected by the great multitude and follow the same logic, neither is determined as certain; therefore, the relative strength or weakness of the positions is not established here through the power of the intellect, and we conclude that there is no contradiction regarding the matter at hand.

Now, one might ask: "By saying that the essence of food (*āhāra-rasa*) and so forth nourish [the body], you have accepted that the production of the essence of food from the essence of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-rasa*) is a distinct process.
Consequently, why have you not stated what its location is or what its measure is? It is replied: because its excellence or deficiency does not correspond to the excellence or deficiency of the food.
In this manner, because there is no fixed measure for such increase or decrease, their location is indeed within the vessels (*dhamanī*).

(32) As for the nourishing nutrient-essence (*poṣaka-āhāra-rasa*), it is not grasped as a separate entity from the constituent elements (*dhātu*) such as *rasa* and the rest, because it is already included by the very term "nutrient-essence" (*rasa*) since it exists in the form of the cause of *rasa* and the other elements.

(33) Although *ojas* here consists of the essence of the seven constituent elements and is thus obtained by the very mention of those elements, nevertheless, by virtue of its function as the sustainer of life, [it is mentioned separately].

However, for those who maintain that *ojas* is produced from *śukra* (semen) and thus read it separately, they would have to apply the principle of extension (*atideśa*) to the position that *ojas* is the eighth constituent (*dhātu*), as he will state later: "That which is the supreme radiance (*tejas*) among the constituents beginning with *rasa* and ending with *śukra* is indeed *ojas*.
(34) He concludes the section on the conformity to the primary nature (*prakṛti*) of the tissues and wastes whose nourishment has been explained, starting with the words "All these... (35).

It has been stated that even those called wastes (*mala*), such as sweat, urine, and so forth, become *dhātus* because they sustain the body when they remain within their own proper measures; thus it is said, "the *dhātus* are also called wastes. Regarding the phrase "according to age and body": this means nourishing the *dhātus* according to whatever measure they possess at a particular age, such as childhood and so on, and likewise according to whatever measure the *dhātus* possess in a particular body, whether by nature it is tall, short, thin, or stout.
The construction is: "they nourish such [a state].
(37) Regarding the passage beginning with "evam" (thus), "established in their own means of valid cognition" (*svapramāṇāvasthitau*) means neither exceeding nor falling short.

(38) Regarding "of the substratum" (*āśrayasya*), which refers to the body: "fully ripened," they subsequently reach the entire substratum through the channels (*dhamanī*); the meaning is that they pervade the whole body. (39)
"Of the element of equilibrium" (samadhātu) refers to that which possesses an equal flavor (*samarasa*) and so forth, as well as equal sweat, urine, and so forth.
"By way of signs" (*nimittataḥ*), etc.:
by this phrase "by way of signs," he refutes the notions of decrease and increase regarding the form of omens (*ariṣṭa*) which are actually signless (*animitta*).

"By means of increase and decrease, which are rooted in food"—this means, respectively, by those [states] produced from increased or diminished food. By this, the meaning is that the *rasa* (nutrient essence), through the increase or decrease caused by specific types of food, brings about equilibrium (*sāmya*).

Although the equilibrium of the *dhātus* (constituent elements) is already established as being health (*ārogya*), the fact that he says "for the sake of health" (*ārogyāya*) serves to exclude an equilibrium resulting from either the depletion or the excessive increase of the natural *dhātus*, because such an equilibrium is itself a cause of disease.

"Kitta (waste) is likewise for the impurities. Just as the nutrient essence (*rasa*) is, so too does kitta, through the aforementioned sequence of the essence, bring about the equilibrium of the impurities for the sake of health.
(45) Regarding another treatment for increased impurities, he says "svamāna" and so forth.

(46) "Emission" (*utsarga*) means external discharge; there is a purification in the form of their emission as taught in the scriptures. Or, they are called "emissive" (*utsargin*) because they carry out emission. (47)
He states another treatment for chronic impurities (malas) in the verse beginning with "cold and hot" (śītoṣṇa), etc.

(48). "Paryaya" means reversal; thus, the meaning is by means of qualities opposite to cold and hot. Therefore, the therapeutic application consists of heat for an impurity arising from cold, and likewise cold for one arising from heat. (49) Furthermore, the word "etc. (ādi) is used here in an elliptical sense; by this, qualities opposite to oily (snigdha), dry (rūkṣa), and so forth are also included. (50)

Alternatively, it should be understood that there are qualities of transformation (*paryaya-guṇa*) and qualities of duality (*dvandva-guṇa*), such as unctuousness, dryness, softness, sharpness, and so forth; and [the treatment] consists of being administered by means of these according to what is appropriate.
By this, the threefold therapeutic intervention for increased *malas*—consisting of avoidance of the cause (*nidāna-varjana*), purification (*śodhana*), and pacification (*śamana*)—is stated.
Among these, avoidance of the cause consists of the abandonment of food that increases the *malas* and the consumption of food that results in little *mala*.
Alternatively, purification is stated by the phrase "of those who have undergone evacuation," and pacification is stated by the passage beginning with "cold, heat," and so forth.
Now, the channels are the pathways for those elements known as impurities (*mala*) and pure essences (*prasāda*);
they fill their respective elements according to their specific divisions.
Thus, this body originates from what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed;
and diseases arise in this body from that which is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed.
However, it is the specific application of what is beneficial or harmful that produces the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome herein.

Regarding the term *ayanamukhāni*: they are both *ayanāni* (courses) and *mukhāni* (gateways), thus "courses and gateways. Here, *ayanāni* refers to the paths by which [the impurities] come (*āyānti anena*), while *mukhāni* refers to those through which they enter. By this it is meant that whatever is the course (*ayana*) of the impurities and the tissues (*dhātus*), that very thing is the gateway of entry (*praveśamukha*).
It is said that there is no entry by another [way] nor departure by another.
(1) Regarding the *rasas* and so forth, their respective channels (*srota*) are both the openings (*mukha*) and the pathways (*ayana*).
(2) Alternatively, "openings of the pathway" (*ayanamukha*) refers to the paths of the pathway (*ayana*); the meaning is "the paths of movement. (3)

And those channels, filled with impurities and clarity, nourish the *dhātus* according to their respective [requirements]. (4) "According to their distribution" means that each *dhatu* is filled by its own specific measure; they nourish only to such a measure, neither more nor less—this is the meaning. (5) Furthermore, this is the function of those [channels] abiding in their natural state; however, it should be understood that for those in a state of disorder, there is indeed the production of *dhātus* that are either deficient or excessive. (6)
And it is said elsewhere: "The constituent element (dhātu) is nourished by its own corresponding stream.
[Thus he] concludes with "in this way," and so forth. [One may ask:
how is it that from food and the like there arises both the body and the disease that harms it, which are contradictory? To this he says: "beneficial and non-beneficial," and so forth.

A specific type of food and so forth that is beneficial in nature produces a specific wholesome result, whereas a specific type of food and so forth that is harmful in nature produces a specific unwholesome result; therefore, the sense is that a contradictory effect does not arise from a cause of a single uniform nature.
[10] To the Blessed One Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "For indeed, O Blessed One, we see things designated as beneficial..."

Even among those who consume food, some are diseased and others are healthy; likewise, there are those designated as having consumed what is unwholesome. When this is observed, how can we perceive the distinction between the auspicious and the inauspicious, which consists of the specific difference in the utilization of the wholesome and the unwholesome?
"For it is observed, O Blessed One," and so forth; the connection is that those who consume [food] as prescribed by such designations are both diseased and free from disease.
[1] "Consisting of specific qualities" means arising from specific qualities.
[2] The Blessed Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, diseases caused by that do not arise for those who consume unwholesome food."

Furthermore, the fear of all diseases is not overcome merely by the consumption of wholesome food; for there are other types of disease even apart from the consumption of unwholesome food, namely: seasonal irregularity (*kālaviparyaya*), intellectual error (*prajñāparādha*), and unwholesome sound, touch, form, taste, and smell (*asātmya*).
These types of disease afflict a person with misfortune even if they consume tastes correctly; therefore, those who consume wholesome food are also seen to be afflicted by disease.
Furthermore, for those who consume unwholesome food, an improper practice does not immediately become harmful due to specific causes.
For not all unwholesome things possess equal defects, nor do all defects have equal strength, nor are all bodies equally capable of withstanding disease.
Indeed, that very same unwholesome thing becomes even more unwholesome through its association with place and time, and through excessive application of potency and quantity.

That very [disease] becomes most difficult to treat and most rapid in its action when it arises from a combination of doshas, has a contradictory onset, has spread deeply, has been present for a long time, originates in the seats of life, strikes the vital points (marmans),

and occurs in bodies that are excessively obese or excessively emaciated, where the flesh, blood, and bones are ill-positioned, which are weak, nourished by unwholesome food, characterized by little food intake and little strength; such bodies are unable to withstand disease, whereas those with the opposite qualities are able to withstand it.

And from these very factors— unwholesome diet, the specific humors (*doṣas*), and the particularities of the body— diseases arise that are either mild or severe, and either quick to manifest or slow to develop.
Thus, O Agniveśa, the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*, when provoked in specific locations, bring about specific diseases.
"Caused by that" means caused by unwholesome food.
"Not only" refers to others.
"The natures of diseases" means the causes of disease.
"Of those who consume unwholesome food," and so forth.

(4) "By reason of" means due to another cause or an obstruction; and that cause should be understood as being contrary to what will be stated in the upcoming text, such as "that very [food] is unwholesome.
(5) "Immediately" means at that very time. (6)

By this, he shows that unwholesome food generally acts as a cause of morbid change after a lapse of time (*kālāntara-vikārakartṛtva*) regarding the production of disease; otherwise, the word "immediately" (*sadyas*) would be redundant, because [unwholesome food] would not produce a disorder even at a later time.

"One who possesses a *doṣa*" means one who generates disease. "Improper conduct" (*apacāra*) refers to the consumption of unwholesome diet; he states the reason for what has been said in the passage beginning with "for not," etc.
"Having equal defects" means producing equal defects.

(9) "Tolerance of disease" means being opposed to the strength of the disease; that is to say, it acts as an obstacle to the arising of the disease. (10) He explains that very [concept]—unwholesomeness, the state of having equal defects, and so forth—with the words "that very," and so on. (11)

In this context, although the causes that obstruct unwholesome [regimen] should have been stated because they are the subject at hand, nevertheless, for the sake of consistency in reasoning (*samānanyāyatayā*), those factors that increase the potency of the unwholesome are now described. (12) Regarding the phrase "due to the association of place and so forth," this refers to association with a favorable place and so forth; for example, rice is unwholesome because it produces *pitta*, yet it becomes even more unwholesome through association with a marshy (*anūpa*) region, whereas in an arid (*dhanva*) region its power is diminished. Likewise, [the effect of] a favorable autumn season...

It becomes strong through combination (*yoga*), as in winter; it is weak through combination, just as that same rice-gruel is strong when mixed with curd, molasses, and so forth, but weak when mixed with honey and the like. It is strong through potency (*vīrya*), as that same substance is strong when made warm but weak when cold;
and it is powerful through excessive dosage (*pramāṇātiyoga*) but weak when the dose is deficient—these and other such principles are to be followed accordingly. // 13 //
He [the author] states that the humors possess equal strength with the words "that very humor" and so forth (verse 14).

"Of mixed origins" means one whose causes are many and combined; alternatively, "of mixed origin" means having a corresponding *dūṣya* (vitiated tissue), such as when pitta becomes difficult to treat and acts rapidly upon reaching blood as its *dūṣya*. (Verse 15)

An example of contradictory treatment (*viruddhopakrama*) is as follows: "Pitta is the initiator of urinary disorders (*meha*); for it has been stated that all types of *pittameha* are palliable (*yāpya*) because of their contradictory treatment. Here, the contradiction of the treatment lies in this: that which removes pitta, such as sweet substances (*madhurādi*), is contrary to the fat (*medas*) which is the primary tissue (*dūṣya*) to be afflicted in *meha*, whereas pungent substances (*kaṭvādi*), which are favorable to fat, are contrary to pitta. // 16

"Deep-seated" (*gambhīrānugata*) means it has entered the deep internal elements such as the marrow; for speech is superficial, being based on the skin and flesh, whereas this [fever] is deep, being based within.

(17) "Long-lasting" (*cirasthita*) means that because it has taken root through its persistence in the body for a long time, it is difficult to cure. (18) "Arisen from the seats of the vital breaths" (*prāṇāyatanasamuttha*) means it relies upon the ten seats of the vital breaths, such as the temples (*śaṅkha*), which will be described in the following chapter. (19)

"Destroying the vital points" (*marmopaghātī*) means that which causes injury to the vital points (*marman*) such as the heart, the *kṣipra*, and the *tala*, which are distinct from the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*). (20) Since the status of being a "destroyer of vital points" already implies that it arises specifically from the seats of the vital breaths, the repeated mention of them is for the purpose of demonstrating that those [afflictions] which rely upon the vital points of the seats of the vital breaths are particularly severe. (21) "Most severe" (*kaṣṭatama*) refers to its causing manifold suffering and its being incurable. (22)

"Most swift-acting" (*kṣiprakāritama*) means most rapidly producing a transformation. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), he shows that due to the smallness of causes such as having a mixed origin (*saṃsṛṣṭayoni*), there are distinctions such as being difficult, more difficult, swift-acting, or most swift-acting; thus, when all the aforementioned causes are combined, it becomes most difficult and most swift-acting.

The "most difficult to treat" and so forth should be understood according to their respective suitability. A disorder that begins with contrary treatment is indeed difficult and does not act quickly. [Verse 24]. He describes bodies unfit for disease in the passage beginning with "and bodies," etc.
[Verse 25]. Those bodies of embodied beings whose flesh and other tissues are "un-settled" (aniviṣṭa)—meaning loose—or alternatively, "un-settled" meaning irregular—are so described. [Verse 26].

"Accumulated" means increased; the sense is that a body nourished by what is unwholesome (*asātmya*) becomes permeated with many defects. (27) "Opposite" means endowed with qualities such as not being excessively corpulent. (28) "Able to withstand disease" means those which act as obstacles to the arising of disease. (29)

And this reversal, presented with respect to the body for the sake of illustration regarding the endurance of disease, should be understood to imply that the aforementioned reversal of the strength of unwholesome factors and the reversal of the strength of the *doṣas* do not immediately cause disease. // 30

Concluding this very point by summarizing the specific characteristics of the body's weakness and strength resulting from the fault of unwholesome diet, according to their respective suitability as causes for mild or other types of diseases, he says: "And from these... and so forth. The specific characteristics are those as previously stated and their opposites. Among them, it should be understood that the characteristics opposite to those previously stated result in diseases that are mild and slow-acting, whereas the characteristics of the unwholesome diet and so forth as previously stated result in diseases that are severe and quick-acting.

In this context, in order to demonstrate the diseases that arise when the *vāta* and other *doṣas* become aggravated in specific locations such as the *rasa* (lymph/chyle) and so forth, he says "ta eva" and so on.

[Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.8] Regarding that, we shall explain in detail, exactly as they occur, those various diseases which manifest in whichever locations the *doṣas* have become aggravated within the sites beginning with *rasa*.

In that context, regarding the passage beginning with "rasa" (taste) and so forth, concerning the aggravated *doṣas*, it is not restricted such that only wind (*vāyu*), or bile (*pitta*), or phlegm (*śleṣman*), or their combinations become aggravated in the taste to produce lack of appetite (*aśraddhā*) and the rest.

Even though there is a difference among the *doṣas*, because the substratum (*āśraya*) here is non-different, lack of appetite and the other symptoms arise solely through the influence of that substratum; however, despite the difference in the *doṣas*, the specific signs of wind and the others appear specifically within the lack of appetite and the rest.

Alternatively, it should be understood that through the wind (*vāta*) and other humors residing in the *rasa*, according to their respective capacities, the causes of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) and so forth are produced; for heaviness cannot occur when the *rasa* is corrupted by wind. However, this [explanation] is not very elegant;
therefore, the former position alone is superior. [Verse 3:
Lack of faith, loss of appetite, distaste in the mouth, and insensitivity to flavors.
Nausea, heaviness, drowsiness, body ache, fever,
darkness of vision, pallor, obstruction of the channels, impotence, exhaustion, emaciation of the limbs,
loss of digestive fire, and premature wrinkles and graying hair [arise]. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.9–10)

In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, it is stated that while food that has entered the mouth is indeed swallowed even in a state of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*), the distinction from aversion (*aruci*) is that one does not swallow what has entered the mouth when there is aversion.
(1) A bad taste in the mouth (*āsya-vairasya*) is a change from the normal taste of the mouth to something else. (2)
The loss of the sense of taste is the non-perception of flavors.
Debility is the exhaustion of the limbs.
The diseases arising from the corruption of the *rasa* will be described [subsequently], as will those arising from the corruption of the blood (*rakta*).
Leucoderma, erysipelas, pustules, hemorrhagic disorders, menorrhagia,
inflammation of the anus, penis, and mouth, as well as splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, abscesses, melanaemia, jaundice, facial freckles, moles, and black spots.
Ringworm (dadru), exfoliative skin disease (carmadala), vitiligo (śvitra), scabies (pāmā), urticaria (koṭha), and circular patches (maṇḍala).
[In the Āyurvedadīpikā:

Since the mention of "leprosy" (kuṣṭha) among those diseases arising from the vitiation of blood already implies ringworm and the others, their explicit mention again is for the purpose of demonstrating their specific manifestations. 1.
Tilakālakas are shaped like sesame seeds. An aśramaṇḍala is a red circular patch. These arise from a disorder of the blood; now hear those born from a disorder of the flesh. Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.13.
Adhimāṃsa, arbuda, kaila, galaśālūka,
śuṇḍikā, pūtimāṃsa, alaji, gaṇḍa, gaṇḍamāla, and upajihvikā.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.14) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
By the word *kīla*, hemorrhoids (*arśas*) are meant here.

We shall now describe those [afflictions] based on the flesh of the *vedī* and those based on the fat, as well as the censured premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) of urinary disorders (*prameha*). (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.28.15)

In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, the "condemned premonitory symptoms of prameha" refer to such things as the mattedness of the hair and so forth, because it is these specifically that are condemned; it does not, however, refer to the bad taste or sweetness in the mouth and other such signs.

Alternatively, "condemned" refers to the eight [symptoms] mentioned in the chapter on "The Condemned" (*Ninditīya*), which pertain to those who are excessively obese, such as the decline of lifespan and so forth; their condemnation arises from their association with the condemned state of excessive obesity.

Thus, in the previous explanation, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "those which and" (*yāni ca*) functions as a restrictive particle (*niyama*), whereas in the subsequent explanation, it serves as a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*). [Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.16]: Adhesions of the teeth and bones, pain from the breaking of teeth and bones, discoloration, and defects of the hair, body hair, nails, and beard—these arise from disorders of the bones.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,
by the term "excessive bone and teeth" (*adhyasthidanta*), both excessive bone and excessive teeth are included;
"pain" (*śūla*) should be understood as specifically bone pain.
There is a spinning sensation in the joints, fainting, and likewise the vision of darkness; furthermore, there is the appearance of red, thick-based eruptions arising from the joints.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.17)
"Rug" and so forth should be understood as resulting from a disorder of the marrow (*majja*).
[1] "Arūṃṣi" refers to ulcers (*vraṇa*).
[2] From a disorder of the marrow and from a disorder of the semen (*śukra*), impotence (*klaibya*) and lack of sexual arousal (*aharṣaṇa*) arise.
Or he gives birth to one who is diseased, impotent, short-lived, or deformed;
or his embryo does not develop, but instead miscarries or is lost. For vitiated semen afflicts a man along with his wife and offspring.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, "impotence" (*klaibya*) refers to:
(1) the non-erection of the penis;
and (2) the inability to engage in sexual intercourse even when the penis is erect.

"For corrupted semen afflicts a man along with his offspring and his wife. In this context, "affliction of offspring" refers to the production of diseased or impotent offspring, while "affliction of the wife" refers to the production of miscarriages and the like.
When the humors (malas) become aggravated by relying upon the sense organs, they afflict those organs through impairment and distress. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.20)
In the passage beginning with "upaghāta" and so forth, *upaghāta* means destruction (*vināśa*), whereas *upatāpa* refers to some degree of impairment (*vaikalya*).
When vitiated, [the humors] afflict a person through the tendons, vessels, and sinews.

Through stiffness, contraction, and cramps; through knots, throbbing, and numbness; [the *āyurvedadīpikā* notes that "from the tendons" (*kaṇḍarābhyaḥ*) is used in the ablative case with the sense of the locative.]
1. *Khallī* is the contraction of the hands and feet.
2. *Granthi* is precisely a knot of the tendons and so forth.
3. [The humors], provoked by resorting to impurities, cause piercing pain, emaciation, and corruption.
The *doṣas* cause excessive retention and discharge of the *malas*.

Regarding the phrase "of the *malas*" (*malānām*) and so forth, it should be understood according to the context as "breaking, drying up, and vitiating"; therein, "breaking" (*bheda*) refers to the breaking up of feces (*purīṣa*).

Emaciation (*śoṣa*) occurs specifically through all the impurities (*mala*), whereas corruption (*pradūṣaṇa*) consists in the impairment of the natural color and other qualities by being endowed with corrupted color and so forth. [1] "Excessive retention and discharge" means excessive retention is non-functioning, while excessive discharge is over-functioning.
[2] From various kinds of unwholesome food that has been eaten, drunk, licked, or chewed...

These aforementioned transformations of human beings come to pass. A wise person, desiring their non-occurrence, should always practice wholesome regimens such as diet and so forth; thus, diseases born of those [transformations] will not arise.
For disorders born of the *rasa* (tissue fluids), lightening therapy (*laṅghana*) is the universal medicine;

for those born of blood, the physician’s remedy is described in the chapter on the purification of blood (*vidhiśoṇitika*). For disorders born of muscle (*māṃsa*), however, purification (*saṃśuddhi*), as well as surgical, caustic, and thermal procedures, are the treatments.
In the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Aṣṭāṅganinditaka*, the treatment of diseases arising from fat (*medas*) is described.
For diseases residing in the bones, the five purificatory procedures (*pañcakarma*) are the remedy,
as are enemas (*vasti*), milk, clarified butter (*sarpis*), and bitter medicinal compounds.

Medicines that are sweet and bitter, food, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, purification, and [eating] at the proper time and in the right measure are the remedies for the arousal of semen and marrow. However, the pacification of disorders arising from the sense organs will be explained in the chapter on the three vital organs (trimarmīya).

The pacification of diseases arising from the sinews and other such tissues will be explained in the section on wind disorders (*vātaroga*). In the chapter concerning the suppression of natural urges (*anegāndhāraṇa*), a compendium of treatments has been provided; furthermore, the successful management of disorders born of impurities (*malaja*) has been stated here and there.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*] Now, demonstrating the defects produced by unwholesome diet, [the author] instructs on what ought to be done with the words beginning "vividhāt" (from various...).
The word "medicine has been declared" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. 1–2.

Although it has been stated that there are "five types of enemas," the specific mention of "vasti" (enemas) is for the purpose of demonstrating the particular efficacy of an enema prepared with bitter substances.
[3] "Purification" refers to cleansing by means of emesis and other such methods.
[4] "Success" (siddhi) is said to occur "in some cases," such as in the treatment of diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and so forth. [5]
Due to physical exercise, the sharpness of heat, the non-observance of wholesome regimens,
and the rapid movement of the vital air (marut), the impurities (malās) move from the visceral cavity (koṣṭha) to the peripheral branches (śākhā).
While situated there, they sometimes linger when not further impelled.
They do not become aggravated at an improper place or time, as they wait for the appropriate cause.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.28.32) [Commentary from Āyurvedadīpikā:

Now, since the *rasa* (tastes) and other factors constitute the "branches" (*śākhā*), [the author] states the verse beginning with "physical exercise" (*vyāyāma*) to explain how the *doṣas* residing in the "trunk" (*koṣṭha*) move toward the branches. 1.28.32.

In that case, due to the agitation caused by physical exercise, the impurities (malas) leave the visceral cavity (koṣṭha) and move to the peripheral tissues (śākhā). Furthermore, the humors (doṣas), having been liquefied by the sharpness of the digestive heat (ūṣman) of the fire, move to the peripheral tissues. It is logical that when a humor increases excessively through the non-observance of wholesome regimens, the indulgence in unwholesome things, or over-indulgence, it—having increased like a flood of water—overwhelms its own site and moves to another location. // 2 //

"Because of the swiftness of the wind" means that due to the mobility of the air, it moves as if impelled by the wind; and the impelling of one wind by another is indeed logical. Otherwise, [one might ask] why the plural "impurities" (*malāḥ*) is used. Now, he explains what those situated on the branches do: "And remaining there," and so forth. (4) "Sometimes they linger" means that at times they cause a delay in the process of the disease. (5)
To the question "Why do they linger?", he says: "Not being provoked" (na samīritāḥ).

Those defects which, due to their smallness, are weak, become aggravated when provoked by another cause; likewise, those same [defects] do not arise in an improper place (*anādeśe*), meaning in a location unfavorable to them, nor at an improper time (*anakāle*), meaning at a time unfavorable to them—this is the construction.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason beginning with "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) and so on.

Because those defects are weak and depend upon further causes, they require [the assistance of] motion and so forth; by contrast, those which are more frequent and do not depend upon further causes do not require motion and so forth because of their strength.
For this very reason, it was said: "at times" (*kadācit*).
Through increase, liquefaction, digestion, and the cleansing of the openings of the channels,
as well as by the suppression of the wind (vāyu), the impurities leave the peripheral branches and enter the visceral cavity (koṣṭha). (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.28.33)
Now he explains the reason for the movement of the *doṣas* from the peripheral branches (*śākhā*) into the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*), beginning with the words "by increase" (*vṛddhyā*) and so forth.

1. "By liquefaction" (*viṣyandanāt*) means by melting; and that which has melted, due to its very fluidity, moves downward into the visceral cavity. 2. "By digestion" (*pākāt*) means that a *doṣa* which has been digested, because it is no longer bound, moves downward into the visceral cavity. 3. [The third point follows as above.]

"By purifying the openings of the channels" means by the removal of obstructions. "By the restraint of the wind" means that through the restraint of the propelling wind, it returns to its natural place, the abdomen. [5] For the non-arising of what has not yet arisen, and for the cessation of what has already arisen.
One who seeks happiness should practice that regimen for diseases which has been observed [by the wise].
All activities of all living beings are considered to be for the sake of happiness;
however, due to the distinction between knowledge and ignorance, there are activities on the right path and on the wrong path.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*: Now, he provides a summary aphorism for the remedy of all diseases, beginning with "Of those not yet born," etc. (1).
"The procedure that has been observed" refers to the entire treatise. (2)]
Now, if the activity of all living beings is for the sake of happiness, why does anyone engage in a wrong path? To this he says "jñāna" and so forth.
The point is that it is solely out of ignorance—thinking "this is a means to happiness"—that the unexamining act, and not because they intend to produce suffering.
The examining, having investigated thoroughly, pursue only what is beneficial.
But worldly people, whose selves are shrouded by passion and delusion, desire only what is pleasant.
Learning, intelligence, memory, skill, fortitude, devotion to the beneficial,
purity of speech, tranquility, and steadfastness— these attend upon the discerning man.
These qualities do not resort to that which is worldly, for it is dependent on the dust of delusion;
many physical and mental diseases arise from that as their root. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.38)

1. "Only what is beneficial" refers to that which is pure in its future consequence even if it causes suffering in the present. 2. "Only what is pleasant" refers to that which causes happiness in the present but is contrary to the future. 3. Worldly people are those who lack discernment.
He praises the examiner with the words "the sacred learning" (*śruta*) and so forth.

(4) They "resort to the examiner" means they exist within the examiner; or rather, the deities of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth resort to the examiner, as it was said: "the deities of knowledge entered [him].
(5) "Rooted in that" means rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*. (6)
For through intellectual error, one pursues five kinds of harmful and disadvantageous things: one suppresses natural urges, engages in rash acts,
and the ignorant person becomes attached to objects that appear pleasant in the immediate moment.
The knower is not stained, for when consciousness has been purified.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.40) [Āyurvedadīpikā]:
The meaning is that the pursuit of things harmful to one's welfare and so forth produces disease.

Although it should have been said "in pleasures of the present moment" (*tadātvasukheṣu*), by saying instead "in those perceived as pleasure" (*sukhasaṃjñeṣu*), he demonstrates that even though they are pleasant at the time, they are in reality not pleasure even at that very moment, because such unwholesome present pleasures produce suffering as their consequence, just as [the example] shows.
It has been stated here that health is designated as "pleasure.
[3] One who has discerned [the truth] is an investigator.
[4] One should not consume foods out of passion, nor out of ignorance.
One should eat wholesome food after careful examination, for the body is indeed born of food.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.28.41) [Āyurvedadīpikā:
"Not out of passion," etc. 1.

Even though one knows something to be harmful, some wicked person engages in it out of passion alone; and some engage in it through ignorance, by perceiving it as beneficial despite its being harmful. Both of these [faults] are prohibited:
"In the prescription for food, there are eight specific factors known as causes;
having examined them regarding the arising of the wholesome and unwholesome, one should employ them. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.42)
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
He asks, "How is food to be examined? and answers with the passage beginning "of food," etc. (1).

Regarding the arrangement—that is, the preparation—of food, there are eight specific factors, such as nature (*prakṛti*), processing (*karaṇa*), and combination (*saṃyoga*), which are to be discussed in the *Rasavimāna* chapter and are designated as "causes" (*hetu*). To the question "Where are they designated as causes?", he replies with the passage beginning "auspicious," etc. (2).

Regarding the arising of the auspicious and the inauspicious: it should be understood that those factors, such as *prakṛti* and the rest, which are auspicious produce what is auspicious, and those which are inauspicious produce what is inauspicious.
[3] A wise man in this world, by always avoiding unwholesome things that ought to be avoided, becomes one who has attained freedom from debt toward the virtuous. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.43)
However, that origin of disease which cannot be avoided by anyone here, having encountered it, should not be lamented by the wise. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.44) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

[Objection: "But even when one is following a wholesome regimen (*pathya*), diseases may still arise due to the power of powerful past unrighteousness (*adharma*). So what is the use of this practice of following a wholesome regimen? [The author] says: "Those things to be avoided," and so forth. 1. "Having attained freedom from debt" means having reached a state of being free from debt. By this, he shows that through the avoidance of what is to be avoided, a person becomes faultless in their human effort (*puruṣakāra*). 2.
