However, regarding a disease that has come about through fate (*daiva*), virtuous people do not blame the one who follows a wholesome regimen. He states this very point with the words: "But as for that which... and so forth. 3. [Note: The commentary explains that while one must strive against what is avoidable, one should not reproach oneself or others for what is beyond human control.]
"It is impossible to avoid" means that it is produced by powerful karma.
"One should not grieve" means that human effort is of no avail against a disease born of destiny (daiva) which is inevitable.
[5] "That which arises from food, and diseases which arise from food..."
The distinctions between what is beneficial and what is harmful, the specific differences between pleasure and pain,
the capacity and incapacity of the body and the mind to endure sufferings,
and the various distinct groups of diseases arising from the bodily constituents (dhātus)— all these are explained. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.28.45–46)

The pacification of these [doshas] as they move from the visceral cavity (koṣṭha) to the peripheral tissues (śākhā), and how the doshas become aggravated as they move from the peripheral tissues back to the visceral cavity;
the distinction between the wise and the ignorant; and that which is beneficial for both the healthy and the diseased.
All of that has been fully elucidated in the chapter on various foods and drinks.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, named "On Various Foods and Drinks," in the Section on General Principles (*Sūtrasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*]
"Substance for collection" (*saṃgraha-vastu*) refers to the body (*śarīra*).

By the passage beginning with "in terms of capacity and incapacity," etc., [the author] makes known the section of the text starting from "the bodies are excessively gross," etc., up to the end of "contrary [to health], yet capable of enduring disease.
*Carakasaṃhitā* [Chapter 1, Section 1]
Nidānasthāna, Chapter 7:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of insanity (unmāda).
Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
In this regard, there are indeed five types of insanity (*unmāda*), namely: those caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, their combination (*sannipāta*), and exogenous factors (*āgantu*).
Among these, the four types caused by the [internal] *doṣas* quickly manifest in men of the following kind:
those who are timid, whose mental constitution is afflicted, whose *doṣas* are aggravated, and who consume types of food that are impure, corrupted, unwholesome, or unfamiliar.

For those who employ medicinal substances according to an improper method of administration, who practice the application of medical systems in a discordant manner, who perform other bodily activities in an irregular way, whose bodies are excessively depleted,

who are agitated by the onset of disease, whose minds are impaired, or who are repeatedly struck down by desire, anger, greed, exhilaration, fear, delusion, exhaustion, grief, anxiety, agitation, and the like; [for such persons, the treatment may fail].

Furthermore, when the mind is impaired and the intellect is agitated, the provoked humors (*doṣas*), having become intense, reach the heart, obstruct the channels carrying the mind (*manovahāni srotāṃsi*), and produce insanity (*unmāda*).
One should understand insanity as a derangement of the mind, intellect, perception, knowledge, memory, inclination, conduct, and behavior. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 2.7.4–5)

Its premonitory symptoms are as follows: emptiness of the head, turbidity of the eyes, ringing in the ears, excessive respiration, salivation from the mouth, lack of desire for food, anorexia, indigestion, cardiac oppression, and constant, inappropriate dhyāna, fatigue, delusion, agitation,
horripilation, fever, frequent insanity of mind, urticaria, and the production of the appearance of facial paralysis (ardita).
Furthermore, there is frequent seeing of disease in dreams, as well as the sight of distorted, trembling, unstable, and inauspicious forms;
mounting a sesame-pressing wheel, being churned by whirlwinds, sinking into turbid waters in a whirlpool, and the rolling away of the eyes. (Caraka Saṃhitā 2.7.6)
Immediately following that, there is the manifestation of insanity itself.
In this regard, the specific cognition of insanity is as follows: constant wandering about; the twitching of the eyes, eyebrows, lips, shoulders, jaws, hands, feet, and limbs;
the sudden and incessant utterance of incoherent words; the spitting of froth from the mouth; and the frequent occurrence of smiling, laughing, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
Furthermore, the imitation of the sounds of the lute, flute, conch, cymbals, and rhythmic clapping at inappropriate times; traveling in vehicles that are not vehicles;

adorning oneself with objects that are not ornaments; greed for foods that have not been obtained and contempt for those that have been obtained; intense envy; emaciation; harshness; having swollen and reddened eyes; and a lack of relief from things that usually alleviate wind (*vāta*) while finding relief in their opposites—these are the symptoms of *vāta*-type insanity.

Impatience, anger, and agitation; striking one's own people or others out of place with weapons, clods of earth, vegetables, wood, or fists; charging at others; a craving for shade, cold water, and food; excessive heat; and a reddish, greenish, or yellowish appearance of the eyes and skin due to the aggravation of *pitta*, along with a lack of relief from things that do not agree with *pitta*—these are the symptoms of intoxication caused by *pitta*.

Staying in one place, remaining silent, wandering about only slightly, the flowing of saliva and nasal mucus, lack of desire for food, longing for solitude, loathsomeness, aversion to cleanliness, constant sleepiness, swelling of the face, and eyes that are white, fixed, and smeared with impurities; and due to the contrary of what is soothing for *śleṣman*, there is a lack of relief— these are the symptoms of *śleṣma*-type insanity.
When there is a combination of the symptoms of all three doṣas, one should recognize that as sannipātika; experts declare it to be incurable. However, for the three curable types, the treatments are:

oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, unctuous enema, pacification, bloodletting, fumigation, smoking, collyrium, nasal drops, insufflation, massage, poultices, affusion, ointments, striking, binding, confinement, terrifying, startling, causing forgetfulness, depletion therapy, and venesection.

The method of dieting should be prescribed according to the specific requirements through proper reasoning, and whatever other medicine is necessary that is contrary to the cause [of the disease] should also be administered.
Regarding this, there is a verse: "The best of physicians should cure curable cases of insanity born of the humors (doṣas)."
By this ritual procedure as it has been proclaimed, [the following is established]:

that madness which arises from causes consisting of the humors (doṣas), and which is characterized by specific features of its onset, premonitory signs, symptoms, sensations, and therapeutic relief, is called exogenous (āgantuka).
Some, however, maintain that its cause is improper action performed in a previous life.

And its cause is indeed the transgression of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*), according to the Blessed One Punarvasu Ātreya. For it is through the transgression of wisdom that one, having disregarded the gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, gurus, elders, siddhas, and teachers worthy of worship, commits harmful acts or undertakes some other such unwholesome action; thus, they strike down one who is already destroyed by his own self.
Gods and other beings cause one to become insane.
These are the premonitory symptoms of one who is possessed by an exogenous insanity caused by the provocation of gods and other deities; namely:
a fondness for harming gods, cows, Brahmins, and ascetics; irritability; cruelty of intent; restlessness; and [the loss] of vitality, complexion, luster, strength, and physical form.
The acquisition [of the disease] occurs through being threatened or incited by gods and other beings in a dream; immediately following that, the manifestation of insanity (*unmāda*) takes place.
In this regard, the specific manner of onset for those spirits (*bhūta*) who cause insanity and intend to produce it is as follows:

the gods produce insanity by gazing [at the victim]; the teachers, elders, perfected ones (*siddha*), and great seers (*maharṣi*) by pronouncing curses; and the ancestors (*pitṛ*) by appearing [before the victim].
The Gandharvas touch him; the Yakṣas enter him; the Rākṣasas cause him to smell their own scent; the Piśācas, having mounted him again, make him carry them.

These are his symptoms, namely: excessive self-confidence, strength, vigor, manliness, prowess, grasping, retention, memory, knowledge, speech, and discernment; and the onset of the insanity is irregular.
Indeed, even among gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, or among gurus, elders, and perfected ones (siddhas),
there are persons who must be approached during these intervals— namely, at the commencement of a sinful deed,
or at the time of the ripening of a previously committed deed, or when one is dwelling alone in an empty house or stationed at a crossroads.

Or during the time of twilight, or in a state of impurity, or at the junctions of the lunar phases, or upon engaging in sexual intercourse, or approaching a woman in her menses, or when the practice of study, offerings, auspicious rites, or oblations is defective; or upon the violation of observances, vows, or celibacy; or in a great battle, or upon the destruction of one's country, family, or city; or when a great planet approaches [the moon], or when a woman is in labor, or upon touching various beings that are inauspicious or impure.
Or after vomiting, purging, or the shedding of blood; or when one is impure or lacks self-restraint; or upon visiting a shrine or a temple of a deity;

or when one has consumed the remnants of meat, honey, sesame, molasses, or liquor; or when one is naked; or at night, upon visiting a city, a market town, a crossroads, a grove, a cemetery, or a place of execution;
or upon insulting a Brahmin, a teacher, a god, an ascetic, or anyone worthy of honor; or upon transgressing the proclamation of Dharma; or upon any other such act.

"By the phrase 'at the commencement of what is praiseworthy,' the times for striking [the patient] are explained. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 2.7.14) Furthermore, there are three purposes for the spirits that cause insanity when they bring about madness: namely, violence (*hiṃsā*), sexual pleasure (*rati*), and worship (*abhyarcana*).
One should recognize these specific purposes through the specific characteristics of the insane person's behavior.
Caraka Saṃhitā, Vimānasthāna, Chapter 1: [The Determination of Taste].
Now, therefore, we shall expound the determination of taste (rasavimāna). Caraka 3.1.1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya.
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

Since the five factors beginning with the cause (*hetu*) must be known through diagnosis (*nidāna*), knowledge of the specific details of the *doṣas*, medicinal substances (*bheṣaja*), and so forth is required for the application of treatment; therefore, the Section on Specific Determination (*Vimānasthāna*) is taught to provide knowledge of those specific details of the *doṣas*, medicinal substances, and the rest that are to be explained.]
He says:
1. And therein, because of the predominance of both the disease and its remedy, he first explains the *rasavimāna* (the specific determination of tastes), which makes known their particularities. 2.
And he himself will demonstrate this connection between the sections (*sthāna*). 3.

That by which the specific nature of the *doṣas*, medicines, and so forth is measured—that is, known—is called *vimāna*; the meaning is that it is the specific excellence (*viśeṣa*) regarding the power and other qualities of the *doṣas*, medicines, and so on. That section in which such a *vimāna* resides as its subject matter is the *Vimānasthāna*. [4] The chapter composed concerning the *vimāna* of the *rasas* is the *Rasavimāna*. [5]

In this context, having entered into the specific details of diseases— namely their causes, premonitory symptoms, clinical signs, therapeutic suitability, enumeration, predominance, treatment protocols, and classifications— as well as their temporal variations,

the physician must subsequently understand, with an attentive mind, the proper measures of the humors, the medicines, the location, the time, the strength, the bodily constitution, the essence, the diet, the suitability, the mental state, the temperament, and the age; for the success of medical action depends entirely upon the knowledge of these measures.
For indeed, a physician who does not know the measure of the *doṣas* and other factors is not capable of suppressing disease;
therefore, O Agniveśa, we shall explain the Section on Measurement (*Vimānasthāna*) for the purpose of knowing the measure of the *doṣas* and so forth.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Vimānasthāna 3.1.3) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
With the words "In this [work]," and so forth, he states the connection with the subject matter (*sthāna*).

By including the distinctions of attainment (*samprāpti*), number, predominance, and so on, he demonstrates that by teaching attainment itself, every form of attainment is thereby explained through its various divisions such as number and the like.

However, there is no such division of the causes (*nimitta*) and other factors that would require even a brief textual exposition; since they could not be described here through such a division, they are stated only in a general sense.
"Having entered" means having understood.
The defects (*doṣa*) and so forth have been explained in detail in the *Sūtrasthāna*.
"Measure" (*māna*) refers to specific qualities such as power (*prabhāva*); he states the cause for knowing this in the passage beginning with "the defects, etc. (*doṣādi*).
"Of action" refers to medical therapy.

In this regard, we shall first describe the potencies of tastes, substances, humors, and morbidities. There are six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. When these are used correctly, they maintain the body; however, when used improperly, they indeed lead to the provocation of the humors. *Caraka Saṃhitā*, Chapter 3, Section 1.4.

He promises to state the subject matter of the chapter with the words "Therein, at the beginning," and so forth. Although, in the passage beginning with "the doshas and the medicines," the *doṣas* were placed first because medicine depends upon the *doṣas*, nevertheless, here [the discussion begins with] medicine in the form of tastes and substances, by virtue of its being the agent that effects the pacification of the diseases required [to be treated].

Likewise, since the *doṣa* (humor) is also a cause only insofar as it pertains to taste (*rasa*) and substance (*dravya*), the *rasa* and *dravya* indicated by the word "medicine" (*bheṣaja*) are treated first; subsequently, however, the *doṣa-vikāra* (disorders of the humors), which are included by the mention of *doṣa*, are addressed. 2. *Prabhāva* is an excellent state; its meaning is "potency. And here, both the inconceivable and the conceivable [types of] *prabhāva* are to be understood. 3.

By the passage beginning with "wherein, indeed, among those of many tastes," he will further explain that the potency (*prabhāva*) of both substances and their transformations must be considered by way of both taste (*rasa*) and the humors (*doṣa*).
(4) "Sustaining" (*yāpayanti*) means they maintain equilibrium.
(5) Here, the word "wrongly" (*mithyā*) refers to deficient application (*ayoga*), excessive application (*atiyoga*), and perverse application (*mithyāyoga*). (6)
Furthermore, there are three doshas: vāta, pitta, and śleṣman.

When they remain in their natural state (prakṛti), they are beneficial to the body; however, when they undergo morbid transformation (vikṛti), they indeed afflict the body with various kinds of disorders.
"Defects" (doṣāḥ) refers to the defects of the body.
The word "again" (punaḥ) excludes the defects of the mind.
In this regard, three tastes each produce one particular defect, and three tastes each pacify it.

For example, pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes generate wind (*vāta*), whereas sweet, sour, and salty tastes pacify it; pungent, sour, and salty tastes generate bile (*pitta*), whereas sweet, bitter, and astringent tastes pacify it; and sweet, sour, and salty tastes generate phlegm (*śleṣman*), whereas pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes pacify it.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"In that regard," and so forth, he states the functions of the tastes (*rasa*) when they are unmixed.
By this instruction on the functions of the tastes, it is also implied that the *doṣas* are produced by their respective tastes and are likewise pacified by those same tastes.

It should be understood that pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] produce *vāta* "provided there is no counteracting factor. Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that even bitter substances such as *arka*, *aguru*, and *guḍūcī* do not produce *vāta*.

For in those cases, a hot potency (*uṣṇavīryatā*) exists as a counteracting factor; thus, they do not produce *vāta*. This principle should be followed accordingly. By the word "this" (*enam*), it is meant that the very same *vāta* produced by pungent and other tastes is specifically countered by sweet and other tastes due to their being diametrically opposed in their entire nature.
He shows that they pacify [the humors]: for when wind (*vāyu*) arises from wakefulness and the like, sleep and the like—which are the opposites of wakefulness and so forth—are especially wholesome.
(5) In this way, he demonstrates the intended meaning of these two words (*ena* and *enat*) regarding bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*) as well.

(6) However, in the case of a combination of tastes and humors (*rasa-doṣa-saṃnipāta*), those tastes which possess qualities identical to, or predominantly similar to, certain humors will increase those [humors]; whereas those with opposite qualities, or predominantly opposite qualities, [will decrease them].
Or, they pacify [the doshas] when practiced repeatedly.
For this reason of systematic arrangement, the number six is taught for the tastes and the number three for the doshas, provided they are not mutually mixed. (Caraka Saṃhitā 3.1.7) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

Now, by what reasoning do the tastes (*rasa*) produce the humors (*doṣa*) and pacify them? To this he says: "The taste-humor," and so forth. 1. "In the combination" (*saṃnipāte*) means within the internal confluence of the body.

2. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction; it shows that those [tastes] which possess contrary qualities, especially when compared to those in which contrary qualities predominate, are what pacify [the humors]. 3. [This is the third point.]

Regarding the qualities that arise from the various combinations of tastes, this has been stated in the sūtra beginning with "The qualities and defects based on [tastes] have not been mentioned," and so forth.
(4) "Being practiced" means being used repeatedly, not being used only once.
(5) Now, as to why the multiplicity of combinations of tastes and *doṣas* is set aside in favor of stating six tastes and three *doṣas*, he says "this [is] as follows," and so forth. (6)
"Vyavasthā" (establishment) refers to the summary of the expansion of the combinations of *rasas* and *doṣas*.
[7] The phrase "not combined with one another" (*paraspareṇāsaṃsṛṣṭānām*) should also be construed with the word "of the *doṣas*" (*doṣāṇām*).
[8] Indeed, the detailed enumeration of their combinations is incalculable, because the distinctions among their variations are incalculable. (Caraka Saṃhitā 3.1.8)
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, he states the reason for not describing the detailed expansion of the combinations of tastes and *doṣas* with the words beginning "saṃsarge" (in combination), etc. (Verse 1):
Since the expansion of the varieties of combinations is incalculable, therefore [the tastes] are said to be six and [the *doṣas*] three. (Verse 2)

"Because the distinctions of conceptual construction are innumerable": the distinction (*bheda*) of the conceptual construction of conjunction (*saṃsarga-vikalpa*) refers to its various heterogeneous types; because those are innumerable.

By this it is meant that just as, for example, although there are internal differences between individual instances of tastes, they are said to be six by means of designations such as "sweet" due to their connection with the commonality (*sāmānya*) of sweetness and so forth, so too, even though there are internal differences among the conjunctions of sweet, sour, sweet-and-salty, and so on—

The argument that, by making a general grouping, the restriction to the number sixty-three will be established, is refuted; for even when there is a mixture of sweet, sour, and other tastes, an incalculable variety arises due to the distinctions of "sweeter," "sweetest," and so forth, which belong to different classes.
For it is said: "Indeed, tastes exceed that number through their degrees of intensity."

In that regard, having observed individually the influence of the tastes (*rasa*) and the humors (*doṣa*) in substances that possess multiple tastes and in disorders (*vikāra*) that consist of multiple humors, one should then determine the true nature of the influence of both the substance and the disorder.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
Now, how then is the influence of combined tastes and humors to be known? To this he says: "In that regard, indeed," and so forth. 1.

In that context, while describing the potency (*prabhāva*) of a substance possessing multiple tastes and multiple doṣic disorders through the combination of the individual potencies of each taste and doṣa,

he likewise describes the potency of the combinations of tastes and doṣas; for here, because the potencies of the combinations of tastes and doṣas depend upon the substance and its disorders, they are spoken of as being the potencies of the substance and its disorders themselves.

By this principle, even though it is not explicitly stated, it should be understood that the potency (*prabhāva*) of a substance consisting of a single taste and a disorder (*vikāra*) consisting of a single humor (*doṣa*) is indeed already expressed through the description of the potencies of unmixed tastes and humors.

"Having observed each one individually" means having observed the combined potency of a substance with multiple tastes and a disorder with multiple humors by means of the potency of each individual taste and so forth previously described.
However, it is certainly not the case that this applies everywhere.

For it is not possible to determine the true nature of the power of a whole by means of an inference based solely on the power of its parts, when those parts are associated with various morbid transformations, possess diverse natures, are mutually impaired, and are further conceptualized by other mental constructs. (Caraka Saṃhitā 3.1.10)

And this determination of the power of substances and their transformations through the door of the influence of the defects of tastes does not apply to every substance or transformation; thus he says, "But indeed, it is not so in all cases.
Here he states the reason for this with the passage beginning with "For not" and ending with "capable of being determined.

Regarding the phrase "of those combined in a modified or unequal manner": it means those combined in a modified state (*vikṛti-samaveta*) as well as those combined in an unequal manner (*viṣama-samaveta*), which together constitute "those combined in a modified or unequal manner" (*vikṛti-viṣama-samaveta*).

"Of those combined" means of the tastes (*rasas*) and humors (*doṣas*) that have been mixed together. (4) Among these, the combination of a taste in a state of transformation (*vikṛti-samavāya*) is as follows: in the case of *taṇḍulīyaka*, which is sweet, sweetness by nature produces unctuousness, aphrodisiac effects, and so forth; however, because it is combined with a state of transformation in *taṇḍulīyaka*, it does not produce those effects. But when tastes are combined in an unequal manner, as in sesame (*tila*), where there are astringent, pungent, bitter, and sweet [tastes], if these tastes were combined in equal proportions—

Consequently, even sesame might either remove *pitta* and *kapha*, or it might remove all three *doṣas*; however, this [sesame] produces *pitta* and *kapha*. Therefore, in this context, a discrepancy is inferred: that the tastes sometimes act as agents [of transformation] and sometimes do not. Furthermore, the three reasons beginning with "because they possess diverse natures" (nānātmakānām) serve only to indicate the presence of modified combinations (*vikṛti-samavāya*) and unequal combinations (*viṣama-samavāya*).

Therefore, by means of [the reasons] such as "because they consist of various natures" (*nānātmakatvāt*) and so forth, there occur *vikṛtisamavāya* (modified inherence) and *viṣamasamavāya* (unequal inherence).

[Regarding the phrase] "of those consisting of various natures": this means [of those] produced from causes of diverse forms; thus, by the very power of the difference in causes, there occurs a modified or unequal blending of the tastes and the humors (*rasadoṣa*).
Alternatively, "of those consisting of various natures" means [of those] having various measures (*nānāpramāṇa*).
And thus, the state of having various measures (*nānā-pramāṇatva*) is the cause for the unequal combination [of tastes].
(11) "Of those mutually impaired" means of those whose qualities have been neutralized by one another.

(12) Although there is generally no mutual impairment of the qualities among the *doṣas*, it should nevertheless be understood that it occurs in some cases due to the power of unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*); however, in the case of the *rasas*, the impairment of one by a stronger [taste] certainly does occur.

"And by other conceptualizations" means by other differentiators. In this context, the differentiators of *rasa* (taste) are its own juices, pastes (*kalka*), and so forth; for even a single substance acquires different qualities through specific modes of preparation (*kalpanā*).
However, in the case of a *doṣa* (humor), it is only the different affected tissues (*dūṣya*) that, through their association with different qualities, become its differentiators.
As it has been said: "That very same provoked *doṣa* [is differentiated] by the particularity of its origin. (16)
"And having moved to another location, it produces many transformations.

(17) In this interpretation, the separate mention of the unequal combination (*viṣamasamavāya*) of the *rasas* and *doṣas* caused by their increase or decrease is not tenable; for even in an unequal combination, the qualities of the predominant *rasa* as well as the *doṣa* remain predominant.
Since the qualities of that which is diminished become diminished, it is possible to infer the power of the whole through inference based on the power of its parts.

Now, if it is argued that in a heterogeneous combination of *rasa* and *doṣa*, those very same qualities do not become superior or inferior, but rather a different quality altogether arises— well then, this aggregate is indeed a transformation (*vikṛta*), because its effect is dissimilar to its cause.

Thus, having observed this objection, it is explained otherwise: the blending (*melaka*) of flavors (*rasa*) and humors (*doṣa*) is of two kinds—concordant with their nature (*prakṛti-anuguṇa*) and discordant with their nature (*prakṛti-ananuguṇa*). Among these, that blending which occurs without the suppression of the natural qualities (*prākṛta-guṇa*) of the combined elements is designated by the term "natural equilibrium" (*prakṛti-sama-samavāya*); whereas that which occurs through the suppression of the natural qualities is [the other].

That is called "dissimilar conjunction with a modification" (*vikṛtiviṣamasamavāya*). The meaning is: a conjunction that is dissimilar—meaning discordant with its own nature—due to a modification acting as the cause;
this is "dissimilar conjunction with a modification.

In this very context of dissimilar conjunction with a modification, the three reasons beginning with "because of having multiple natures" (*nānātmakatva*) should be applied exactly as they have been explained.

However, those who treat *vikṛti* (transformation) and *viṣamasamavāya* (unequal combination) as entirely distinct—on the grounds that because the degree of inequality in *viṣamasamavāya* is so extensively elaborated, it is difficult to infer the qualities of the constituent parts from the whole—also designate that [inequality] solely by the power of the substance's transformation (*dravyavikāra*). For when such a collection is thus constituted, having perceived the true nature of the collection's power in this very way, one should then determine the true nature of the power of the substance's transformation. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 3.11)
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

Now, [the author] asks, "How then is there knowledge of the manifestation resulting from a morbid and discordant combination? and answers with the verse beginning "tathāyukte hi," etc. 1. "In such a combination" (*tathāyukte samudaye*) refers to a morbid and discordant combination (*vikṛtiviṣamasamavāya*). 2.
The reality of the power of the aggregate (*samudayaprabhāvatattva*) is the reality of the power of the combination (*melakaprabhāvatattva*).

For when honey and ghee are held in equilibrium, or in the case of the plant called *sūryāvarta*, there is neither the intoxicating quality resulting from the sequence of the qualities of the honey and ghee being combined,
nor the tendency to increase with the rising of the sun belonging to the *sūryāvarta* due to the influence of the humors such as wind (*vāta*).
However, the meaning is that this is indeed produced by the power of their conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

And as for the two types of movement of the combination of the humors (*doṣa-rasa*), he has described them in the section on the etiology of fever (*jvara-nidāna*) as *saṃnipāta*, which consists of the equal concurrence of the humors, precisely through the combination of the symptoms of the humors.

As it is said: "One should recognize a dual fever (*dvandvika*) or a fever arising from the combination of all three (*sāṃnipātika*) from the conjunction of the characteristics previously described individually. (6)

As for the fever produced by the three *doṣas* when they are combined in an unequal manner (*vikṛti-viṣama-samaveta*), its symptoms were stated in the section on treatment as "burning at one moment, coldness at another," and so forth.
(7) Indeed, the appearance of dark or reddish eruptions (*koṭha*) and the like mentioned therein are not found anywhere in fevers caused by *vāta* and the other *doṣas* individually.

(8) Similarly, regarding taste (*rasa*), where sweetness is inherent in the mango fruit through natural equilibrium (*prakṛti-sama-samaveta*), it is stated merely that "the mango is sweet. By this alone, its quality of removing *vāta* and *pitta*, which follows from the general property of sweetness, is also understood.
It is indeed so obtained.

For instance, although in the case of the eggplant (*vārtāka*) pungency and bitterness would normally result in its causing wind (*vāta*), because of a specific combination of modified qualities (*vikṛti-viṣama-samavāya*), that effect does not occur; therefore, the Teacher has stated that "the eggplant subdues wind."
Thus, and so forth; each respective example should be followed as it appears in the treatise.

However, that which speaks of the qualities of substances and their modifications—though these have already been established by way of the faults, qualities, and tastes produced through the combination of similar constituents (*prakṛti*)—should be understood as being for the sake of excellence and for the sake of clarity.
"Reality" (*tattva*) refers to the reality of the potencies of taste and so forth.

As for the formal promise made earlier— "First, therein, we shall teach the potencies of tastes, substances, humors (*doṣa*), and morbid transformations"— that was indeed made as a promise to explain the potencies of taste and so forth, since the potency of a substance is described precisely through the inference of the potency of its taste, and likewise through the potency of the humors.
[The previous section] would have fulfilled its purpose by describing the influence of the modifications [of taste].

However, in this case, since there is no inference of the influence of substances or their modifications based on the inference of the influence of tastes and *doṣas*— given that a substance consists of a combination of modified and non-modified [tastes]— there is no tautology, because the promise is made to state the true nature of the influence of tastes and so forth individually.

In this context, the power of potency (*vīryaprabhāva*) and the power of post-digestive transformation (*vipākaprabhāva*) of substances should be included within either the power of the substance (*dravyaprabhāva*) or the power of the taste (*rasaprabhāva*). Among these, those potencies and post-digestive transformations that are consistent with the tastes should be understood as belonging to the taste; however, those potencies and post-digestive transformations that are contrary to the potency and post-digestive transformation described according to the sequence of tastes should be understood as belonging to the power of the substance. "We shall teach" means that we shall teach the reality of the powers of taste and so forth individually throughout the entire treatise. The detailed exposition of the powers of taste and so forth must be stated throughout the whole treatise.
In this regard, the potency of tastes has been taught;
now we shall teach the potency of substances.
Oil, clarified butter, and honey are substances intended for the pacification of Vata, Pitta, and Kapha, respectively.
Demonstrating that this very [work] is a concise exposition, he says "tatraiṣa" and so forth.
(1) "Eṣa" means that which has been stated by the text beginning with "rasāḥ ṣaḍ" and ending with "tattvam upadekṣyāmaḥ. (2)
"It is taught" means it has been stated in brief.
Others, however, read: "In that regard, this power of taste (rasaprabhāva) is indicated.
In this view, the power of substances, defects, and morbid humors (doṣavikāra) is also indicated here; since that too occurs by way of taste, it belongs to taste alone.

Because it has been described through elaboration (*prapañca*), one should understand that he concludes the mention of that [subject] alone, and not of substances (*dravya*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the power of substances" (*dravyaprabhāva*) and so on, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) means: since the power of substances was previously stated in a general sense, we shall now describe the power of specific substances such as oil (*taila*) by way of individual specification (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*). // 5 //
"For the purpose of pacification" means having pacification as their objective.

In that regard, oil—because it is endowed with moisture (*sneha*), heat (*uṣṇya*), and heaviness (*gaurava*)—conquers the wind (*vāta*) when practiced continuously; for the wind is endowed with dryness (*raukṣya*), coldness (*śaitya*), and lightness (*lāghava*), and thus possesses contrary qualities. Indeed, when there is a meeting of contrary qualities, the greater overcomes the lesser.
Therefore, oil conquers *vāta* when practiced continuously;
clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) likewise conquers *pitta* because of its sweetness, coolness, and mildness, for *pitta* is indeed non-sweet, hot, and sharp.
And honey conquers *śleṣman* because of its dryness, sharpness, and astringency, for *śleṣman* is indeed unctuous, mild, and sweet.

Furthermore, whatever other substance there may be that is qualitatively opposite to wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha), it overcomes these [doshas] when practiced continuously. [Commentary:
"Practiced continuously" means being used without interruption.]
"Having contrary qualities" means having qualities opposite to those of oil.
"In the meeting of contrary qualities" means in the conjunction of two things with contrary qualities.

Now, one might object: "Between two things of contrary qualities, the smaller is overcome by the greater; how then does oil conquer *vāta*, for it is not logical that oil should possess a greater degree [of power] relative to *vāta*? To this he replies: "When practiced constantly."
Thus [it is said].
For, by constant application, oil becomes superior to wind; the meaning is that it thereby conquers the wind.
Ghee is indeed exactly the same; the meaning is that ghee also, when practiced constantly, [conquers wind]. 6.
"Non-sweet" (amadhura) means the opposite of sweet due to qualities such as roughness, lightness, and lack of aphrodisiac effect; that is to say, it refers to the bitter taste (*kaṭu-rasa*).

Here, by the word "potency" (*prabhāva*), the general power of a substance (*dravya-śakti*) is expressed, not an inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*). Therefore, even though substances like oil possess qualities such as unctuousness and heat, their pacification of *vāta* and other humors occurs solely through the potency of the substance itself.

Furthermore, although the sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*) in ghee (*sarpiḥ*) is active in pacifying *pitta*, the pacification of *pitta* by ghee is indeed its specific action (*kārya*) due to its sweetness, coldness, and mildness; thus, this is the potency of the substance.
Thus it should be stated.
However, when the effect of a substance is considered by way of its rasa, then the designation "rasaprabhāva" (the influence of rasa) occurs.
In this same manner, the resolution regarding astringent aftertastes and honey should be stated.
Others, however, say that regarding the fact that oils and such things pacify wind (*vāta*) and the other humors, this is called an inconceivable power (*prabhāva*).
In that regard, when oil and wind—which possess contrary qualities—are combined, it is the oil alone that overcomes the wind, and not the wind that overcomes the oil;

thus, the power of the oil is indeed inconceivable. In the same way, the powers of clarified butter (*sarpis*) and honey (*madhu*) in removing bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*) are also to be understood as arising from their [inconceivable] power. 12.

Others do not accept this, because by the phrase "oil and so forth, when practiced constantly," it is stated that only an increase [of the substance] is the cause for conquering wind and the other humors;

likewise, by the passage beginning with "and whatever other substance," setting aside the inconceivable power of substances, it is stated in general that the reversal of qualities through practice alone is the cause for conquering wind and the others. [13]
Now, indeed, one should not consume three substances in excess compared to other substances; namely, long pepper (*pippalī*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and salt (*lavaṇa*).
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
Having stated the substance that is habitually consumed as an illustration of its potency, he speaks of those not habitually consumed with the words "Now," etc.]

By the statement "more than others," it is shown that other substances of this kind, such as *citraka* and *bhallātaka*, should not be used in excess; however, substances like *pippalī* and the like, being even more [potent] than others, must be avoided when used in excess. For *pippalīs*, though pungent, have a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), are heavy, not excessively unctuous or hot, and are moistening (*prakledinī*).

And those [substances] regarded as medicines produce immediate beneficial or harmful effects; they appear auspicious at first due to the excellence of their application, yet they are followed by an accumulation of morbid humors (*doṣa*). For when used constantly, they aggravate *śleṣman* (phlegm) because of their heaviness and moistness, and they aggravate *pitta* (bile) because of their heat; furthermore, they are not conducive to the pacification of *vāta* (wind) due to their slight unctuousness and heat. However, they are indeed "carriers of the formulation" (*yogavāhinī*)—[provided they are used correctly].
Indeed, such things occur; therefore, one should not consume long peppers (*pippalī*) in excess.

[The *Āyurvedadīpikā* explains that the description of the qualities of long pepper—such as being pungent in taste yet sweet in post-digestive effect (*vipāka*)—is intended to show the opposite of the defects that arise from unaccustomed use.]

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the pacification of the *doṣas*, as well as for the purpose of demonstrating the suitability for producing the defects mentioned in the text—such as "in the case of excessive application, because they cause heavy moisture, they excite the *śleṣman*," and so forth. 1.
The word division is *bheṣajābhimatāśca sadyaḥ*. 2.

"Sadyas" means in the absence of repeated practice. (3) They become performers of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; thus, they are "performers of the auspicious" when practiced immediately, but "performers of the inauspicious" when employed with excessive repetition.
(4) He demonstrates this very capacity for performing the auspicious and the inauspicious by means of the passage beginning with "appearing auspicious at first," and so forth. (5)

"Due to the excellence of the balanced application" (*prayogasamasādguṇyāt*) means that because the application is balanced, when the application of *pippalī* and other such substances is equal—meaning moderate in both duration and quantity—they possess excellent qualities.
(6) Those which have a continuous accumulation of the *doṣas* are called "those with a continuous accumulation of *doṣas*" (*doṣasaṃcayānubandha*).
(7) He explains this very state of having a continuous accumulation of *doṣas* with the words beginning with "constantly" (*satatam*). (8)

In the context of describing the properties of long pepper (*pippalī*), he states another quality, beginning with "But they are *yogavāhinī*s," and so forth. (9) Because they are *yogavāhinī*s—meaning they carry along other substances—even pungent long peppers find application in aphrodisiac formulations; likewise, in formulations for curing fever, abdominal tumors, skin diseases, and so on, long pepper destroys the fever and other ailments.
(10) And this prohibition against the excessive use of long pepper should be understood as applying after setting aside exceptions. (11)

Therefore, the administration of the *pippalī-rasāyana* formulation, as well as the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen for conditions such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), does not involve any contradiction. For it is inferred from the words of the Sages that, regarding the subject matter already mentioned, *pippalī* fruits are indeed free from defects when used according to the prescribed method.
Others, however, maintain that while *pippalī* and other such substances may be used in abundance for seasoning food, they should not be used independently.
"Being used constantly" should be understood as both by way of excessive quantity and by way of continuous application.

Furthermore, alkali (kṣāra), being endowed with heat, sharpness, and lightness, first moistens and subsequently dries; it is employed for the purposes of cooking, burning, and splitting. When used excessively, however, it becomes a cause of injury to the hair, the eyes, the heart, and virility.
For those villages, towns, market towns, and provinces that constantly consume this [alkali] become subject to blindness, impotence, baldness, and premature graying,
and suffer from heart disease— just as, for example, the people of the East and China do; therefore, one should not consume alkali in excess.
"Those who cut out the heart" means those possessed of sensations characterized by the cutting away of the heart.
Furthermore, salt is endowed with heat and sharpness; it is neither too heavy nor too unctuous, it is moistening, capable of causing loosening, and it stimulates the appetite for food substances.

It is beneficial at first sight due to its excellence when combined in a formulation, yet it is followed by an accumulation of the *doṣas*. It is employed for the purposes of stimulating the appetite, digestion, moistening, and loosening.
When that [salt] is used in excess, it brings about exhaustion, flaccidity, and weakness of the body.
For those villages, cities, market towns, and provinces that consume it constantly become for the most part exhausted, with their flesh and blood becoming flaccid, and incapable of enduring hardship.
This is the case, for example, with the Vāhlīkas, Saurāṣṭrikas, Saindhavas, and Sauvīrakas; for they eat salt even along with milk.
Even those regions of this earth that are excessively saline do not produce herbs, creepers, trees, or large forest trees, or they become weak in vitality due to being afflicted by salt.
Therefore, one should not consume salt in excess.
For those persons who have become habituated to excessive salt, baldness, graying of hair, and wrinkles appear prematurely.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"Fatigue, wasting of the muscles, or loss of vigor.
1] Not only does excessive use of salt cause injury to the body, but it also causes injury to the earth; thus [the author] says, "Those also here," and so forth. 2.
"Ūṣara" refers to those [lands] where salt is predominant.

(3) "One should not consume salt excessively" means one should not constantly consume salt in excessive measure; however, as a seasoning for food substances, it may indeed be consumed even habitually in small quantities.
(4) He states the defects even for those in regions other than Vāhlīka and so forth who eat too much salt, beginning with the words "Those who... (5).

By this same reasoning, even in other regions, the defects such as looseness (śaithilya) occurring in those accustomed to excessive salt is understood to be caused solely by the overuse of salt, not by the inherent nature of the region itself.
Therefore, for them, it is best to gradually eliminate that habituation;
for even habituation, when being withdrawn gradually, results in no harm or at most only slight harm. (Caraka Saṃhitā 3.1.19)
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"Of them" refers to those for whom excessively alkaline and salty substances are habitual (*sātmya*).
"Due to that habituation" means due to the habituation to excessive alkali and excessive salt.
"Gradually" means that one should not suppress the urges, but rather follow the sequence of abandoning what has become habitual (*sātmya*).
Here, by the word *sātmya*, the habitual nature of one's dwelling place (*okasātmya*) is intended.
Regarding the two positions—that it may have little fault or no fault at all—the determination is as follows: extreme habituation results in little fault, while any other degree results in no fault.
That which is agreeable to one's own self is called *sātmya*; for the meaning of *sātmya* is the same as the meaning of *upaśaya*.
It is threefold according to the division of superior, inferior, and middling; however, it is sevenfold according to each individual taste and through the use of all tastes combined.
Among these, that which contains all tastes is superior, that which has only a single taste is inferior, and that which lies between the superior and the inferior is middling.
In that regard, one should gradually establish a superior suitability by means of inferior and intermediate levels of suitability.

Furthermore, having attained a state of suitability even for all tastes, and having duly considered the eight factors—beginning with the individual constitution—that determine the specific rules for dietary regimen, one should adhere strictly to what is beneficial.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 3.1.20) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
"Sātmyam" means "that which is agreeable to one's own nature"; that is, it refers to what is habitually agreeable to the individual. "Okāt" means "from habitual practice.
"Upaśayārtha" means "that which is designated by the term *upaśaya* (therapeutic suitability)."
"That" refers to the suitability of one's habitat (okasātmya).
"Threefold" means according to the divisions of superior, inferior, and middling.
It is "sevenfold," however, because there are six types based on each individual taste and one type based on the consumption of mixed tastes; thus, it is sevenfold.
By the word "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), those [foods] beginning with two tastes and ending with six tastes are included.
(7) "Situated among the superior, inferior, and middling" refers to those beginning with two tastes and ending with five tastes.
(8) A person is characterized by the inferior and the middling. (9)
"Excellent" means containing all tastes.
"One should bring about suitability" means one should practice it.
"Gradually" means according to the sequence of practice as previously described.

Even for one who has established a suitability for all tastes, food should be prepared only when endowed with excellent qualities such as those of its natural constitution (*prakṛti*); thus he says "all tastes," and so forth.
(13) "Having thoroughly examined" means having deliberated upon whether something is beneficial or harmful.
(14) By the word "only that which is beneficial," the meaning is that one should follow and consume only that which is beneficial according to one's constitution and other factors. (15)
The meaning is that the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of a type of food are caused by factors such as its *prakṛti* (nature).
[2] Those things for which the consumer is the eighth are "those with the consumer as the eighth.

[3] In this context, *prakṛti* refers to the inherent nature (*svabhāva*); furthermore, it is the natural endowment of qualities such as heaviness and so forth belonging to foods and medicinal substances, as in the case of black gram and mung bean, or the wild boar and the deer.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, [the author] analyzes [the factors] beginning with "nature" (*prakṛti*) by means of the passage starting with "therein" (*tatra*), etc.
1. "Natural" (*svābhāvika*) means not produced by refinement (*saṃskāra*) or other such means. 2.
Regarding "of black gram and mung bean": by nature, there is heaviness in black gram and lightness in mung bean; likewise, there is heaviness in the boar and lightness in the antelope.
Furthermore, processing (*karaṇa*) is the refinement of naturally occurring substances;
for refinement is said to be the imparting of a different quality (*guṇa*).

Those qualities are acquired through contact with water, fire, purification, churning, place, time, storage, processing, and so forth, as well as through the duration of time, the type of vessel, and other factors.

[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, although it should have been stated "of substances," the author uses the term "of those that are natural" (*svābhāvikānām*); by this he indicates that the imposition of its own qualities by the productive primary elements occurs at the time of origination, whereas *saṃskāra* (processing) is the imparting of further qualities to that which has already originated by means of water and other agents.]
He demonstrates this:

and that [transformation] is performed precisely by the suppression of the natural qualities (*guṇa*), just as the heaviness inherent in rice is destroyed by contact with water and fire and by cleansing, so that lightness is produced in the cooked grain.
As it has been said: "Rice that is well-washed, drained, steamed, and heated becomes light. (1–3)
Likewise, even for light substances such as red rice (*raktaśāli*) and the like, lightness increases through contact with fire and other means.
(4) The acquisition of qualities through churning is illustrated by the fact that curd which causes swelling becomes a destroyer of swelling when churned, despite being oily.
(5) By way of location, as in the instruction "one should place [it] beneath a heap of ashes," and so forth. (6)

Infusion (*vāsana*) is the imparting of qualities, such as the imitation of fragrance by water through the infusion of blue lotuses and the like. (7) And through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), performed by means of one's own natural effort, there occurs an intensification of the very quality present in substances such as the *āmalaka* fruit. (8) Through the passage of time, as in the instruction, "one should drink [the medicine] whose potency has developed after a fortnight," and so forth. (9)
As in the case of the statement, "One should smear an iron vessel with a paste made from the three myrobalans using a ladle," and so forth;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), grinding, consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), and other such acts are included.

Now, one might ask: how can an inherent quality (*svābhāvika-guṇa*) be destroyed by a quality produced through refinement (*saṃskāra-adheya-guṇa*), since an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is unalterable?

If it is argued that natural heaviness is counteracted by a *saṃskāra* (latent impression), then we ask: how can one say that "nature is unalterable"? For nature is not altered in the production of entities; otherwise, it would not be their nature.

Therefore, the heaviness of beans and the like is bound to their specific genus (*jāti*) and cannot be destroyed by a *saṃskāra* within that genus. However, the alteration of that [heaviness] by a *saṃskāra* is indeed admitted, because it is observed to occur.

However, some quality of substances is not altered even by processing (*saṃskāra*) and the like, such as the heat of fire, the mobility of air, the viscidity of oil, and so forth. (14) For these qualities indeed persist as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*). (15) On the other hand, qualities such as heaviness (*gaurava*) do not persist as long as the substance exists, because they are observed to disappear even in old grain and similar things. (16)

For it has been said: "A quality undergoes destruction either through the destruction of its substance, or through the imposition of another quality. However, in a case where a distinct substance characterized by water is produced from rice by means of a refinement (*saṃskāra*), the production of another quality there is perfectly logical.

Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the state of aggregation of two or many substances; it initiates a specific quality which the individual substances do not initiate separately, such as the conjunction of honey and clarified butter, or of honey, fish, and milk. [Āyurvedadīpikā]
He states [the definition of] conjunction with the words "Conjunction, however," and so forth.
(1) "It initiates a particularity" means that it initiates an unperceived effect in a specific part of the substances being conjoined.
(2) "Which is not produced by each one individually" means that particularity which the substances being conjoined do not initiate when taken one by one. (3)
For honey and clarified butter are individually non-lethal, yet when combined they become lethal; likewise, the combination of milk, fish, and so forth causes leprosy and other diseases.

Here, however, "combination" (*saṃyoga*) is intended specifically as the union of substances that are directly perceived; therefore, although there is a form of combination even in cases such as *bhāvanā* (infusion), it is not classified as a "combination" because the substances involved in the infusion are not primarily perceived therein.
The "heap" (*rāśi*), however, refers to the grasping and the encompassing of all [food], for the purpose of determining the measure and the non-measure of its results.

In this context, "grasping all" (*sarvagraha*) is the taking of the entire quantity of food as a single mass; "encompassing" (*parigraha*) is the taking of each individual food substance by measure one after another.
Indeed, "grasping all" is the grasping of everything, and "encompassing" is said to be the grasping from every side.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, "quantity" (*rāśi*) refers to the measure [of food].

It is for the purpose of determining the results of both adequate and inadequate measures; that is, the auspicious result of food and medicine taken in the proper measure, and the inauspicious result of what is either deficient or excessive in measure. (1–2)
Regarding what was stated— that for the sake of knowing that [quantity], there is a suitable measure and an unsuitable measure known as a *rāśi*—
he explains "all the [food]" and so forth. Therein,
"of all" refers to the measurement by a single lump of mixed items such as rice, meat, and soup.

He explains *parigraha* with the words "Furthermore, *parigraha*... and so forth. (6) "By each [item]" means the measurement of the whole preceded by the measurement of its parts, such as one *kuḍava* of rice, one *pala* of soup, two *palas* of meat, and so on. (7) In the case of *sarvagraha*, there is no restriction regarding the measurement of each individual part; therefore, *sarvagraha* is the determination of the total quantity of food by means of any food whatsoever, where each individual item is of an unrestricted measure. (8)
He demonstrates this very point through the etymology of the word, beginning with "sarvasya hi" and so forth.
[9] "From all" means from each individual component.
[10] Furthermore, "place" (deśa) refers to location; it denotes the production and movement of substances, as well as what is appropriate to that place (deśasātmya).
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,] he analyzes "region" (*deśa*) with the words beginning with "region" (*deśa*): 1.
By the mention of "place" (*sthāna*), he indicates the location of both the food substance as well as the consumer. 2.

"He explains" means that [the treatise] becomes the cause for the knowledge of qualities produced by the origin, distribution, and so forth of substances. 3. Among these, by way of origin: that which is born in the Himalayas is possessed of quality (heavy), while that born in the desert is light, and so on. 4. By way of distribution: lightness is perceived in the food of animals that roam in such [light] environments, as well as in those that move in arid lands and perform many activities; conversely, heaviness is perceived in the opposite case. 5.

By means of regional similarity (*deśasāmya*), suitability (*sātmya*) is understood as that which possesses qualities opposite to those of the region; for example, hot and dry qualities are suitable in marshy (*anūpa*) regions, while cold and unctuous qualities are suitable in arid (*dhanvan*) regions. Habitual suitability (*okasātmya*) is included within the category of the user (*upayoktṛ*).

Time (*kāla*) is both ever-moving (*nityaga*) and situational (*avasthika*); therein, the situational time depends on the specific pathological condition (*vikāra*), whereas the ever-moving time depends on seasonal suitability (*ṛtusātmya*).
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,
"constant" (*nityaga*) refers to that which consists of the day-and-night cycle and so forth;
"occasional" (*āvasthika*) means characterized by specific states such as illness, childhood, and the like.
"Depends on modification" means that it depends on modifications such as those caused by phlegm (kapha) or fever, which arise from childhood and other stages, for the purpose of regulating diet.
[3] "Seasonal suitability" refers to that which depends on the season; thus, it is "dependent on seasonal suitability.
[4] "The rule of application" is the regulation of the method of consumption; that depends on the signs of digestion.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, it is stated:
"The rule regarding consumption—namely, that food should be consumed in this manner and not in that manner—is primarily taught as being dependent upon the signs of digestion (*jīrṇalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, even rules concerning the manner of consumption, such as 'not talking, not laughing, not too fast, not too slow,' must certainly be observed here. For if one eats while suffering from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), a great disorder arises characterized by the provocation of all three *doṣas*."

Thus has [the recipient] been described. Furthermore, the consumer is he who partakes of that food, depending upon which one’s habituation to a particular diet is established. In this way, the eight specific bases for the rules of dietary practice have been explained. (Caraka Saṃhitā 3.1.22)
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, it is stated:

"That which depends on the individual is suitability (*sātmya*). For suitability through habituation (*abhyāsasātmya*) is dependent upon the person who consumes; for indeed, due to habituation, something may become suitable as wholesome or unwholesome for a particular individual.

The specific qualities of these [foods], which yield auspicious or inauspicious results and act as mutual auxiliaries, one should desire to know; and having understood them, one who seeks his own welfare should indeed act accordingly. Out of delusion or negligence, one should not consume any food or anything else that is pleasant yet harmful and resulting in unhappiness.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*,

regarding the passage beginning with "of these" (*eṣām*), it should be understood that specific qualities resulting in auspicious fruits and those resulting in inauspicious fruits are mutually supportive.
Among them, lightness (*lāghava*) and so forth are auspicious by nature, while heaviness (*guru*) and so forth are inauspicious.
Even a specific quality produced by the instruments [of preparation] and so forth is auspicious if prescribed in the scriptures, but it is inauspicious if prohibited.
(3) Unwholesomeness of place (*deśāsātmya*)—such as a substance originating from a censured region—and other such factors result in inauspicious effects for the substance.

(4) Likewise, unwholesomeness of time (*kālāsātmya*) resulting in inauspicious effects, such as eating during indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), as well as unwholesomeness of location (*okāsātmya*) leading to inauspicious results, should be understood as such; conversely, that which is the opposite yields auspicious results. (5)

"Out of delusion" means out of ignorance; "out of negligence" means even knowing [the consequences], [acting] out of attachment—this is the meaning. (6) "Pleasant" means pleasant only for the immediate moment. (7) The explanation of "harmful" is "having an unpleasant result. (8)
"Unpleasant" means having the nature of suffering; "whose future result" (*udarka*) refers to that which occurs at a later time.
[9] "Or something else" refers to medicine, a dwelling, and so forth.
[10] In this regard, this rule for the preparation of food is most beneficial by its very nature at the proper time for both those who are healthy and certain of those who are ill.

For those eating, the food should be warm, unctuous, and in the proper quantity; it should be digested without conflict of potencies and be pleasant. In a desirable place, with all desired accessories, one should eat neither too fast nor too slowly, without talking or laughing, being single-minded and properly considering oneself. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 3.24) [Āyurvedadīpikā]
Regarding the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*): "this" (*idam*) refers to what is about to be described.

(1) That by which the rules for diet are prescribed—namely, by means of the [qualities] such as hot and unctuous which are about to be described—is the "prescription of the rules for diet. (2) By the phrase "and of certain patients," he demonstrates exceptions [to the general rule], such as that for those suffering from *rakta-pitta* only cold [food] is beneficial, and for those with diseases of *kapha* only dry [food] is beneficial. (3)
The construction is as follows: for some who are eating, this arrangement of the rules for food becomes most beneficial.

Regarding the phrase "by its very nature" (*prakṛtyaiva*), it means "most beneficial by its own inherent character. Thus, that which is beneficial by nature may, on certain occasions, become harmful upon encountering a particular person; however, because such instances are merely occasional, they are disregarded.
The intention is that, because it is the most common case, we shall describe this as the most beneficial.
[5] In the passage beginning with "hot," the word "samyak" (properly) is the required division.
[6] We shall teach its excellence: one should eat hot food, for hot food tastes better when being eaten, and once consumed, it kindles the digestive fire.
It quickly stimulates the appetite, leads to easy digestion, harmonizes the wind (*vāta*), and diminishes phlegm (*śleṣman*);
therefore, one should eat warm food.
One should eat unctuous food, for unctuous food is pleasant to consume while being eaten, and once consumed, it stimulates the digestive fire that has not been provoked.

One attains youthfulness quickly, one harmonizes the bodily winds (*vāta*), builds up the body, strengthens the sense organs, produces an increase in strength, and brings about clarity of complexion; therefore, one should eat what is unctuous.
[Āyurvedadīpikā]
"Of that" refers to food endowed with qualities such as heat.
"Excellence" (sādguṇyam) means the possession of praiseworthy qualities.
"Causing it to diminish" means making its constituent parts disintegrate.

One should eat in moderation; for food eaten in moderation does not afflict the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, but increases life-span alone, moves comfortably through the rectum, does not impair the digestive heat (*ūṣman*), and reaches full digestion without distress. Therefore, one should eat in moderation.
[Āyurvedadīpikā]
1. "Measured" (*mātrāvat*)—the suffix *matup* here denotes praise; thus, the meaning is "that which is praised as being measured. 2.
"It does not oppress" (*apīḍayat*)—by virtue of not being excessive, it remains in its own place and does not provoke the *vāta* and other humors by not displacing them from their locations.
3. "It moves around the anus" (*gudam anuparyeti*)—this means that having been digested, it exits in a manner consistent with its nature.
[One should eat when the heat has become fire. For if one eats while [the previous meal] is undigested, the food being ingested mingles with the undigested essence (*rasa*) of the prior meal;
this quickly provokes all the humors (*doṣa*). However, for one eating when [the previous meal] is digested, [the humors] remain in their own places.

When the humors and the digestive fire have been excited, when hunger has arisen, when the openings of the channels are dilated, when eructation is pure, when the heart is clear, when the downward movement of wind is restored, and when the urges of flatus, urine, and feces have been discharged, the food that is consumed nourishes the life-force alone without vitiating any of the bodily tissues; therefore, one should eat only after [the previous meal] has been digested.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"Of the previous" means that which was performed on another day;
"untransformed" means improperly produced.]
"By the essence of food" means by the sweet and other tastes resulting from the transformation of food, or else by the essence produced from food.
[3] "When the humors (*doṣas*) are situated in their own locations," and so forth, is the definition of digested food.

[4] One should eat that which is not contrary in potency (*vīrya*); for by eating what is not contrary in potency, one is not afflicted by disorders born of food with contrary potencies; therefore, one should eat what is not contrary in potency.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

"Born of incompatible potencies and foods" refers to conditions such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), blindness, and erysipelas (*visarpa*), as described in the chapter on the teachings of Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya.
One should eat in a desired location with all desired accessories; for one eating in a desired location is not afflicted by the mental disturbances arising from an undesired location.

One suffers mental distress through undesirable things, and likewise through desirable objects and all types of requisites; therefore, one should eat in a desirable place and with all desirable requisites.
[Commentary on the Āyurvedadīpikā:

"By things that cause mental distress" means by those factors such as desire and so forth, which cause affliction of the mind and produce mental disturbances, as will be described in the chapter on the Three Divisions of the Stomach (Trividhakukṣīya). 1.
The construction is as follows: by eating with all desired requisites, one does not experience mental distress; for mental distress arises from eating what is undesirable and so forth.

One should not eat too quickly; for in one who eats too quickly, there is excessive salivation, depression, and instability of the food, and the perception of the defects or qualities of the food is not certain; therefore, one should not eat too quickly.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*: Utsnehanam is the movement [of the humors] onto the wrong path;
avasādanam is exhaustion. 1–2.
Non-abiding means not entering the stomach by virtue of being situated within the heart.

(3) The perception of defects in food, such as hair and the like, as well as the perception of its good qualities, such as its deliciousness, is not constant; it is perceived at times and not at others.
(4) In that regard, through the non-perception of defects, one consumes that which is indeed defective; and through the non-perception of good qualities, there is an absence of pleasure. (5)
One should not eat too slowly; for one who eats too slowly does not attain satiety, eats excessively, the food becomes cold, and it is digested irregularly. Therefore, one should not eat too slowly.
(Āyurvedadīpikā)

And it is digested unevenly; the meaning is that this is due to the irregularity of the connection with the digestive fire caused by eating over a long period of time. Not talking, not laughing, and being focused on that [food], one should eat while not talking or laughing and with a mind fixed on nothing else; for those very same faults that occur in one who eats too quickly occur in one who eats while talking, laughing, or having a mind elsewhere. Therefore, one should eat without talking or laughing and with a mind fixed on that.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"The defects that arise for one who eats too quickly" refer to excessive oleation and so forth.

One should eat after having carefully observed oneself, thinking, "This is wholesome for me; this is not wholesome. For in this way, one's own individual suitability (*ātmasātmya*) becomes known to him. Therefore, one should eat after having carefully observed oneself.
By the word "of oneself" (ātmanaḥ), he shows that the suitability for oneself is known by the self alone for each individual, and not through the instruction of the scriptures.

"He who knows the tastes, the substances, the humors (doṣas), and the disorders by their inherent power (prabhāvataḥ), as well as the place, the time, and the body—he is our physician. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 3.1.26)
[The author] praises the knowledge of the potency and other qualities of tastes as taught in this chapter with the words "rasān" and so forth.
"He is our physician" means he is approved by us. // 1 //
The purpose of the treatise on weights and measures; tastes, substances, defects, and diseases according to their specific potencies;
substances that should not be consumed excessively; the three types of suitability (*sātmya*); the eight bases of diet; and the excellence of food. *Caraka Saṃhitā*, Chapter 3, Verse 27.
All this has been elucidated in the Vimāna [section] numbered by the tastes.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of Tastes" (Rasavimāna), in the Vimānasthāna of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
[From the Āyurvedadīpikā]

Although the disorders of the *doṣas* should have been explained in detail regarding their specific potencies within the section on the "Three Parts of the Stomach" (*trividhakukṣīya*), they are nevertheless stated here in brief. Therefore, it is correct to say that the potencies of the *doṣa*-disorders are also included in this summary (*saṃgraha*).
Furthermore, the mention of the three substances beginning with oil is not listed separately in the summary, as it is already encompassed by the discussion of the potencies of substances.
Caraka Saṃhitā, Śārīrasthāna, Chapter 1:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise titled "The Manifold Nature of the Person" (Katidhāpuruṣīya).
Thus spoke the Blessed Ātreya:
"O wise one, in how many ways is the person divided according to the division of the constituent elements?
Why is the person the cause, and what is the source of the person?"
Is he ignorant or is he wise? Is he eternal or is he shown to be non-eternal?
What is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), what are its transformations (*vikāra*), and what is the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the person (*puruṣa*)?
[He is] actionless, independent, sovereign, all-pervading, and omnipresent.
Those who know the self describe it as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and likewise as the witness (*sākṣin*).
O Blessed One, how can there be activity for that which is actionless?
If it were independent, how could it be born in undesirable wombs?
If he is the master, why is he forcibly overcome by unpleasant states?
And since all sensations are omnipresent, why does he not perceive them all?
Why does the all-pervading one not see what is obstructed by mountains or walls?
There arises the doubt: which came first, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) or the field (*kṣetra*)? For without the field to be known, the knower of the field is not logically possible;
and if the field were prior, the knower of the field would be non-eternal.
And as a witness, whose agent is this, for no other is found?
And how could there be a distinction produced by sensation in that which is changeless? Furthermore, O Blessed One, among the three types of suffering, which one does the afflicted person treat?

The physician [examines] past sensation, present sensation, and future sensation. There is no attainment of what is yet to come, no arrival of what is past, and even for the present one, there is no stability; therefore, there is indeed uncertainty regarding suffering.
What is the cause of sensations, and what is said to be their basis?
Where do all these sensations completely cease without remainder? [The Blessed One replied:
"The All-Knowing One, the renouncer of all, who has emerged from all attachments."
"By what signs is the one, tranquil self of beings perceived?
Having heard these words of Agniveśa, Punarvasu, the best among the wise and himself tranquil in soul, explained everything exactly as it is.
The elements consisting of the five objects of sense and consciousness as the sixth are known as the person (*puruṣa*);
furthermore, the single element of consciousness (*cetanā-dhātu*) is also known by the name "person.
Moreover, according to the division of elements, it is known as twenty-fourfold.
The mind, the ten sense organs, their objects, and the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti)—these constitute the body.
The characteristic of the mind is both the absence and the presence of cognition;
for even when there is contact between the self, the senses, and the objects, [cognition] does not occur.
Cognition occurs through the withdrawal of the mind, and it proceeds through its presence;
moreover, minuteness and oneness are remembered as the two qualities of the mind.
That which is to be thought about, deliberated upon, inferred, meditated upon, and even resolved—[all these depend on the mind].

Whatever is to be known by the mind, all that indeed bears the designation of "object" (artha). The function of the mind is the apprehension of the senses; its own restraint consists of reasoning (ūha) and deliberation (vicāra), after which the intellect (buddhi) operates.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, having described the qualities of the mind (*manoguṇa*), he states the objects of the mind (*manoviṣaya*) beginning with "the thinkable" (*cintya*), etc.
(Verse 1). That which is thought by the mind as something to be done or not to be done is the "thinkable" (*cintya*). (Verse 2)
That which is deliberated upon through reasoning and the lack thereof is *vicārya* (3);
that which is inferred through probability, thinking "it must be thus," is *ūhya* (4);
and that which is the object of the knowledge of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) is *dhyeya* (5).
6. That which is to be conceptualized is the object of determination, whether by way of its possession of qualities or its possession of defects.
7. By the phrase "whatever it may be," objects not previously mentioned, such as pleasure and so forth, are included.
8. "Cognizable by the mind" means that which is grasped by the mind independently of the sense organs.

And these objects of the mind (*manas*) consist precisely of sound and the other [sensory qualities]; therefore, by including them as the sixth category of objects, there is no excess over the number twenty-four.

(9) However, pleasure and the other [mental states] are objects of the mind distinct from sound and the rest, and they are to be grasped only through the apprehension of specific modifications of the intellect (*buddhi*).
(10) Having explained the object of the mind, he states its function with the words beginning "the sense organs" (*indriya*), etc. (11)
The restraint of the senses, the control of the sense-bases, and likewise the subduing of one's own mind are all functions of the mind.

For the mind, when it has strayed toward undesirable objects, is restrained by the mind itself; and the mind, being endowed with another quality (guṇa), restrains itself from other objects—so say some. 12.

As it has been said: "The mind, being inclined toward sense objects, cannot be restrained from harmful matters due to the loss of fortitude; for fortitude consists of self-restraint. (13–14) Therefore, by means of fortitude acting as the cause, one restrains oneself; thus, there is no contradiction regarding an action directed toward itself. (15)
He states another function of the mind (*manas*): "namely, *ūha* (inquiry) and *vicāra* (deliberation).
(16) Here, *ūha* is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception, while *vicāra* is conceptualization (*vikalpana*) in terms of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.

(17) For the Sāṃkhyas consider that there are four causes of conceptualization: among them, the external cause is the sense organ (*indriya*), while the internal causes are the triad consisting of the mind (*manas*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the intellect (*buddhi*). (18)

In this context, the sense organs "observe," which means they perceive without conceptual construction; the mind, however, "volitions," which means it conceives of things in terms of what is to be rejected or accepted;
the ego-sense "identifies," which means it thinks, "this is mine," "I am authorized here";
