and the intellect "determines," which means it forms a resolution such as, "I shall abandon this faulty thing" or "I shall accept this virtuous one."
The meaning is that it acts.

(19) Although *ūha* (deliberation) is an external activity such as that of the eyes and other senses, nevertheless, because the mind is the presiding factor even there, it is described as an activity of the mind.
(20) For the intellect (*buddhi*), accompanied by the internal organs, penetrates every object. (21)
Therefore, the instrument is threefold: the doorkeeper is the [intellect], while the rest are the doors.
(22) Subsequently, the intellect functions; this means that following deliberation and reflection, the intellect performs determination.

(23) Furthermore, the function of the ego-sense, which is self-conceit, should be understood as being indicated by the very function of the intellect, even though it is not explicitly mentioned here. (24)

For the intellect (*buddhi*), while forming the determination "I am abandoning this" or "I am taking this up," exists only within the object as conceived by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); thus, the activity of the ego-sense is also grasped through the very activity of the intellect, since the offering of the activities of all the instruments occurs within the intellect.
As it has been said: "These specific qualities of the *guṇas*, distinct from one another, are like lamps."
Having illuminated the entire object of the person, they deliver it to the intellect.
For an object of the senses is perceived by the sense organ together with the mind;
thereafter, it is conceptualized by the mind as possessing qualities or defects. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Śārīrasthāna 5.22)
In that regard, whatever cognition arises toward an object that is determinative in nature,
by means of that one resolves to speak or to act with conscious deliberation.
(Caraka Saṃhitā 5.1.23)
He explains this very fact—that cognition is preceded by *ūha* (inferential deliberation)—in the passage beginning with "by the sense-organ" (*indriyeṇa*).
1. "Is apprehended" (*gṛhyate*) means it is apprehended by mere *ūha* through non-conceptual [perception].
2. "By way of its quality" (*guṇataḥ*) means by way of its being something to be accepted (*upādeyatayā*).
"By way of defect" means by way of being something to be abandoned.
He explains the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect with the words "is born," and so forth.
"In that object" refers to the object constructed by the mind.
"Of the nature of certainty" means having a stable form; that is to say, it consists of ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*).
"It determines" means it performs an undertaking; that is to say, it becomes engaged. In other words, it proceeds to speak or act upon the object as determined by the intellect.
By the phrase "preceded by the intellect," he shows that only such an undertaking as is preceded by the intellect is of this kind, whereas the undertaking of one who is insane and so forth is not.
The sense organs, beginning with that of space (ākāśa), are each increased by one;
these five are to be inferred from their functions, and it is from them that cognition proceeds. (Caraka Saṃhitā 5.1.24)

Having designated the mind, he now designates the sense organs; therein, because of their superiority, he first mentions the organs of cognition (buddhīndriyas) with the words "one by one" and so forth. Among the elements beginning with ether (khādi), the five organs—vision and the rest—are joined with each element in turn as an additional constituent. By the phrase "one by one additional," he indicates that all five are composed of the five elements (pāñcabhautika), while implying that fire (tejas) is predominant in vision, and so on.
"They are inferable from their effects" means they are inferable from their products; the product is the visual cognition and so forth.
By the phrase "from which cognition proceeds," he shows that these [faculties] are five, namely the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*).

Furthermore, although in the Sāṃkhya system the faculties are said to be derived from the *ahaṃkāra*—as it is stated: "The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the modified (*vaikṛta*) [ahaṃkāra]"—[the author here refers to them as such].

"From ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra)"—nevertheless, due to differences of opinion, one should understand that the elemental nature of the senses is either literal or figurative. This elemental nature of the senses is to be understood as figurative; and the basis for this metaphor is as follows: whichever sense grasps that which is most abundant in a particular quality is said to be "abundant in that [quality]. For example, the eye grasps light (tejas), and therefore it is said to be "fiery" (taijasa), and so forth. Thus it should be understood.
The two hands, the two feet, the anus, the generative organ, and likewise the organ of speech—these are the five organs of action. The two feet are for the act of going;
the anus and the generative organ are for the purpose of excretion; and the two hands are for grasping and holding.
The tongue and the organ of speech, as well as speech itself, are truth; light is truth, and darkness is untruth.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 5.26) [Commentary from Āyurvedadīpikā:
The two hands and the two feet constitute one sense organ each, by virtue of performing a single type of action.
The anus and the generative organ likewise constitute one each.
Regarding speech, he states "and speech," etc., to explain its division according to the purposes of acquisition and relinquishment. 4.
It is like light within light, because by being the agent of dharma it illuminates both worlds; its opposite is darkness, which is untruth.
[5] The great elements are space, wind, fire, water, and earth;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities. Caraka Saṃhitā 5.1.27.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

Now, in accordance with the order of enumeration, since the subject matter to be explained is dependent on others—because the qualities of the five elements are grasped through the grasp of their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*)—he first speaks of the elements themselves, which are grasped within the nature of the eight constituent factors (*dhātu*), beginning with the words "the great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*), etc. (1).
Sound and the other [qualities] are to be known as the natural qualities of ether and the other [elements], respectively.
As for the excellence of qualities that must be explained, it arises precisely from the connection with the elements that have entered [into them].
Therefore, because the four elements enter into earth, it possesses five qualities; likewise, in water and the others, one should understand the possession of four qualities and so forth.
Among them, each preceding one possesses a single quality, while there is an increase in qualities for each subsequent one; furthermore,
each preceding quality is said to exist sequentially within the succeeding substances.

Having described the inherent quality, he speaks of the quality produced by the entry of other elements, beginning with the words "teṣām" (of these), etc. 1. "The preceding has one quality": the preceding element, ether (*kha*), has sound as its sole quality. 2. And the masculine gender of ether and the others is due to their being conceived as having the nature of *dhātus* (elements); for it is said: "Ether and the rest, with consciousness as the sixth, are the *dhātus*. 3.
In whatever measure there is remoteness, in that same measure there is an increase of qualities (*guṇavṛddhi*) according to their respective order.

[Objection: Even by this much, the specific nature of having one quality, two qualities, and so forth is not definitively known as to which quality resides in which element. To this he says "the first" (*pūrva*), and so on. Among the elements beginning with space (*khādi*), the first quality exists sequentially according to their respective order; moreover, it is not only the first [quality] itself, but also the quality of that first one—the "first-quality"—which exists in the subsequent element.

Therefore, in space (*kha*), the prior quality of sound (*śabda*) exists; in air (*vāyu*), however, touch (*sparśa*) is the quality obtained by sequence, and thus becomes "prior," while sound is the "prior quality"—thus there is a state of having two qualities (*dviguṇatva*). This should be understood similarly for fire and the other elements.

As for odor (*gandha*), because there is no other subsequent quality, it does not become "prior"; nevertheless, with respect to the phrase "its qualities" (*tadguṇāḥ*) in the text "odor and its qualities," one must either conceive of odor as being "prior" in relation to that word, or interpret "prior" [as referring to the whole] like the expression "the umbrella-bearers are going."

Therefore, it has been stated according to logic that even a previously non-existent odor should be understood as having arrived sequentially in the earth. [8] Solidity, fluidity, mobility, and heat are the observed marks of earth, water, air, and fire respectively; the absence of resistance is the observed mark of space. Caraka-saṃhitā 5.1.29.
All of this is indeed the characteristic of the domain of the tactile sense organ;
for touch, along with its opposites, is to be known by the tactile sense organ. (Caraka Saṃhitā 5.1.30)
He states the uncommon characteristic of the elements, beginning with "hardness" (*khara*) and so forth.

1. Non-obstruction (*apratighāta*) means non-resistance; that is to say, the state of being intangible (*asparśatva*). For that which possesses tangibility obstructs movement, whereas space does not, because it lacks tangibility. 2. "All this" refers to hardness and the other [characteristics]. 3.
"Within the range of the tactile faculty" means that which is to be known by the tactile faculty.
How is all this known by the tactile faculty? To this he says "tactile," and so forth.
"Along with its opposite" means the absence of touch.

Whatever sense faculty apprehends a certain object, it also apprehends its absence; therefore, it is logical that even the intangibility (*asparśatva*) of space is apprehended by the tactile faculty (*sparśanendriya*). (7) Fluidity and mobility, according to the Sāṃkhya system, are properties of the gross element of air because they are apprehended by the tactile faculty; indeed, whatever is apprehended by touch is merely a transformation of the gross element of air. (8)

These subtle elements, beginning with space (ākāśa), should be understood as being in the form of *tanmātras*; however, the gross elements, beginning with space, are mentioned therein as their transformations.

In the category of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the *tanmātras* are said to be of a subtle form. For it is stated: "The *tanmātras* are the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*); from those five [tanmātras] arise the five gross elements."

These are known as the specific qualities (viśeṣas), being calm, terrible, and delusive; therefore, even here, the subtle elements such as ether and the rest, denoted by the term *tanmātra*, are to be understood. [12] (Carakasaṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna)
1 [Chapter on Rasāyana] Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on Rasāyana concerning *abhayā* and *āmalakī*.
Thus said the venerable Ātreya. *Caraka Saṃhitā*, Chapter 6, Section 1.1–2.

Since medical treatment that brings about dharma, artha, and fame must be performed for one whose longevity has been determined by the absence of the characteristics mentioned in the *Pūrvasthāna*, the section (*sthāna*) that expounds upon medical treatment is stated immediately thereafter.
(1) Furthermore, he will explain later on how even the means of *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa* are called "medical treatment" (*cikitsā*). (2)

Even therein, among the treatments for fever and other ailments, rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) and aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*) are mentioned first because they yield great results. Of those two as well, rejuvenation alone is described first because it yields the greatest result by being the cause of a lifespan of a thousand years and so forth. Even within that [treatment], the chapter on *Abhayāmalakīya* is mentioned at the beginning because it sets forth the essential aphorisms regarding the meaning of the Section on Therapeutics (*cikitsā-sthāna*).

Therapeutics (cikitsita) is that which removes disease; it is the wholesome regimen, the means of accomplishment, the medicine, the expiation, the pacification, the restoration to the natural state, and the beneficial treatment. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.3) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

In this regard, first, for the sake of conventional usage, he states the synonyms of the medicine (bheṣaja) denoted by the term "location" (*sthāna*), beginning with "treatment" (*cikitsita*) and so forth. 1. And thus, at the outset, he provides the synonyms for the primary subject matter, just as in the *Nidāna* [chapter] there is a statement of the synonyms for cause (*hetu*), form (*rūpa*), and so on. 2.

Furthermore, this enumeration of synonyms applies primarily to the four-pillared medicine (*catuṣpāda-bheṣaja*), as it is said: "Physicians declare that medicine consists of four pillars and sixteen components. 3.

However, because it takes the form of a constituent part of such medicine, the medicinal quality of medicine—which consists of both stationary and moving substances—should be understood as being established by internal convention.
(4) The designation "medicine" (*bhaiṣajya*) is [also applied to] "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*), because like expiation, medicine removes the disease that is the effect of unrighteousness (*adharma*).
(5) One should know the names of medicines; and that medicine is of two kinds.
For one who is healthy, it provides some invigorating effect; for one who is afflicted, it alleviates disease.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.1.4) [The Āyurvedadīpikā explains this twofold nature with the words beginning "svasthasya" etc.]
"Not everything" means not all [medicines].

For a person who is being treated as healthy, it promotes vigor (*ūrjas*) by removing natural diseases such as old age and the like, and by removing unwholesome bodily states such as excessive exhilaration, emaciation, consumption, and unsuitable seminal flow; thus, it is "vigor-promoting for the healthy" (*svasthasyorjaskaram*). 3.
By the qualification "the dispeller of disease for the afflicted," it means that for one afflicted by fever and so forth, she is the remover of that fever and so forth.

(4) Since the state of being "afflicted" is already obtained through the very expression "dispeller of disease," the fact that he specifies "of the afflicted" shows that she excludes the non-distressing pain caused by natural old age and the like, and instead refers to one tormented by an unnatural disease such as fever. (5)

And non-medicine is of two kinds: that which causes affliction and that which causes subsequent affliction. [In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, following the discussion on medicine, he states the twofold nature of non-medicine with the words "non-medicine" and so forth. 1.

In this context, "affliction" (bādhana) refers to that which causes harm only in the immediate term, such as a small amount of unwholesome food (1); and "accompanied by affliction" (sānubādhana) refers to that which produces chronic disorders such as leprosy and the like (2). That which promotes vigor for one who is healthy is aphrodisiac (vṛṣya), and that is an elixir (rasāyana) (3). *Caraka Saṃhitā*, Chapter 6, Verse 5.
Generally, for most diseases, the second [measure] is considered the means of pacification;
for the word "generally" (prāyas) has a specific meaning, as both [words] serve the purpose of expressing both meanings. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.6) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

Medicine is said to be of two kinds; [the author] analyzes this with the words "of the healthy," and so forth. 1. The division is as follows: "That which is generally an aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) and that which is generally an elixir (*rasāyana*). 2. That which is generally an aphrodisiac, and likewise that which is generally an elixir, [and] that which for the afflicted person is predominantly a remover of disease.

That which promotes well-being and vigor is called *svasthorjaskara*. That which is second, however, removes affliction and disease; it generally consists of *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa* treatments that pacify fevers and other ailments. For example, the clarified butter, jaggery, and other substances mentioned under the treatment for chest-wounds and emaciation (*akṣatakṣīṇa*) serve as both *rasāyana* and aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*).

Likewise, the "King of Formulas" (*yogarāja*) mentioned under the treatment for anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*) is described as a *rasāyana*. Similarly, the *Agastyaharītakī* mentioned in the section on cough (*kāsa*) [is also such].
One should follow the passage beginning with "described as a rasāyana," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is perfectly evident here that those [substances] described as rasāyanas also alleviate fever and other diseases; this is well-established in the rasāyana treatises.

Others, however, maintain that what merely removes disease is not a rasāyana, but rather that which is designated as such because it removes disease only figuratively, due to its possession of the common property of producing longevity through the strengthening of the body's integration.

"Thus, the elixir (rasāyana) is described here. [Objection: Now, if that which promotes vigor for the healthy also removes disease, and that which removes disease also promotes vigor for the healthy, then why is it designated by the term "something specific" (*kiṃcit*) as an indicator of the classification of medicinal actions? We reply: it is because its primary function is the promotion of vigor for the healthy.

Furthermore, the quality of removing disease is established here; however, it is not asserted that everything which removes the diseases of the afflicted possesses the quality of promoting vigor in those who are healthy.

Therefore, when it is said that even substances such as *pāṭhā* and *saptaparṇa*—because they possess the power to be proven as rejuvenatives (*rasāyana*) by virtue of their ability to remove the diseases of the afflicted—are both rejuvenatives and aphrodisiacs (*vājīkarana*), this is merely presented as a partial illustration.
The capacity to act for the benefit of both those who are healthy and those who are afflicted [is established].
(6) He explains the intended meaning of the word "mostly" with the words beginning with "mostly.
(7) "For the sake of a specific purpose" means for the sake of abundance. (8)
Through this elixir (rasāyana), one obtains long life, memory, intelligence, health, youthfulness, majesty, complexion, a resonant voice, nobility, supreme strength of body and senses,
mastery of speech, humility, and luster.
For the elixir (*rasāyana*) is indeed the means for obtaining the tastes and other qualities taught by the Sages.
[The *Āyurvedadīpikā* states:
He describes the effects of the elixir with the verse beginning "long" (*dīrgha*), etc. 1.8.1.
The three qualities beginning with radiance (*prabhā*) should be understood as pertaining to the body (*audarya*).
2. Accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*): the meaning is that whatever is spoken necessarily comes to pass. 3. Reverence (*praṇati*): being honored by the world. 4.

He explains how this is accomplished by means of *rasāyana* with the words beginning "lābha" and so forth; by the mention of "taste" (*rasa*) and the rest, memory (*smṛti*) and other faculties are also included. [Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.9] That which produces a lineage of offspring, which provides immediate exhilaration, and by means of which one becomes like a stallion—possessing extreme strength and proceeding unimpeded toward women.
By whatever means one increases [in vigor], one becomes exceedingly dear to women;
even as one grows old, the semen remains inexhaustible, and by this it is seen to be fruitful,
like a great sacred tree with abundant branches.
He becomes worthy of honor and highly esteemed by his subjects, and he possesses many offspring.
Since it is the root of progeny, by means of which one enjoys infinity both in this world and after death,
that very [practice] is an aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa) that brings fame, prosperity, strength, and nourishment.
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
Regarding the purpose of aphrodisiac therapy (*vājīkaraṇa*), it says "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth.

"Offspring-continuity" (*apatyasaṃtāna*) means the succession of offspring; thus, the meaning is that it produces sons and grandsons. The sense is that a son born from semen produced by aphrodisiac therapy becomes capable of fathering sons himself.
And his extreme dearness here is due to his having accumulated semen and thus being a constant practitioner of sexual intercourse, as it is said:
"Kings desire even a deformed warrior as a servant, just as women desire a husband who is habituated to sexual intercourse, though he be a fool and impudent. (3)
Thus [it is said]. 4.
"It is accumulated" means it attains nourishment. 5. "As if inexhaustible" means inexhaustible. 6.
"Productive" means that which generates an embryo; 7.
a *caitya* is a shrine for a deity; 8. "venerable" means worthy of worship; 9.
"Endlessness" means, as it were, an endlessness, that is to say, a long continuity [of life].
This medicine, which promotes vigor for one who is healthy, is said to be of two kinds;
that which destroys disease will be discussed in the section on therapeutics. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.13)
The entire purpose of medical treatment for disorders consists of these:
medicinal therapy, the procedure for rejuvenation (rasāyana), and the method for aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa).
Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.14 [Āyurvedadīpikā]

"Cikitsita" refers to the treatment of fever and other such diseases. Now, one might object: since *rasāyana* (rejuvenation therapy) and *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy) are also indeed treatments for fever and other diseases, why are they mentioned separately? To this he replies with the words "cikitsitārtha" and so forth. The meaning is: it is true that *rasāyana* and *vājīkaraṇa* are also designated by the term "treatment" (*cikitsita*) because they remove diseases such as fever.

Now, since they cure diseases and because they are subjects to be discussed in the section on therapeutics (cikitsita), he asks where the Rasāyana and Vājīkaraṇa [sections] should be stated, and says "Rasāyana... and so forth.
"Method" (vidhi) means the procedure or the exposition of Rasāyana.
"First" (agre) means immediately following [this].

The aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa) will be described first—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. That which is contrary to medicine should be known as non-medicine; it must not be used. However, I shall now declare that which is medicine and should be used. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.15)
[From the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:

He explains "non-medicine" (*abheṣaja*), which was previously mentioned, with the words beginning "non-medicine" (*abheṣajam*) etc. [1] It is the opposite [of medicine], characterized by producing disease and performing harmful functions. [2]
The sages know that there are two types of application for rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana):
namely, the indoor method (kuṭīprāveśika) and the outdoor method involving wind and sun (vātātapika).
First, the procedure for the indoor method will be taught.
In a city that is secure, auspicious, well-supplied with necessities, and inhabited by kings, physicians, the twice-born, virtuous people, and those of meritorious deeds,
one should have a small hut constructed on a good plot of ground in the northeast direction.
It should be endowed with ample width and height, consisting of three chambers, with fine latticed windows,
thick walls, pleasant in all seasons, very well-constructed, and pleasing to the mind;
it should be inaccessible to undesirable sounds and the like, and devoid of women.
Provided with desirable implements, and accompanied by ready physicians, medicines, and Brahmins; then,
during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious lunar day and asterism,
at a favorable moment and under a propitious conjunction, having performed the ritual shaving of the head.
Having established the power of fortitude and mindfulness, being full of faith and composed in mind,
having shaken off the defects of the mind and contemplating loving-kindness toward all beings,
he should first worship the deities and circumambulate the twice-born.
Having paid homage to the gods, cows, and brahmins, he should then enter that hut.
Having been purified by cleansing therapies within it, being healthy and having regained his strength, he should employ the elixir (rasāyana); I shall now describe those cleansing procedures.
That which is performed by entering a small chamber (kuṭīpraveśa) is called *kuṭīprāveśika* (1).
That which is performed even by resorting to wind and sun (*vātātapa*) is called *vātātapika* (2).

"Trigarbhā" means that first there is one house, and inside of that is a second; thus, it is called "trigarbhā" because it has three inner chambers (garbhas) or internal spaces within it—meaning it has three interior courtyards at its center.
"Sūkṣmalocanām" means having small latticed windows.
"Śukle" refers to the bright fortnight (the waxing moon). "Sajjā" means that in which physicians and other [necessary persons] are present. Thus it is.
"Adored on an auspicious lunar day and asterism" means being honored through the conjunction of an auspicious *tithi* and *nakṣatra*.
"Having performed the shaving" means having had one's hair cut.
"Mental faults" refers to desire, anger, and so forth.
"By means of purificatory therapies" refers to emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and head-purgatives.
"Happy" means free from disease.

"Having regained strength" means that, because the impurities have been removed by the purificatory therapies, strength has been restored again through the sequential process of dietary rehabilitation (*saṃsarjana*) and so forth.

Although all types of purification therapies (*saṃśodhana*) are intended here by the use of the plural form "by purifications," nevertheless, because they are specifically appropriate for this *rasāyana*, only the administration of *harītakī* and so forth is mentioned. Others, however, say that the supreme purification must be performed solely through the administration of *harītakī* and its like; the plural "purifications" is used, moreover, to include [all methods] until complete purification is achieved.
[13] He demonstrates the method of preparing the formulation of *harītakī* and other ingredients:

Powders of *harītakī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *āmalaka*, jaggery (*guḍa*), *vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, turmeric (*rajanī*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*viśvabheṣaja*). (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.25)
A person who has undergone oleation and sudation should drink [the medicine] with warm water.
For one whose body has been purified by that and who has performed the gradual reintroduction of food (*saṃsarjana*),
one should administer barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) mixed with clarified butter for three nights or even for five days.
Or for seven days, until the stool becomes pure and bright; then,
knowing his digestive tract to be purified, one who understands age, constitution, and suitability should administer a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that is appropriate for him.
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"Yāvaka" means barley-food.
The three options beginning with "three nights" pertain to inferior, middling, and superior purification respectively.]
One should know that the five-tasted *harītakī* is hot, non-saline, auspicious,
a downward mover of the *doṣas*, light, an appetizer, and a digestive;
it promotes longevity, nourishment, and fortune, and is supreme for stabilizing youth.
It pacifies all diseases and bestows strength upon the intellect and the senses;

it cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal tumors (gulma), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), consumption (śoṣa), anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), intoxication (mada), hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi), disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇīdoṣa), chronic conditions, and irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
Heart disease along with diseases of the head, diarrhea, loss of appetite, cough, urinary disorders, abdominal distension, splenic enlargement, and acute abdominal dropsy;
excessive salivation due to phlegm, hoarseness of voice, discoloration of the skin, jaundice, and worms.
Harītakī quickly overcomes swelling, asthma, vomiting, impotence, exhaustion of the limbs,
various obstructions of the channels, coatings on the heart and chest,
and the confusion of memory and intellect. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.33–34)
Those suffering from indigestion, those who eat dry food, those emaciated by women, wine, or poison,
and those afflicted by hunger, thirst, or heat— these should not consume āmalakī.
One should know that those same qualities and actions apply to āmalakī as well.
Those properties which were stated for *harītakī* are reversed in its potency (*vīrya*). Therefore, one should know that through such actions, the fruits of *harītakī* and *āmalaka* are like nectar.
Thus, the physician should praise the fruits of both *harītakī* and *āmalaka*.

Although there are other substances prescribed for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) that grant a lifespan of a thousand years, nevertheless, it is specifically *harītakī* and *āmalaka* that are mentioned at the beginning of this chapter by way of their qualities and actions;
for they alone possess the dual characteristics of being both disease-removers and life-prolongers. Furthermore, in that regard:

Although the *āmalaka* fruit has been described as the foremost among those that maintain youthfulness, nevertheless, because the *harītakī* is superior in its capacity to remove diseases, it has been mentioned first.

(1) Regarding the *harītakī* and other such substances, the production of the five tastes and so forth is caused by the specific power of the particular arrangement of the elements (*bhūta-saṃniveśa-viśeṣa*) through the influence of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); therefore, logical arguments (*upapatti*) do not apply here. (2)
"Śivā" means she who brings about auspiciousness, because she is endowed with praiseworthy qualities.
"The alleviator of all diseases" refers to [her power] through combination, processing, and so forth.

Although her quality of removing all diseases has already been stated, the specific mention of her being a destroyer of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and other ailments is for the purpose of demonstrating her particular efficacy in destroying leprosy and similar conditions.

Even though it is a promoter [of natural urges], its capacity to cure diarrhea and grahaṇī disease should be understood as being due to its power to promote the discharge of obstructed morbid humors (doṣas), as it has been said: "One who passes stools that are scanty, or obstructed, or accompanied by pain, should be purged with lukewarm pastes of abhayā and pippalī. (6–7) Furthermore, although its quality of bestowing intellect and memory was already stated, the subsequent mention of its removal of confusion of memory and intellect is intended to demonstrate its specific potency in that regard. (8)
By the phrase "the opposite of *vīrya*," the cold *vīrya* of the *āmalaka* fruit is stated.
[9] "Grains" refers to fruits that are devoid of hard seeds.
[10] The Himalayas, the best of mountains, is the supreme ground for medicinal herbs.
Therefore, one should cause the fruits produced from that [tree] to be gathered when they are seasonally ripe,
possessing fully developed juice and potency, at the proper times according to the prescribed rule,
and nourished by the sun, wind, shade, and water.
I shall now describe the application and the supreme medicinal action of those fruits which are un-eaten, non-putrid, free from blemishes, and devoid of disease. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.40)

Although it has been stated that the Himavat is the source of medicinal plants, nevertheless, in order to demonstrate that for the purpose of rejuvenation (rasāyana) only those medicines originating from the Himavat should be taken, he uses the expression "of medicinal plants" (auṣadhīnām).
"At the proper times" means at the time when the fruit is ripe.
"According to the prescribed method" means that the administration of the elixir must necessarily be performed preceded by the taking of medicine, the worship of auspicious deities, and so forth.
By the term "remedies," he demonstrates that the fruit is free from defects such as wind or fire.
Take ten *pala* measures each of the five groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*),
one thousand *harītakī* fruits, three thousand fresh *āmalaka* fruits,
*vidārigandhā*, *bṛhatī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, and *nidigdhikā*.
One should know the group beginning with Vidārigandha with Śvadaṃṣṭrā as the fifth;
likewise, Bilva, Agnimantha, Śyonāka, Kāśmarya, Pāṭalā, Punarnavā, the two Śūrpaparṇīs, Balā, and Eraṇḍa.

One should prepare these five roots: *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *medā*, *jīvantī*, and *śatāvarī*, as well as the roots of *śara*, *ikṣu*, *darbha*, *kāśa*, and *śāli*. Thus, one should procure these five groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*).
All those aforementioned parts should be processed in ten times the amount of water;
when reduced to one-tenth,
that strained decoction should be taken along with all those *harītakī* fruits and all the *āmalaka* fruits.
Having crushed all those boneless fruits and strained them with brushes into that decoction,
one should cause these powders to be added:
of *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *pippalī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, and *plava*.
Having taken four-pala portions each of mustā, viḍaṅga, candana, aguru, madhuka, haridrā, vacā, and kanaka, as well as of sūkṣmailā and tvac; Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.48–49.
One should add one thousand powdered sugar cubes, weighing more than a *tulā*,
along with one *āḍhaka* of oil and three *āḍhakas* of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
All of this should be cooked over a gentle fire in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood.
Having ascertained that it is licked, not burnt, and cooled, one should mix it with honey.
The quantity of honey should be half that of the fat; all of this should remain in a vessel of ghee until it has fully blended, and one should administer its dose at the appropriate time.
That which does not obstruct digestion, taking food in a single measure according to one's age;
in this regard, sixty-day rice with milk is desired as the meal once [the previous meal] has been digested.
The Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and others whose wealth is their austerity [follow this practice].
Having consumed this elixir, they became possessed of immeasurable lifespan;
casting off their worn-out bodies, they attained a preeminent and youthful state.
Free from drowsiness, fatigue, and labored breathing, they were devoid of disease and composed in mind.

Endowed with intelligence, memory, and strength, those whose wealth is penance practiced for a long time the Brahma-penance and celibacy with ultimate devotion. One who desires longevity should employ this Brahma elixir.
One attains long life, pre-eminent youth, and enjoys desired objects.

Regarding the statement "of the five" and so forth, Jātūkarṇa has stated that ten *palas* of each substance are to be taken; thus, there are five groups of the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and for each of these substances, ten *palas* are prescribed.
"One thousand *harītakī*s" means one thousand *harītakī* fruits. 2. "The two *śūrpaparṇī*s" refers to *mudgaparṇī* and *māṣaparṇī*. 3. "*Vīrā*" is the *jālaṃdhara* potherb. 4.
*Kūrcana* is the means of causing decay, such as a stone-son (*śilāputraka*), a pestle (*musala*), and so forth. *Vinīya* means having cast in.
*Plava* is the *kaivartamustaka* plant. 7.
Kanaka is nāgakeśara (Mesua ferrea). 8. Tvak is guḍatvak (cinnamon). 9. "Audumbara" means made of copper. 10.
"Half a measure of fat" means half a measure each of ghee and oil. [11] One meal, not taken in the afternoon.

[12] One should grind a thousand *āmalaka* fruits possessing the aforementioned qualities according to the method of grinding and steaming, well-steamed by the heat of milk, dried in the shade, and de-seeded; then one should powder them.

Then, one thousand fresh *āmalaka* fruits, having been thoroughly saturated with their own juice, should be combined with a powder consisting of one-eighth part each of *sthirā*, *punarnavā*, *jīvantī*, *nāgabalā*, *brahmasuvarcalā*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *śatāvarī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *pippalī*, *vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, *svayaṅguptā*, *amṛtā*, *candana*, *aguru*, *madhuka*, *madhūkapuṣpa*, *utpala*, *padma*, *mālatī*, *yuvatī*, and *yūthikā*.
This mixture should again be thoroughly saturated with the juice of one thousand palas of *nāgabalā*, dried in the shade, and then combined with double the amount of clarified butter and honey.

Or, having fashioned it into the shape of a small ball of jaggery, one should place it inside a clean, sturdy jar smeared with ghee, beneath a heap of ashes underground. After performing the protective rites, one who is learned in the *Atharvaveda* should leave it there for a fortnight. At the end of the fortnight, having extracted it, one should consume it every morning according to the prescribed method—increasing the dose by half a *karṣa* at a time and combined with the eight parts of the powder of gold, silver, copper, coral, and iron—while carefully observing the strength of one's digestive fire (*agni*).
When that [milk] has been digested, by consuming sixty-day rice with milk and clarified butter, one obtains the aforementioned benefits.
This is the Brāhma elixir, practiced by hosts of great seers;
by employing it, one becomes free from disease, long-lived, and possessed of great strength.
Beloved by his subjects, Siddhārtha possesses a splendor equal to the moon and the sun;
he retains what he has heard, and the noble nature of the ṛṣis arises within him. He is as firm as the essence of the earth, and his prowess is equal to that of the wind.
He becomes free from poison, and the poison is neutralized within his body.
[Commentary on Āyurvedadīpikā:

Regarding the method of steaming flour (*piṣṭasvedanavidhi*), the meaning is that it should be steamed just as flour is steamed when placed upon grass or similar materials set over a vessel filled with water.
"Swarasaparipītam" means saturated with its own juice (*svarasabhāvita*).
The medicinal herbs such as *brahmasuvarcalā* and others will be described in the section on the origin of Āyurveda.
"Yuvati" refers to the *navamālikā* flower.
"An eighth part" means one-eighth.
"In the form of small lumps of jaggery" means in the form of molasses.
"By an increase of half a karṣa" means one should increase starting from half a karṣa.
"By the method as stated" means by the method of entering the hut (*kuṭīprāveśika*).
"The qualities as stated" refers to those recited in the scriptural passages concerning the fruits of the preliminary practice (*pūrvaprayoga*).

"Having the essence of the mountain-supporter" (*dharaṇīdharasāra*): just as in the case of "camel-faced" (*uṣṭramukha*), [the compound is analyzed as] "the mountains are the supporters of the earth (*dharaṇīdharāḥ*)," and their "essence" (*sāra*) is iron; thus, the meaning is that he has an essence like that.
"Non-poisonous" means that which is poison without causing transformation.
[11] Bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, pāṭali, balā, the four *parṇīs*, pippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and the two types of *bṛhatī*. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.1.62)
Śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, drākṣā, jīvantī, puṣkara, aguru, abhayā, amṛtā, ṛddhi, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka,
śaṭī, musta, punarnavā, medā, elā, candana, and utpala.
One pala each of vidārī, vṛṣamūla, kākolī, and kākanāsikā, along with five hundred āmalaka fruits, should be placed together and boiled in one droṇa of water. Caraka Saṃhitā 6.1.64–65.
Having ascertained that these medicinal herbs have lost their potency,
the physician should then remove the pulp from that *āmalaka* fruit and fry it in twelve *palas* each of oil and clarified butter; having done so, he should add half a *tulā* [of sugar].
One should properly prepare purified sugar-candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*) like a linctus (*leha*). Once it is prepared and cooled, one should add six *palas* of honey,
four *palas* of *tugākṣīrī*, and likewise two *palas* of long pepper (*pippalī*).
One should add one *pala* each of cinnamon bark (*tvac*), cardamom (*elā*), cinnamon leaves (*pattra*), and saffron (*kesara*).
This is called *cyavanaprāśa*, which is declared to be a supreme rejuvenative (*rasāyana*);
it specifically prescribes the cure for cough and dyspnea.

It promotes the growth of the limbs of those who are emaciated, wounded, aged, or young; it alleviates loss of voice, diseases of the chest, heart disease, vāta-śoṇita (blood disorders caused by wind),
thirst, and the defects located in the seminal receptacle.
One should administer its dose in such a quantity that it does not obstruct one's meal.
By its use, the very aged Cyavana became young again.
It bestows intelligence, memory, luster, freedom from disease, longevity, strength, and vigor of the senses.

By the use of this elixir (*rasāyana*), even an old man who has entered the inner chamber (*kuṭīpraveśa*) shall obtain supreme delight with women, an increase in digestive fire, clarity of complexion, and the downward movement of the vital wind (*pavana*).
Casting off all the forms produced by old age, he bears the appearance of fresh youth.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, "the four parṇīs" refers to śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, mudgaparṇī, and māṣaparṇī.
*Tāmalakī* is the same as *bhūmyāmalakī*. 2.

*Kākanāsā* is *nāsāphalā*; others call it *kākatuṇḍaka*. 3. Here, the loss of flavor in substances occurs when they are kept in water that occupies one-fourth [of the vessel]. 4. *Niṣkula* means "without seeds" (i.e., seedless). 5.
Because of the compound designation "of oil and ghee," twelve palas are for both together, not separately.

(6) Matsyaṇḍikā is a concretion of sugar-candy. (7) Here, although honey and ghee are equal in measure at six palas each, there is no contradiction because they are combined with other substances. (8)

Then, one thousand palas of *āmalaka*, *harītakī*— either *āmalaka* and *vibhītaka*, or *harītakī* and *vibhītaka*, or *āmalaka*, *harītakī*, and *vibhītaka*— wrapped in *palāśa* bark, smeared with clay, and steamed in a kiln (*kukūla*), should be pounded in a mortar until they are free of husks;
this should be consumed by one who abstains from other food, combined with curd, ghee, honey, meat-paste, oil, and sugar, according to the prescribed method.
At the conclusion of that procedure, one should restore the patient with gruels and similar foods; anointing and massage should be performed with clarified butter and barley flour.

This is the excellence of the application of this rejuvenative therapy (*rasāyana*); having carefully considered the strength of the digestive fire, one should eat twice as much as usual, followed by a meal of *ṣaṣṭika* rice with clarified butter and either vegetable broth or milk.
Beyond this, one may live according to one's pleasure and eat whatever one desires.

By this practice, the sages regained their youthfulness and became long-lived for many hundreds of years, free from decay, endowed with the strength of other bodies, intellects, and sense organs, and they pursued austerity with extreme dedication.
*Kukūlaka* is a fire of dried cow-dung.
"Of the *akulakas*" means those that are boneless.

The measurement for the substances and so forth is not stated here; therefore, it may mean that the primary powder is equal in measure to the curd and other ingredients combined, or else that each of the curd and other ingredients is individually equal in measure to the powder.

The choice between using broth or milk is made according to the strength of the digestive fire.

Having prepared a jar of ghee by cooking it with a decoction of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *vibhītaka*, and the five groups of five roots (*pañcapañcamūla*), combined with a paste (*kalka*) of *pippalī*, *madhuka*, *madhūka*, *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *ātmaguptā*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *kṣīra*, and *śuklā*, along with the fresh juice of *vidārī* and eight times the amount of milk— one who uses this [attains the desired results].

One should consume a dose equal to one's digestive fire, and once it has been digested, eat *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk and ghee, followed by warm water as a post-drink. Thus, freed from the fear of old age, disease, sin, and malevolent spells, and having attained incomparable strength of body, senses, and intellect, one may achieve the supreme lifespan with all undertakings unimpeded.

Having consumed a palmful of this [mixture] combined with one-fourth part of iron powder every morning according to the prescribed method, one should eat at evening rice or *ṣaṣṭika* grain mixed with ghee along with mung-bean soup or milk. By using this for three years, one's age remains free from decay for a hundred years; learning is retained, all diseases are pacified, and even potent poison is neutralized.

The limb becomes as firm as stone; he becomes unassailable by all beings. Just as there is nectar for the immortals and ambrosia for the enjoyers of pleasure, so was the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana) in ancient times for the great seers.

In ancient times, those devoted to *rasāyana* did not undergo old age, nor weakness, nor disease, nor death for thousands of years. One who practices *rasāyana* according to the prescribed rules enjoys not only a long life in this world, but [attains other benefits as well].
He attains that auspicious state frequented by divine sages, as well as the imperishable Brahman; thus it is said.

In this chapter on Abhayāmalakī, six formulations have been proclaimed—perfected elixirs by means of which one may prolong life. Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on rejuvenation (rasāyana) concerning those who desire vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus said the venerable Ātreya.

In the previous chapter, the *āmalaka* rejuvenation therapies (*rasāyana*) were taught; since there are also *āmalaka* rejuvenation therapies here, this "Chapter on Those Desiring Vitality" (*prāṇakāmīya*) is stated immediately thereafter.
It is called *prāṇakāmīya* because it was composed with reference to the term "those desiring vitality.
O you who desire vitality, listen to this which is being spoken—like another nectar, beneficial to the sons of Aditi, and possessing inconceivable and wonderful power.

This is the procedure for the elixir (*rasāyana*): it promotes longevity, brings about health, stabilizes youth, removes sleepiness, drowsiness, fatigue, exhaustion, laziness, and weakness; it balances the wind (*vāta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and bile (*pitta*), provides stability, removes loose flesh, kindles the internal digestive fire, and produces excellence in luster, complexion, and voice.
By means of this, the great sages such as Cyavana and others attained renewed youth and became most desired by women, possessing firm, even, and well-proportioned flesh.
They possess well-knit and firm bodies, with very clear strength, complexion, and sensory faculties; their prowess is unimpeded everywhere, and they are capable of enduring hardships.
All bodily defects arise from village food—that is, for those who eat sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, *śukra*, potherbs, meat, sesame paste, and flour-based foods;

for those who eat sprouted grains, new awned cereals, *śamī* beans, incompatible foods, unwholesome foods, dry, alkaline, and obstructive foods; and for those who eat damp, heavy, putrid, and stale food.
For those who habitually consume irregular or excessive food, who constantly sleep by day, indulge in women, or drink liquor; whose bodies are agitated by irregular and excessive physical exercise;

and who are full of fear, anger, grief, greed, delusion, and exhaustion—for these reasons, their muscles become flaccid, their joints loosen, the blood becomes inflamed, and the fat is excessively liquefied; furthermore, the marrow is no longer replenished within the bones.

Semen does not flow and vital energy (ojas) goes to waste; being in such a state, he becomes exhausted and dejected, possessed by sleep, drowsiness, and laziness, lacking enthusiasm, and breathes heavily. He is incapable of physical or mental activities, his memory, intellect, and luster are destroyed, he becomes a vessel for diseases, and he does not attain a full lifespan.

"Therefore, observing all these aforementioned defects that are detrimental to health, one should discard those foods and activities and proceed to employ rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana)," having said this, the Blessed Lord Punarvasu Ātreya spoke again.

for the man who consumes this yoga, there arises great strength, supreme purity of complexion, and a voice that resembles the thundering of a mass of clouds, as well as abundant and stable progeny. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.2.5–6)

One should place [the preparation] in a vessel of clarified butter and keep it buried underground for six months.

Thereafter, one should consume a dose equal to the strength of one's digestive fire (agni-bala) in the forenoon; this is the application, not in the afternoon, and the rules for diet should be observed according to what is suitable to the individual.
From the use of this, the age remains free from decay for a hundred years; the rest is the same as previously stated.

One should place it in a jar for twenty-one nights; beyond that is its application. By this application, one remains free from decay for a lifespan of a hundred years; the rest is the same as before. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.2.10) [Āyurvedadīpikā]

These [doses] should be administered by increasing or decreasing one *bhallātaka* at a time, starting from ten up to thirty; there is no increase beyond this.
According to the prescribed method of administration, the maximum dose for the *bhallātaka* regimen is indeed one thousand.

When the medicine has been digested, the regimen consists of eating *śāli* or *ṣaṣṭika* rice with ghee and milk. At the conclusion of the administration, the regimen of milk alone should be followed for twice that duration.
By its application, one remains free from decay for a hundred years; this is the same as what was stated previously.

Regarding the "application of *bhallātaka* up to one thousand": when the total number of *bhallātaka* fruits consumed reaches one thousand by way of cumulative addition, at that very moment the practice must be discontinued. Furthermore, the abandonment of the application may indeed occur even before reaching the count of one thousand, depending on factors such as one's physical constitution (*prakṛti*). Moreover, the completion of the count of one thousand does not occur here through a single progressive sequence of increase and decrease; rather, it is achieved through repetition.

The application should be carried out up to a limit of thirty; just as the completion of the count of one thousand occurs through the practice of the application of *bhallātaka*, having done so, the cessation [of the treatment] should be performed.

The juice of those fruits which enters the jar should be mixed with one-eighth part honey and double the amount of clarified butter.

By consuming that [preparation], one remains free from decay for a hundred years; the rest is the same as previously stated. pitta and vāyu become aggravated and dry up the somatic constituents (*saumyadhātu*) and the channels carrying the nutrient fluid (*rasavāhinī-nāḍī*), as well as the roots of the tongue, the throat, the palate, and the *kloman*.
These two very powerful [doshas], having dried up the bodies of men, produce thirst;
for even as water is drunk again and again, it is consumed by them and does not reach a state of peace.
For those emaciated by terrible diseases, that [thirst] arises as a secondary complication (upasarga).

From the statement beginning with "due to agitation" (*kṣobhāt*) and so forth, the causality of *vāta* and the causality of both *vāta* and *pitta* should be inferred according to their respective appropriateness.
1. The section beginning with "bile and wind" (*pittānilau*) is the passage on the pathogenesis (*samprāpti*) of all types of thirst. 2.
"Saumyān dhātūn" (the mild elements) refers to phlegm, tastes, and water, which possess qualities exceeding those of Soma.
"Pradūṣayataḥ" (they vitiate) means they vitiate through desiccation.
"Klomnaḥ" is the accusative plural form.
By the word "in the body" (dehe), he shows that these thirsts constitute the body itself.

For that mental thirst which was previously described as being of the nature of desire and aversion within the body and proceeding from pleasure and pain, this [present thirst], however, being caused by the defects residing in the body, is born of the body alone—this is the sense.
Even in the case of natural thirst, wind and bile are indeed its initiators; so why is that [natural thirst] not included here?

"Do not say so; for since that [type of thirst] is pacified simply by drinking the appropriate liquid intended for it, it has no place here in this discussion of natural (asvābhāvika) diseases"—keeping this in mind, [the author] states "drunk, drunk," etc., to explain the distinction between the wind and bile that initiate the natural thirst and those wind and bile that initiate the thirst to be described below. The wind and bile that initiate the present thirst dry up the water as soon as it is drunk; therefore, because of this drying up of the water, the person does not find relief, whereas in the case of natural thirst, one attains peace by drinking water.
The state [of being]. 11.
He speaks of the production of thirst in the form of affliction with the words beginning "ghora" (terrible), etc. 12. "Becoming calamities" means having the form of afflictions. 13.
The premonitory symptom is dryness of the mouth; its specific characteristic is a constant desire for water.
Lightness and the disappearance of all these signs indicate the subsiding of thirst.
He states the precursor (*prāgrūpa*) of craving with the words "the precursor," and so forth.

(1) In the very course of explaining the precursors, he states the non-deviating characteristic (*avyabhicārilakṣaṇa*) of cravings among them with the words "its own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
(2) "Its own characteristic" means the non-deviating characteristic; for example, fever has heat as its [own] characteristic, and swelling has protuberance as its [own] characteristic. (3)
He states the natural premonitory symptoms (prāgrūpa) once again: "The lightness of the signs is their departure.

This means that the lightness—the smallness or even the absence of some—of the signs of thirst arising from vāta and other [doṣas] which will be described hereafter, constitutes the premonitory symptoms of thirsts.
Consequently, during the stage of premonitory symptoms, some of the characteristics to be described do not occur at all, and those that do occur are indistinct due to their paucity.

And it has been said: "The unmanifest characteristic of that [thirst] is known as its premonitory symptom (*pūrvarūpa*). Or rather, this premonitory symptom—namely, dryness of the mouth and the constant desire for water—is both the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the premonitory symptom of thirsts; therefore, dryness of the mouth and the desire for water constitute both the specific characteristic and the premonitory symptom.
In the stage of premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpāvasthā*), however, the dryness of the mouth and the desire for water should be understood as being mild.

(8) As for those who read the premonitory symptoms as "dryness of the mouth, loss of voice, and constant desire for water," in their view, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of thirst would not have been stated.
(9) And it has also been stated by Hārīta regarding the specific characteristic of thirst: "The specific characteristic of thirsts is indeed a constant state of thirsting for water. (10)

Or rather, the premonitory symptom (*pūrvarūpa*) consists solely of dryness of the mouth and loss of voice, while the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the constant desire for water. Furthermore, the "diminution of signs" (*liṅgānāṃ ca lāghavam*) means the departure or cessation of the form of the disease, namely thirst. This very cessation of thirst is the slight manifestation of the symptoms that will be described hereafter; for there can be no total eradication of these characteristics as long as one is seized by innate thirst (*sahajatṛṣṇā*).
Because they persist for only a short duration.

However, some maintain that the lightness of the signs (*liṅga*), their rapid onset, and their subsequent disappearance constitute death; thus, they claim this is the definition of the incurability of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*). That [view] is not very convincing.
[The symptoms are: dryness of the mouth, hoarseness of voice, vertigo, burning heat, delirium, and rigidity.
Roughness of the palate, lips, throat, and tongue, as well as loss of consciousness;
protrusion of the tongue, loss of appetite, deafness, pain in the vital organs (marmans), and exhaustion—thirst produces these fivefold symptoms; hear them now.
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, [the author] states the complications (*upadrava*) of all thirsts, beginning with "dryness of the mouth" (*mukhaśoṣa*), etc. (1).
"Manifested" (*udbhūta*) means increased (*vṛddha*). (2)

However, in the opinion of those who state that dryness of the mouth and other such symptoms [constitute thirst], there would be no mention of thirst as a complication (*upadrava*); yet complications are included in the summary of this chapter.
Therefore, the established rule is that dryness of the mouth and so forth, when excessively increased, are complications, whereas their simple increase constitutes the primary symptom (*liṅga*).
When the wind (*vāyu*), becoming aggravated, dries up the water element (*ap-dhātu*) residing in the body, [thirst arises].

When that [watery element] is dried up, the weak person becomes parched; then, as he continues to dry up, he suffers from thirst. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.22.11) [Commentary: With the verse beginning "The watery element" (*abdhātum*), the author explains the onset (*samprāpti*) and other characteristics of the five [doshas].]
"Situated in the body" means existing within the body in the form of various tastes and so forth.
[Verse 2] "It dries up in the dry watery element"—this is how it should be construed.

[Verse 3] The loss of sleep, dizziness of the head, a dry and tasteless mouth, and obstruction of the channels—these are the symptoms of thirst caused by *vāta*. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.22.12)
[In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*:
"Obstruction of the channels" means excessive injury.
Pitta is considered to be of fiery nature; if it becomes aggravated, it heats the water-element (ap-dhātu).
For when it is aggravated, it produces in men a thirst characterized by intense burning.
A bitter taste in the mouth, a burning sensation in the head, a craving for cold things,
fainting, and yellowish eyes, urine, and feces— this is the clinical presentation of thirst caused by pitta.
With the verse beginning with "pittam" (bile), [the author] describes the bile-born [fever]. 1.

Regarding the enumeration of the bodily constituents, it is stated that bile in the body is of the watery element (*āpya*), consisting of fluid, clear, unctuous, slow, soft, and slimy; it includes chyle, blood, fat, phlegm, bile, sweat, and so forth.

Although it has been stated that *pitta* is dual-natured by the statements "the watery element (*āpya*), taste (*rasa*), and the sense of taste (*rasana*)" as well as "whatever is of *pitta* and whatever luster (*bhās*) exists in the body— all that is fiery (*āgneya*"), nevertheless, because its fiery form predominates, he says "pitta is considered fiery" to show that *pitta* is indeed fiery. This is despite its dual nature.

Moreover, because bile (pitta) is characterized primarily by its fiery (āgneya) component, even among other distinct modifications of the lunar (saumya), fiery, and windy (vāyavya) types, disorders of the bile are indeed categorized as being of a fiery nature. 2. "For that [water-element] when heated... refers to the water-element (abdhātu) being heated. 3.
In the reading "saṃtaptaṃ hi" (for it is heated), it should be understood that it produces bile itself.
4) When the water element produces [thirst], it does so only when heated by bile; thus, bile alone is the agent.
5) Thirst arising from the stomach is also of the nature of fire, because it is produced by the bile of the stomach-fire.
Its symptoms are a beautiful complexion, flatulence, and excessive salivation of phlegm.
(Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.22.15) [The Āyurvedadīpikā states:
By the verse beginning with "thirst" (tṛṣṇā), he describes the non-nativ thirst.]

And here, by the word *āma* used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*), phlegm (*kapha*)—which shares the same treatment and characteristics as *āma*—is also included. Thus, by the exposition of [the fever] originating from *āma*, that which arises from phlegm mentioned by Suśruta is also indeed included here. Furthermore, by the phrase "it is also fiery" (*sāpy āgneyī*), he reaffirms what was previously understood: that all [types of fever] are produced by wind and bile (*vātapitta*).
Although vāta is mentioned as a cause of thirst, it is understood from its omission here that pitta alone is the primary [cause], while vāta is secondary.
It is also stated elsewhere: "Vision, digestion, heat, hunger, thirst, softness of the body, radiance, clarity, and intelligence—these are the functions of pitta arising from its normal state. (5–6)

"Because it is produced by *āma* and *pitta*" means because it is produced by *pitta* increased due to the obstruction of *āma*. The body is born from *rasa*, and *rasa* is born from water; therefore, upon its depletion, one indeed suffers from thirst, with a feeble voice, fainting, and with the heart, throat, and palate completely parched. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.22.16)
In the passage beginning with "The body is born of rasa," [the author] describes that which arises from depletion (kṣayajā). 1.

From the essence of food (āhārarasa), the essence of the bodily constituents (dhāturasa) is produced, which nourishes all the constituents; and that rasa, being born of water, is aqueous—meaning it is of the nature of water (āpya). 2.

"From its depletion" means from the depletion of the *rasa*; one becomes thirsty due to the depletion of the *rasa*, and from that depletion of the *rasa* there occurs a depletion of water (*ambu*). It is logical that by that depletion of water, a person becomes possessed of thirst in the form of a longing for drink;
thus he demonstrates. For it is said in the *Suśruta*: "A human being whose *doṣas*, *dhātus*, and wastes are depleted, and whose strength is also depleted... (4).
It has been stated here as well: "One desires that food and drink which increases one's own bodily constituents," and also, "Indeed, from its depletion, one becomes thirsty.

Furthermore, there is indeed a thirst arising from a secondary affliction (upasarga) which is emaciating and painful for those whose bodies are afflicted by fever, urinary disorders, wasting, consumption, dyspnea, and so forth. (Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 6.22.17)
In the *Āyurvedadīpikā*, the phrase beginning with "bhavati" explains that which arises from secondary afflictions (*upasarga*).
1. "From a secondary affliction" (*upasargāt*) means from complications such as fever; that is to say, in the form of complications such as fever. 2.
"Difficult" means difficult to treat.

Thus, the five types of thirst—consisting of wind, bile, undigested matter (*āma*), depletion of water, and complications (*upasarga*)—have been explained as previously outlined in the aphorisms. Herein, the type arising from phlegm (*kaphaja*) mentioned by Suśruta is subsumed under that arising from *āma*, the type arising from injury (*kṣataja*) is subsumed under that consisting of complications, and the type arising from food (*annaja*) is to be included within that arising from *āma* itself.

In all cases, however, thirst associated with those emaciated by disease and those suffering from persistent vomiting, when accompanied by severe complications, should be known as leading to death. (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.22.18)
Now he states the characteristic of the incurability of craving, beginning with "all, however," and so forth.
"Endowed with terrible afflictions" means possessed of distressing calamities that cause suffering. [1]
